#1375. Guimaraes looks a £75m bargain as ‘super sub’ makes difference

Arsenal have played six Premier League games this season and Bruno Guimarães has been a match-winning force in two of them. At this rate, he might justify his enormous £75m transfer fee by Christmas.

The Brazilian was not signed to be Arsenal’s super sub but that is the role he appears to be playing in these early days in north London. Against Leeds United here, as it was against Sunderland last month, he came off the bench when the champions were struggling. And as it was at Sunderland, he produced a thumping finish to put Arsenal on their way to three points.

Liquid football from Arsenal 😮‍💨 Bruno Guimarães finishes off a well-worked team move! 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/fbLJiaZbX5

This is the value of signing a 28-year-old with significant Premier League experience. As Arsenal laboured against an impressively organised and courageous Leeds side, Mikel Arteta knew that Guimarães was capable of coming into the game and adjusting to its demands. There has been no adaptation period required for Guimarães, who is fast becoming one of the most popular players in north London.

The finish, which put Arsenal 2-1 ahead at the Emirates Stadium, marked an emphatic conclusion to a fabulous passing sequence. Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard and Declan Rice all combined at speed before Guimarães charged on to Rice’s flick. “It was a beauty,” said Arteta of the goal. The move had actually begun at the feet of Guimarães a few moments earlier, when he nutmegged an opponent in style.

The winning goal came just eight minutes after Riccardo Calafiori, Arsenal’s thrilling left-back/centre-forward hybrid, had pulled them level in the game. James Justin had struck for Leeds shortly after half-time, creating a horrible anxiety among the home fans here, and for much of the afternoon Daniel Farke’s side were the better team.

Leeds finally have their opener! 🤩 James Justin arrives at the back post to fire them ahead. 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/ITjUMSlrG1

Leeds, though, could not compete with Arsenal for depth. The arrival of Guimarães as a 63rd-minute substitute represented a flexing of Arteta’s managerial muscle, in his first match since signing a new long-term contract, and the Brazilian offered a moment of attacking quality that his opponents were unable to replicate.

It was actually the first competitive home game that Guimarães had played for Arsenal since his transfer from Newcastle United, as a result of a few niggles and the club’s unusual run of four consecutive away matches before the international break. The most recent of those was the 3-0 thrashing by Brighton, which was one of their worst defeats of the last few seasons.

This gritty victory represented a necessary response to that defeat, even if the performance was far from dominant. “We had a point to prove,” said Arteta. “Something was touched in our identity against Brighton.”

Guimarães, too, clearly felt that some wrongs needed to be made right. For all his brilliance in this game and against Sunderland, he had produced a horrible showing at the Amex Stadium a few weeks ago. “He was not at that level against Brighton,” said Arteta. “This is the level for Arsenal. Every week, every game, every minute, every action you have to be at that level. At Brighton, he wasn’t. Today, he was much better.”

Leeds had not lost in their opening five Premier League matches of this season and it was easy to see why. They were willing to press Arsenal high up the pitch, taking risks and engaging in physical duels, and the strategy proved hugely effective for an hour.

If they had been more precise in the final third, they could have been a few goals ahead by the time Justin converted Gabriel Gudmundsson’s left-wing cross after 55 minutes. Anton Stach, who was accidentally blocked by team-mate Jayden Bogle, and Gudmundsson both went close in the first half.

David Raya at his very best to deny Leeds the opener 😳 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/hOB8RMapxw

“I am heartbroken and gutted for my players,” said Farke. “They deserved to travel back with points today. The defeat has to do with the quality of the players they [Arsenal] could bring in. It is down to the mentality Mikel has created here that even on a tough day they find a way to win the game.”

The early kick-off, the long international break, the slow start and the memories of the Brighton defeat made it a strange atmosphere at the Emirates. You would not have known they were the champions, based on the reaction of the fans to the first-half performance, but the achievements of last season clearly do not guarantee fervent support at all times.

Calafiori’s equaliser, which marked his fifth goal involvement in 10 games for club and country this season, changed the momentum of the game. The Italian is such an unusual player but this was a simple goal, converted from close range after Ben White had headed the ball back across the penalty area. “The energy changed immediately,” said Arteta.

It doesn't take long for Arsenal to respond through Riccardo Calafiori! 🎯📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/WPrcA5ZrQ1 https://t.co/qwwNHAJvZ8

From that moment on, it was a matter of time before Arsenal found their second. On came Guimarães, Viktor Gyokeres, Jurrien Timber, and the home side suddenly had renewed energy. Saka, Odegaard and Rice found each other in a flowing move, before Guimarães powered his low finish into the corner of James Trafford’s net. “That is the quality that is needed at this level,” said Arteta.

Before the game we talked about two things, the challenge ahead against a team that had not lost in the Premier League. They full deserved to be where they are and it was going to be really tough. The second was to restore our identity and be ourselves again.

We weren’t pleased with our performance against Brighton and we wanted to put it right. But the context is that this was a difficult one [opponent]. But we reacted in a way that was unique and made it so special.

[Leeds] are very well organised, very physical and very committed in everything that they do. They are a threat. They are incredible the way they attack the ball and set-pieces, with belief. They came close to punishing us. They have individual quality and they are in a good moment.

When you play at 12.30 at home and you go one-nil down there’s a lot to do. You have to restore a lot of things. Energy is one of them. We had an incredible response. The crowd changed. You could see it.

We brought a lot of leadership on [with his three subs]. We brought goal threat, to win duels, people who can play forward and penetrate against their high press.

The timing, movement and execution of it [the winning goal], yes, it was a beauty.

Unbelievable. Against Brighton we were not at the level. This was all about bouncing back. This is my first official game at home. Great finish, I am very happy. My job if on the bench is to give a headache to the manager.

I have been proving myself in the Premier League but it was important for me today.

Leeds have a great team, a top game. Glad we could get the three points.

A game of three thirds, two of them with Leeds in the ascendancy, the last with Arsenal showing their class and wealth. The winning goal was glorious but Leeds, who have lost their unbeaten record, were impressive.

Gabriel gets his head on a couple of crosses, knocking the second of them away from Calvert-Lewin.

Saka, with the last kick of the game, and through one one one with Trafford, shoots into the stands.

Ampadu’s long throw is headed away by Bruno and on by Merino who knocks it safe and out of play.

Trafford comes 20 yards out of his box to try to keep Leeds going but miscontrols with his chest. Gyokeres takes it round him and has an open goal but checks and goes wider and Leeds manage to move enough bodies back to thwart him.

Five minutes of stoppage time are signalled. Ally McCoist names the substitute Bruno as the man of the match. He was certainly the catalyst for a revival.

Odegaard had just fizzed a cute pass to Bruno in the left of the Leeds box but he couldn’t control it.

Calvert-Lewin is played in over the top and squares for Aaronson to shoot into a defender. He would have been better off leaving it for Nmecha.

Fair to say Leeds were the better side for an hour but have suffered a slow puncture since the equaliser.

Odegaard is booked for delaying Leeds’ goal-kick.

Odegaard misses an open goal, flicking his finish to Trafford after two brilliant touches from Rice to trap a deep cross from the left and roll it across the six-yard box.

Bruno Guimarães has now scored two goals for Arsenal and they have both been beauties. The first was a long-range screamer at Sunderland and this was more of a team effort. Saka to Odegaard, Odegaard to Rice, Rice to Bruno. Gorgeous football. The first time Arsenal have produced such a move all afternoon.

Aaronson does well to get back and block Saka’s shot after being put through by Bruno’s sharp pass.

The difference between the two sides today has been the ability to throw £50m players on off the bench.

After some confusion as the fourth official initially put up Gudmundsson’s number.

Right, where were we? Three weeks on from the fifth round of Premier League fixtures in which the champions Arsenal were beaten 3-0 by Brighton and todays’ visitors, Leeds United, who remain unbeaten, drew in a tepid goalless fixture with Crystal Palace, we finally get to the sixth. As worrying as the result was at the Amex, Arsenal still created a shedload of chances and last season they were the one club that battered Leeds in both games – first early in the season when they were playing four at the back and before Dominic Calvert-Lewin, a late signing, was fully fit, and then later after they had successfully switched to a “base formation” of three centre-backs and the tactical flexibility that allowed.

It was a 5-0 tanking in August and 4-0 in January, so to say Leeds travel to a ground at which they have never won more in hope than expectation would be as true as much as it is hackneyed. Adding to a sense of foreboding and thanks to Opta’s excellent Jonny Cooper, we also have to take into account the fact that Leeds, floodlight kings, have not won a Premier League match kicking off before 3pm since August 2022 and have not won a match in London since beating Brentford in May that year to save themselves from relegation. However, they do boast the division’s best defensive record – three goals conceded – and the No1 ranked goalkeeper in James Trafford who has a save percentage of 87. For all the sense of doom, though, Leeds have become a very good side and their spine – Trafford–Muharemovic–Ampadu–Calvert-Lewin marries steel and class.

Arsenall need no fanfare. Until the set-back in dear old Sussex by the sea, they had looked formidable most of the time and will have been champing at the bit to get back out there and prove it was an aberration. Mikel Arteta mentioned he has doubts about Declan Rice, Kai Havertz and Ezri Konsa but Ben White, Max Dowman and Chrsthian Mosquera are all available. For Leeds Joe Rodon is still out and Dan James was injured on international duty but Harry Wilson and Jean-Matteo Bahoya returned to training after knocks this week and Daniel Farke was relatively optimistic about their prospects.

#1374. Unai Emery open to new Aston Villa deal: Manager holds talks with club bosses over extending £15m-a-year contract amid links to Man United job

Published: 14:07 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 15:28 EDT, 4 November 2026

Unai Emery is open to signing a new deal with Aston Villa that would take him to close to a decade at the club.

Emery is one of the most successful Villa managers of modern times and co-owner Nassef Sawiris wants him to guide the club into an even brighter future.

According to a statement on the Villa social media channels, Emery held talks with Sawiris on Wednesday, with his key lieutenants Damian Vidagany and Roberto Olabe attending.

The post read: ‘Aston Villa held an important working meeting today to plan the club's future and lay the foundations for its long-term sporting and institutional project.

'The meeting brought together Nassef Sawiris, the club's Chairman and Unai Emery alongside President of Football Operations Roberto Olabe and Director of Football Operations Damián Vidagany.

'The discussions focused on jointly planning the club's long-term strategic direction, with positive discussions establishing a clear commitment beyond 2029 for the joint development of the club under the sporting leadership of Unai Emery based on the shared ambitions and common goal to reach excellency and keep growing during the next years.

Unai Emery is open to begin talks with Aston Villa over signing a new contract at the club

The Spaniard, who is earning close to £15million-per-year, has been linked with Man United too

'The objective is clear: to build an ambitious, competitive Aston Villa capable of taking on the biggest challenges and achievements.'

Emery is already one of the best paid coaches in the top flight, earning close to £15million annually.

The Basque was said to be on a shortlist for the Manchester United job if Michael Carrick is sacked.

Villa recently threatened legal action against television pundit Jamie Carragher, who had told ‘Aston Villa fans’ to ‘shut the f*** up’. Carragher apologised for his choice of language.

#1373. My Everton #178: What Makes It The People's Club

It all started with my dad who used to go to both Everton and Liverpool games well before my time.

Over the years, he started a family and, thankfully, his allegiances started to move towards Everton.

Jimmy, my eldest brother, came along years later and he started following the Blues straight away, going to the games as soon as he was allowed to.

I came along in 1984 and soon became the newest Blue in the house.

From the age of around 10, Jimmy took me to my first game at Goodison and I fell in love with Everton from that day. Me and Jimmy went to every home game and a few of the local away fixtures as well.

Our dad didn’t really go to many games with us. He did start coming again around 1999 but had a heart attack after one of the games. He never went again – but followed from the couch at home.

Moving forward some years Jimmy met his future wife, Christine, who at the time was a Leeds fan... not for long, though! It took only three games watching the Blues to convert her and extend our home seats by another.

We loved the tradition of a home game day: the meet-up at my mum and dad's house and the drive listening to Radio City’s football talk.

We had season tickets for many years until Christine became ill and needed constant treatment. We all decided to give them up and buy each game separately if and when we could around her treatment.

Unfortunately, after a year, Christine lost her battle and left us. Jimmy needed to get back to Goodison as soon as possible, so again, we all started going to every game together.

Skip through to 2024 and our dad passed away. Another blue light gone out.

Me and Jimmy made sure to remember him at the new stadium with a stone and photo inside.

Jimmy was obsessed with the new stadium build, watching drone progress daily. He waited so long for a new stadium. Unfortunately, Jimmy also passed away just two months after our dad, not getting to step inside the new stadium he always dreamed of.

Again, with losing my dad and Jimmy, who I always went the game with, I decided that I would also stop going.

For the past two seasons I've supported from home, but all while still singing the Blues!

Family is what makes Everton the People's Club.

Its love is passed down through each family member. All those years ago my dad could have chosen the red side but didn’t.

Since then, at least 15 family members have supported and followed the Blues.

I still haven't been a game at our new stadium, but Jimmy and Christine's grandkids do, singing in his name.

My Everton shares first-hand accounts describing the most-treasured memories of fans, players, and staff both past and present.

#1372. Man Utd make worst start in 40 years after being hauled back by 10-man Spurs

Manchester United fans were never going to pass up the opportunity to aim a volley of abuse in the direction of their bitter rivals.

By the end of another deeply unconvincing performance, though, they were more preoccupied by the problems afflicting their own team than the cheating scandal engulfing Manchester City.

Against City at Old Trafford last month, United lost to a team who were down to 10 men after just 23 minutes.

This time around they could not hold on to a lead against a Tottenham Hotspur side also navigating a numerical disadvantage following Rodrigo Bentancur’s sending off.

Rodrigo Bentancur dives in on Luke Shaw and it's all kicking off at Old Trafford! 🫨 https://t.co/uJUAMuZNzc

The sum total of it all is that United have now made their worst start to a season for 40 years, which is saying something given the traumas of the post-Ferguson era, and perhaps more disconcertingly, look to all intents and purposes like a team going backwards.

The bounce they enjoyed under Michael Carrick last season en route to Champions League qualification is over and, after just six points from as many games, it is hard to shake the feeling that it is going to be anything but a serious battle to finish in the top four or five.

The supporters did not hide their disgruntlement. There were boos around the half hour mark after an insipid opening when Spurs did everything but score and a slow, sluggish, dishevelled United almost looked impervious to their troubles.

Carrick had called for his players to show some “fire” coming into this match, but instead watched them ambling around like it was all a terrible inconvenience. The ease with which Spurs ran around them was alarming. There were more jeers at the interval and again at full time.

Carrick admitted that “hurt” although not as much you suspect as the sight of players feigning interest and then throwing away three points when they had finally summoned some fight to lead courtesy of Bryan Mbeumo’s goal.

Bryan Mbeumo slots it home to give Manchester United the lead against Spurs! 🎯 https://t.co/7yKnpyhfUe

It was a lovely finish after good work by the largely anonymous Matheus Cunha, and when Bentancur was sent off five minutes later after butting Luke Shaw, it should have been the cue to see out the game. To fail to do so against a side as toothless as Tottenham made it all the worse. Leading late on against Everton last month, they also failed to get over the line. It cannot keep happening.

Equally, United cannot play like they did in the first half here when they face Atlético Madrid in the Spanish capital on Tuesday night or at Elland Road against bitter rivals Leeds five days later and expect to get anything from either game. They are not the sort of matches Carrick would want with his team in this shape, but they need to find some inspiration from somewhere.

Carlos Baleba coming on around the hour mark and making a difference on his debut will at least offer Carrick some grounds for encouragement. The £65m midfield signing from Brighton offers some energy and urgency and looks a more natural bedfellow for Kobbie Mainoo than Youri Tielemans, who was woeful against Spurs and should have come off earlier.

In truth, Tielemans was not alone. Throughout the team there was a disconnect and unease and Carrick admitted it became contagious.

“We just couldn’t find a way to get ourselves into the game, whether that was with the ball or without the ball,” the United manager said. “We were a little bit slow with the decision-making, didn’t quite see the passing areas, the space. You don’t want it to happen, but sometimes it can and it probably spread through the team a little bit too much.”

It does not help that Bruno Fernandes is being hampered by an injury he has been carrying for weeks or that Carrick has no natural centre-forward to call upon with Benjamin Sesko again sidelined by the recurrence of a worrying shin problem. Amad Diallo did return here after a lengthy lay-off of his own, but did not look match fit.

In defence, Lisandro Martínez did enough to put off Dominic Solanke, who fired over from Sávio’s cross in the second half, but this was otherwise another poor showing from the Argentine centre-back, one of several positions where United need upgrades.

United needed shaking badly, but when Carrick turned to his bench he called upon Joshua Zirkzee, a fitful forward the club wanted to sell this summer, and right-back Diogo Dalot in addition to Baleba.

Marcus Rashford cannot have been fit given he was only introduced in the 95th minute and perhaps the same was true of the unused Mason Mount. As for £50m summer signing Andrey Santos, this was another league game when the Brazilian midfielder did not get a look in.

United fans had taunted Spurs when a goal and a man up. “You’re going down with the City,” they crowed, a nod to the possibility of City being expelled or relegated from the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching more than 100 financial rules.

United fans had also revived their Stretford End “ticker” after reaching the conclusion that none of City’s titles under Abu Dhabi ownership had been won fairly so, in their eyes, it is now 50 years since their rivals last won anything legitimately. City, of course, continue to maintain their innocence and have lodged an appeal.

But United fans were unable to crow for too long once Solanke levelled.

Spurs are level in stoppage-time! 😳 https://t.co/NoivNchgWw

It had been similar early in the game when the home fans had trained their sights on City. “You cheating b--------, you know what you are”, they sang lustily.

But as the match wore on, those chants began to quieten as the crowd, taking their lead from the team, fell decidedly flat.

Carrick is going to have to find a spark from somewhere and quickly.

Speaking to BBC Match of the Day, Carrick said: “It was a mixed game. We found it tough to start with. For a number of reasons, we were not quite there. You could see it was a challenging time.

“But the lads grew into the game, in the second half I thought we were better in everything. To get the game as we wanted it, in such a good position - we should see it through. We have to manage those situations. That’s two late goals which have hurt us, and things look very different. That’s the reality.”

When asked about the boos at half-time and full-time, he replied: “It’s not nice, it hurts a lot because I care about this club. But I understand the disappointment, the reality is what it is, we need to get back to winning games.”

3 - Manchester United have failed to win any of their last three Premier League games against sides that have received a red card (D1 L2). Disadvantage? https://t.co/DuSpvymZfu

The Tottenham boss told Sky Sports: “I think we played very well against a great team. We had many chances to score in the first half. Three or four. The second half is normal to suffer against this quality. I am very happy because I have seen the right spirit and character.

“We suffered in the game but every situation of the game. I like the situation we were in with the red card. We need this situation. We have not accepted the defeat. We have to react in all ways we can. It is a bad way, it is not the right way. I kiss Bentancur in the dressing room. Football is character.

“We win the game if we play as a team. We didn’t win this game playing as a team. Every game like today, we will win many games.”

When asked about Solanke, he replied: “He is a good player for Tottenham. There for not too many strikers better than Solanke. Today he was captain because he deserved it, especially in this moment because he suffer because Tottenham didn’t score or win any games. He is a great guy, great player and we are behind him.

“We have to believe in ourselves and this football way. If we believe, improve and play as a team, we will score many goals and win many games. If we don’t play as a team, it is impossible.”

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of this mouthwatering Premier League game between Manchester United and Tottenham at Old Trafford.

If Manchester City had not entered a legal battle with the Premier League after being found guilty of breaching 114 charges relating to financial regulations by an independent panel, then surely there would be more pressure on the two head coaches in the dugout this evening?

Man Utd and Tottenham have undoubtedly both endured extremely disappointing starts to their respective top-flight campaigns. The hosts sit just inside the bottom half of the table after picking up just five points from their opening five matches. It’s going even worse for Tottenham, who languish in 20th with zero wins and just two points.

The perilous landscape leaves only one reasonable conclusion: this has all the ingredients for an early season six-pointer.

The strain is perhaps less intense on Michael Carrick, with the Englishman having built up a bundle of goodwill after cleaning up the mess left by Ruben Amorim last season as Man Utd eventually finished third, qualifying for the Champions League. Fans were left slightly underwhelmed by the club’s transfer window, with the players at Carrick’s disposal having not forged any momentum so far in this campaign.

The spotlight is definitely shining more intensely upon Roberto De Zerbi after big-spending Tottenham splashed over £300m in the summer on the likes of Sandro Tonali, Mateus Fernandes, Jan Paul van Hecke and Savio. However, the Italian boss is yet to strike the correct rhythm with his newly-formed squad. An encouraging performance backed up by a positive result here at Old Trafford could be the perfect antidote to ease the worries of fans fearing that Tottenham could be embroiled in another relegation battle.

All eyes are on this one. Kick-off is at 17:30, with team news coming shortly.

#1371. Hearts dealt ANOTHER injury blow as winger Calvin Miller is ruled out for two months with knee injury

Published: 15:47 EDT, 4 November 2026 | Updated: 16:07 EDT, 4 November 2026

Hearts boss Wouter Vrancken has revealed star winger Calvin Miller will require surgery on a knee injury that will keep him out for two months.

Both Tomas Magnusson and Miller came off during the first half of Hearts’ Premier Sports Cup semi-final defeat to Edinburgh rivals Hibernian at Hampden on Sunday.

Icelandic midfielder Magnusson was taken to hospital with concussion, while former Celtic, Morton and Falkirk attacker Miller left the national stadium on crutches with his knee in a brace.

Vrancken, who will be without ten first-team players for Thursday’s Conference League game against FC Thun in Switzerland, was asked about Miller and said: ‘It will be two months, let’s say, depending on what the surgery says because it’s a meniscus injury. It’s a pity, but it is what it is.

‘Tomas is doing good. The day after was already a lot better. There is a protocol, of course, with concussions. He will be for sure back after the (international) break.’

Vrancken will attempt to put together a side capable of getting a first win in the competition, following a 1-1 home draw against Nordsjaelland and a 2-0 defeat away to Trabzonspor. He added: ‘Yes, it’s a puzzle. I’m always happy to see that the players we work with and play out of position are always motivated to do it. They know how much they help the team by doing it.

Calvin Miller holds his injured leg before being taken off in Hearts' League Cup defeat to Hibs

‘It’s good to see because they take responsibility and they don’t live by excuses. They have already done it for weeks. That’s how we also get good results and good performances.

‘Now we have to try to do it two more times before the break. I’m confident in the players that they are mentally ready to play the game.

‘They (Thun) have a good team, they have a lot of energy, a lot of intensity. We will have to be spot on, we have to be on our level to make the result. But the aim is to try to get a win here.’

Meanwhile, the Tynecastle club yesterday announced a loss of £2.4million after investing heavily to return to European football this season. However, the club reported they are also in ‘positive’ discussions about further investment in the January transfer window and are confident of a ‘significantly improved financial result’ in a year’s time.

#1370. Everton's Remembrance Day Plans

Everton and Coventry City will come together ahead of Friday’s Premier League fixture at Hill Dickinson Stadium to remember the fallen and honour the sacrifices made by servicemen and women during conflict.

The pre-match Remembrance ceremony will involve players and staff from both clubs, as well as representatives of the Royal Navy, British Army, Royal Air Force and Merchant Navy.

Those taking part in the tribute will include serving personnel from the Tri-Service Toffees Supporters’ Club and former servicemen and women supported by Everton in the Community’s Veterans Programme.

Supporters are requested to arrive to their seats from 7.50pm, ahead of the ceremony, which will follow the walk-out by the teams and match officials.

As part of the Remembrance ceremony, the captains of Everton and Coventry City will lay commemorative poppy wreaths on the pitch ahead of kick-off, along with representatives from the Armed Forces, the Tri-Service Toffees and Everton in the Community.

Players from both sides will wear shirts bearing the poppy emblem, in memory of the fallen.

We will proudly welcome the following service personnel to take part in our pre-match tribute:

The following former service personnel will also participate in the tribute through Everton in the Community’s Veterans Programme:

Following the laying of the wreaths, The Last Post will be performed by bugler Andrew Manning.

As a mark of respect, the traditional pre-match siren will not sound before the teams enter the pitch, though Z-Cars will play as normal.

As part of the Club’s recognition of serving personnel, Steve McCann and Danny Jackson, both members of Tri-Service Toffees, will take part in the half-time Hit the Bar competition.

The Tri-Service Toffees is an affiliated Everton supporters’ club for those serving in the Royal Navy, British Army and Royal Air Force, whether regular or reservist. Evertonians interested in joining or finding out more about the supporters’ club should email triservicetoffees@gmail.com.

Shirts worn by Everton’s Men’s and Women’s players during the Remembrance period will be auctioned to raise vital funds to support the work of the Royal British Legion. To find out more – or to bid for a shirt – click here.

What Remembrance Means to Me – A Message From The Tri-Service Toffees

Remembrance is about remembering. It really is that simple.

Remembering the sacrifices made by so many, from the First World War through every conflict since. Not just those who served in uniform, but the families, friends, colleagues and civilians whose lives were forever changed.

It is about taking a moment to acknowledge those sacrifices, both great and small, and the individuals who made them.

Having served for over 37 years, including numerous operational tours in conflict, I don’t reflect on my own sacrifices. Those will be for others to remember when I am gone.

Instead, I remember my mum, who served in the Royal Navy, and my uncles Tony and Frank (her brothers). All three have now passed away, but each played a significant part in inspiring my own military career. I also remember the friends and colleagues who have made the ultimate sacrifice in the hope of making a difference.

But perhaps the person foremost in my thoughts is my wife, Shirley.

Throughout my military career, she has made countless sacrifices of her own, often quietly and without recognition. Like so many military spouses and families, she has carried burdens that others rarely see, whilst asking for little in return.

Their sacrifices deserve our remembrance, too.

So, when you pause to remember, think not only of those who gave their lives in service to our nation, but also of those closest to you, whose sacrifices may never have been publicly acknowledged.

At the going down of the sun and in the morning, we will remember them.

Major Anthony John Sandle RLC, Second-in-Command, 156 Regiment, The Royal Logistic Corps(pictured above with Everton Ambassador Graham Stuart)

#1369. The cheats prosper: Man City thrash 10-man Liverpool

Just when the Premier League and the world outside of east Manchester and Abu Dhabi needed Liverpool to step up, to strike back, to make a point, they faltered. Maybe it was unfair to expect them to do so, given the circumstances. But unfairness, lack of clarity and uncertainty are all prevailing moods in English football at present.

How we had rubbed our hands in anticipation of Manchester City having to play their first league fixture here at Anfield after being found guilty of industrial-scale fraud with 114 of the 115 financial charges being proven against them.

It felt apt that it was at the home of Liverpool, who, along with Arsenal, possess the strongest sense of grievance at having been denied trophies and glory by City’s cheating. As expected, there were banners everywhere at Anfield. “A generation of supporters cheated,” one read and it summed up the depth of the anger.

Their fans would surely create the kind of bear-pit atmosphere that would leave City in no doubt at the vitriol that will rain down on them from now on. At every away ground. Liverpool could set the tone. The defiance.

This is a team who can stir the blood, surf the emotion and triumph against the odds more than any other; who have a proud history of doing so. Who feel the injustice at its most acute and could feed off that.

In the end Liverpool suffered their first defeat of the season. Their first under Andoni Iraola. And comprehensively so. It could not have come at a worse time for them and for the Premier League, and for the fans of every other club who wanted to see City humbled. On the pitch.

There was another sense of injustice. Up until the dismissal of Ryan Gravenberch, Liverpool were the better side. Especially as they attacked the Kop in the second half, drawing saves from Gianluigi Donnarumma, and began to build the kind of momentum that has, over the years, appeared to suck the ball into the net.

Ryan Gravenberch is OFF 🟥 https://t.co/IVIHNzqw6k

The midfielder’s first yellow card looked harsh. His second, for a foul on substitute Jérémy Doku was less so (but still not clear-cut) and it meant Liverpool had to play the final third of the game with 10 men. Instead of weaponising that; they wilted and the fans directed their frustration at referee Chris Kavanagh, believing he was lenient towards City.

This is not a slight on Iraola, but it is hard to imagine Jürgen Klopp not riding that wave of emotion more effectively and wringing more out of the available players. Turning to the fans; imploring them; cajoling them.

Instead it was City making the statement with an extraordinary power play as they scored three times in 13 minutes, inspired by Doku, whose cameo made him man of the match. That City could hold the winger back, on the bench, only to introduce him with such devastating effect again pointed to their phenomenal strength in depth.

They are again three points clear at the top, with six wins from six games, ahead of champions Arsenal and there is a frightening awesomeness about them at present that will make the Premier League shudder. For several reasons. What if they run away with it this season before being sanctioned, probably sometime in the spring? Where will that leave the competition?

In the face of City’s power and the adversity of losing Gravenberch, Liverpool simply could not cope. They were already depleted – without Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak, Hugo Ekitike and Cody Gakpo – and needed some of their other big signings to respond.

But this was not a good day for Bradley Barcola or Florian Wirtz, in particular, and it felt telling that the latter was withdrawn soon after Erling Haaland opened the scoring. He could, in fact, have also been sent off after catching Elliot Anderson late. The German’s contribution was once more woefully negligible; worryingly marginal. He was lightweight and so, ultimately, were Liverpool.

Erling Haaland gives Manchester City the lead against Liverpool 🎯 https://t.co/cELo5y60Fk

In fact, Liverpool’s best performers were the young attackers Victor Muñoz and, making his first league start as a makeshift centre-forward, Lewis Koumas, who is just 21. Against that, City unleashed a battery of forward talent.

Was it an unfair advantage? It appears City have been thriving off that for some time and, while this team were not signed during the years the club have been found guilty of cheating, the argument is, of course, that they would not have joined without the sporting supremacy.

Certainly not Haaland, despite his avowed love for City. That cannot be doubted as his father, Alf-Inge, a former midfielder for the club, stood celebrating in the away end. The striker missed one chance when he should have scored, sent through on goal, shaking his head in disbelief at getting his angles wrong. It felt like a warning and that went unheeded as Doku, who had replaced one of their big summer signings in Iliman Ndiaye, cut in from the left with his shot deflecting into Haaland’s path. He made no mistake with a powerful, first-time finish.

Doku soon added a second, a sublime strike, as he dribbled goalwards, defenders backing off, and he arced a right-footed shot high beyond Alisson Becker’s grasp.

There were delighted chants of “olé” from the City supporters and that arrogance was rewarded by a strutting, emphatic third goal. It was finished by the mercurial Rayan Cherki after he was sent clear by a backheel from Josko Gvardiol, another substitute.

A moment of individual brilliance from Rayan Cherki to put the game beyond all doubt 🤯 https://t.co/wvmTMZcGhW

It captured City’s swagger, their sense of responding to what they regard as an injustice – that they maintain will be overturned on appeal – the sense they are going to continue to create an almighty headache for the Premier League. In a sea of uncertainty as to what will now happen, that is something we can be sure of.

“Cheats,” loudly boomed around Anfield from the home fans before the PA played Fleetwood Mac’s Tell Me Lies at the final whistle, as the players walked off. Those signs of defiance were not matched on the pitch. Although it may be a song City will get used to hearing for the rest of this extraordinary, unprecedented campaign.

Enzo Maresca hailed Manchester City’s ability to “make our own noise” after their emphatic 3-0 win at Liverpool.

In the first fixture since being found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges laid against them for serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, City made their statement on the pitch as they re-established a three-point lead at the top of the table.

“It was not easy for the players after the last two, three weeks, but they dealt with it very well,” Maresca, the head coach, said. “I said during the week we need to learn to deal with the outside noise because of the situation, because that will be there. But we have to make our own noise.

“Zero-three at Anfield away is a great result, for sure. I think all the organisation needs a win like this. It’s good for all [of] the club.”

Maresca said City will have to get used to such hostile occasions, with Liverpool fans making clear their anger over the judgment, and added: “All the away games are going to be with noise.”

Maresca confirmed that chief executive Ferran Soriano and director of football Hugo Viana had travelled on the team bus to Anfield in a sign of unity.

“Ferran was there, Hugo was there. We were all together,” Maresca said. “For the importance of the game, Liverpool away, Anfield away. It’s good to be together.”

The Italian claimed that despite the verdict, and the attention and uncertainty as to what will happen next, it had not affected his squad.

“The players just focus on the football. They are not thinking about the future,” he said. “It’s how we learn to deal with the noise. It’s our duty to make noise and to do that we win games. You cannot imagine how happy I am. Hopefully I am going to speak about this situation when we are going to win the appeal.”

The Liverpool boss told BBC MOTD: “I think the first part is that we played two different games. One until the red card, and then after. For 60 minutes, the players were very good. The second game from the red card was where City were better than us.

“The first yellow card was just a kick in the toe. It was nothing. It was a normal foul. It was the moment when we were pushing more. The momentum was coming for us and the atmosphere in the stadium was so nice. We conceded very little in the first half. We did a really good job. The second half, we were translating into chances.

“You learn a lot in games like today. I am very proud of my players. They put the work rate and everything in today. It’s a loss and we didn’t get anything from the performance but I liked it a lot.”

News breaks that City had been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges brought by the Premier League over breaches of its financial rules.

Telegraph Sport understands that Manchester United, Liverpool, Arsenal and Tottenham Hotspur were contacted in advance of the email to the other 15 clubs.

In a letter to fans, a defiant Khaldoon Al Mubarak, City’s chairman, expresses complete confidence that his club would be vindicated.

“There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club,” he writes. “We will not give them that opportunity.”

With the football world still making sense of the news, Tony Pulis admits to feeling “cheated”. His Stoke City side were defeated by Manchester City in the 2011 FA Cup final, during the 2009-23 period.

Hull City owner Acun Ilicali then likens City’s transgressions to “doping” before Mauricio Pochettino, whose Spurs side were often in the hunt with City for major trophies during his time as manager, says that football has “lived through a period of deception”.

The Premier League reveals that City’s owners inflated “sham” sponsorship deals by £830.69m between 2009-10 and 2017-18.

It also discloses that image rights had been inflated and key witnesses had lied.

Ferran Soriano, chief executive of City Football Group, appears helpless when questioned about the verdict’s findings at the European Football Clubs’ general assembly in Copenhagen by Sky News.

An unblinking Soriano then features in a video statement published by City in which he claimed their guilty verdict was based on “a single false accusation”.

With City on the ropes, Pep Guardiola releases a statement in support of his former club, assuring supporters that “we will get through this together”.

The Prime Minister says that he would be “really concerned” to lose City’s owners, but after significant backlash, No 10 moves to clarify his reaction saying that “if wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences”.

It later amends the statement to “wherever wrongdoing is established”.

The UAE then warns Andy Burnham that it will pull billions of pounds of investment out of the UK in retaliation for the guilty verdict against City.

City argue that their sponsorship deals were part-funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club’s owners, in their appeal, which claims bank statements and witness accounts provide “irrefutable evidence” to support their case.

There were four days between the news leaking that Manchester City had been found guilty of the majority of charges first levelled at them by the Premier League in February 2023 and the independent commission findings dropping.

Staff, then, had had a bit of time to process a guilty verdict although little, it seems, could adequately prepare them for the excoriating tone and content of the commission’s ruling.

“The thing that has shocked me more than anything is the language the commission used to describe the club’s conduct,” one staff member told Telegraph Sport this week.

“We had been waiting for a very long time to see what came out of these Premier League charges and lots of different things go through your head. But I just wasn’t expecting that. I’m still a bit shell-shocked by the ferocity of what the commission said. I think that’s what’s worried me.”

“The international break is good because we can review what we have done and what we can do better,” Enzo Maresca said after Manchester City’s harum-scarum 5-3 victory over Sunderland. “But at the same time we can relax a little bit more.” One wonders how much respite Enzo Maresca and Manchester City actually enjoyed in the intervening 21 days.

Since City last kicked a football in anger, they have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges levelled at them by the Premier League in a verdict that has shaken professional football to its very core. The club have appealed and the extent of their punishment now rests with an independent panel. Until then, though, the show goes on and City’s players and staff must compete knowing that their every move now comes with a caveat.

City have put up a united front and on Thursday Maresca and Haaland duly delivered the party lines, the City head coach revealing that the feeling among his charges was “fantastic”. “[My players] know what we can control is the football side – they are not worried at all about different things,” Maresca said, before adding that he trusts the club “completely”. The Italian doubled down on his remarks in his Friday press conference.

City maintain their innocence and many of Maresca’s peers have remained tight-lipped on the case, though Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick admitted this week he has questions, while Régis Le Bris urged football’s governing bodies to be “relentless” in safeguarding competitive integrity.

Given all that has happened, it would be easy to forget that this is, for now, a top-of-the-table clash and has been one of the Premier League’s marquee rivalries since the days of Guardiola-Jürgen Klopp. Liverpool fans have never been ones to roll out the red carpet when City are in town, but the ill feeling and belligerence will only intensify at Anfield this time around owing to the events of the past weeks.

City are top of the league having won all five of their league matches so far, while Liverpool have huffed and puffed to sixth, remaining unbeaten.

#1368. Microbiome-wide PheWAS links gut microbial SNVs to health and exposures

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Alterations in the microbial composition of the human gut have been associated with a wide range of chronic diseases1,2. Yet species-level composition alone can obscure extensive within-species genetic diversity and functional variation. This has driven a shift towards strain-resolved, genetic-level analysis of the microbiome, leveraging microbial genetic variation to identify disease-relevant genes and pathways3,4,5,6. Here we conducted a phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) analysing 12.8 million gut microbial single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) with 244 host health phenotypes and environmental exposures in 10,781 individuals from 6 independent cohorts. We identify 940 independent associations across 69 host factors, including age, sex and cardiovascular and metabolic parameters. Structural analyses identified host-phenotype-associated SNVs in functionally important regions of proteins, findings that inform mechanistic hypotheses about how microbial genetic changes relate to environmental and host physiological factors. For example, we identified an age-associated SNV in Faecalibacterium prausnitzii that affects an amino acid within the protein pocket that binds glutathione. To support future efforts, all study summary statistics are provided in an online catalogue (https://fulab.web.rug.nl/SNV-MWAS/). Together, these results identify new biological connections between the human host and microbial genetic variants at base pair resolution and provide a resource for hypothesis generation that will aid future understanding of the strain-level functionality of the gut microbiota.

The gut microbiome exhibits large variations in its composition and genetic landscape. Within-species genetic variation underlies strain differences in fitness, metabolic capacities, pathogenicity and other biological properties. Thus, the field of microbiome research is moving towards strain-level or genetic-level dissection of the microbial contributions to human health (Supplementary Information). Structural variations in the gut microbiome have been linked to human body mass index (BMI), bile acid concentrations, the human plasma metabolome and host genetics, thereby identifying bacterial genes involved in glucose metabolism, bile acid biosynthesis and biotransformation, and N-acetylgalactosamine utilization3,4,5,6.

However, gut microbial genomes also contain abundant SNVs that can modulate microbial function and host interactions. For example, a SNV in the blc gene of Escherichia coli disrupts the intestinal barrier by decreasing the amount of lysophosphatidylethanolamine, a metabolite that aids remission of inflammatory bowel disease7. In the stomach, a SNV in Helicobacter pylori increases gastric cancer risk by enhancing the proteolytic activity of the serine protease HtrA (ref. 8). In Bacteroides coprocola, SNVs in glycosyl hydrolase genes have been associated with type 2 diabetes9. A SNV-based metagenome-wide association study (SNV-MWAS) in an Israeli population identified BMI-associated SNVs that were replicated in a geographically independent Dutch cohort10. Despite these examples, systematic explorations of the relationships between gut microbial SNVs and host phenotypes have not, to our knowledge, been carried out at phenome-wide scale. Such analyses require large-scale human cohort data with both metagenomic and deep phenotypic data, and they need to overcome a number of technical challenges. For example, microbial species exhibit complex population genetic structures, and these strong lineage effects may lead to false discoveries in association studies if population structure is not properly controlled.

In this study, we compiled shotgun metagenomic sequencing data of 11,831 faecal samples from 5 independent cohorts from the Netherlands and a cohort from Tanzania. Gut microbial genotypes were characterized using GT-Pro11, yielding 12.8 million SNVs in core genomic regions. We further developed a linear mixed-model (LMM)-based analysis workflow that controls for within-species population genetic structure to ensure that SNV–phenome associations detected are independent from the cumulative effect of strain lineage. We then conducted a PheWAS to identify associations between common metagenomic SNVs and 244 host phenotypic and exposure factors, using LMM in each cohort, followed by meta-analysis. In total, we detected 940 independent association signals supported by multiple cohorts that link 39,663 SNVs across 101 species to 69 host phenotypes or exposures, and the full set of results are available in an online catalogue. We also performed protein structural analyses to interpret the biological relevance of these associations.

We compiled faecal metagenomic sequencing data for 11,831 samples from 10,781 individuals from 6 cohorts (Fig. 1). Five cohorts are from the Netherlands—the Dutch Microbiome Project (DMP; n = 7,955)12, Lifelines-DEEP (LLD; n = 1,135, plus 340 followed up after an average of 4 years (designated LLD1 for baseline samples and LLD2 for follow-up samples))3,13, the 500-Functional Genomics Project (500FG; n = 529)14,15, the 1000 Inflammatory Bowel Disease Project (IBD; n = 544)16 and 300-Obesity (300OB; n = 298)15,17—and one is from Tanzania (300-Tanzania Functional Genomics Project (300TZFG), n = 320)18 (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 1). For LLD2 and 500FG, we have additional datasets from some of the same individuals (nLLD2 = 251, nFG500 = 459) with samples processed using both DNA extraction methods19 that allowed us to assess the effect of extraction protocol on SNV profiling and the robustness of microbial genotyping (Fig. 1, Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Note 1). The extensive phenotypic information for the corresponding samples was also curated and harmonized. We integrated 244 phenotypic and exposure factors (92 binary and 152 continuous or ordinal traits) available in the DMP or in at least 2 other cohorts for analysis (Fig. 2a and Supplementary Table 2). Among these, 131 phenotypes were available for at least 2 cohorts, whereas 113 were only available for the DMP. Across the whole dataset, the sample size per phenotype ranged from 593 to 11,706 (Supplementary Table 2).

We then conducted meta-genotyping for the WGS data from stool samples and generated the gut microbial genotype profile, keeping 12.8 million common biallelic microbial SNVs for the LMM-based SNV-MWAS. SNV-MWAS analyses were conducted separately for the six independent datasets from the six cohorts and then integrated through meta-analysis. Linkage disequilibrium-based grouping was conducted to extract independent signals, and an LMM-based permutation test was used to screen for robust association signals. We genotyped 50,945,657 biallelic SNVs in the core genome of 881 species using GT-Pro11, which conducts reference-panel-based SNV detection using k-mer searching and exact matching. The number of SNVs detected in the DMP was higher than in other cohorts, probably owing to its larger sample size (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). The total number of SNVs detected in at least 1 sample for each species ranged from 1 to 342,230 (mean = 58,131) (Extended Data Fig. 1c). The average density of SNVs in the core genomic region of gut bacteria was 32 SNVs per kilobase pair (Extended Data Fig. 1d), which is close to previous reports20. To keep only informative species for downstream analysis, we selected ‘common’ SNVs that were present in more than 10% of samples and had a minor allele frequency (MAF) of more than 5% in at least one cohort. Among the 50.95 million SNVs that were detected, 12,761,497 SNVs were common (Supplementary Table 3). As the distribution of common SNV counts per species was bimodal, with two peaks separated by approximately 1,000 SNVs (Extended Data Fig. 1e), we selected species with at least 1,000 common SNVs, resulting in 433 species with 12,706,564 common SNVs (Fig. 2b, Extended Data Fig. 1f,g and Supplementary Table 4). These 433 species collectively accounted for, on average, 84.3% (s.d. = 9.4%) of the total abundance of the gut microbial community. After filtering, 300TZFG had the highest number of species for analysis (327) and the most common SNVs (7,369,266) (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 1f–h). The average density of common SNV sites in the core genomic region of gut bacteria was 16 SNVs per kilobase pair (Extended Data Fig. 1i). The within-species population structure of the 433 species and the effect of technical factors are described extensively in Supplementary Notes 2 and 3 (Supplementary Figs. 1–4 and Supplementary Tables 5–8). We also pre-calculated the Bonferroni-controlled threshold for study-wide significance by dividing 0.05 by the total number of phenotype–SNV pairs tested (922,497,753), yielding a threshold of 5.42 × 10−11 (Methods).

To understand the functional consequences of SNVs, we annotated genes from reference genomes and predicted the potential functional effect of SNVs on bacterial gene products (synonymous, missense, start or stop codon, and non-protein-coding)21 (Fig. 2c, Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 9). Most SNVs (11,819,660, 93.02%) were located in protein-coding regions, including 9,579,907 (75.39%) synonymous, 2,216,969 (17.45%) missense and 22,784 (0.18%) start or stop codon variants (Fig. 2c). The distribution of the proportion of codon-altering SNVs (missense or start or stop codon SNVs) varied across different bacterial species (Extended Data Fig. 2), reflecting the genetic diversity and evolutionary pressures experienced by these species.

We next performed an SNV-MWAS of 244 factors by linking them to 12 million common SNVs using LMMs fitted separately for each species, phenotype and cohort. These LMMs controlled for population structure by including the species-level between-sample genetic linkage matrix as a random effect. Age, sex, species abundance and clean read count were included as fixed-effect covariates, except in the analyses for age and sex themselves. Given that reference and alternative alleles may coexist within a sample with differing abundances, we encoded gut microbial genotypes as a dosage value ranging from 0 to 1 to represent the frequency of the alternative allele.

Following the per-cohort SNV-MWAS, we conducted a meta-analysis weighted by sample size for the SNV–phenotype pairs available in at least two cohorts to integrate the SNV-MWAS results derived from different cohorts (Fig. 1). This included only the independent datasets—that is, excluding LLD2 and 500FG-APK. This analysis identified 49,346 significant and robust associations that passed the study-wide significance cut-off (meta-analysis P < 5.42 × 10−11; Extended Data Fig. 3 and Methods) and were supported by at least 2 cohorts based on a permutation-based robustness test (cohort permutation P < 0.05 with 999 permutations), with the same association direction. These associations involved 39,663 SNVs of 101 species and 69 phenotypes.

As a resource for further validation and hypothesis generation, we have constructed a catalogue (https://fulab.web.rug.nl/SNV-MWAS/) that includes all 49,346 robust associations as well as the suggestive signals that passed the species-wide significance level (species-specific, defined by Bonferroni correction based on the number of tested SNVs within each species; Methods) in the meta-analysis and the largest cohort DMP (see examples in Supplementary Note 4 and Supplementary Fig. 5).

Most SNV associations (85.76%) were supported by two cohorts, and 14.24% were supported by three or more cohorts (Fig. 3a). Although all associated SNVs showed a similar ratio of start or stop codon or missense SNVs (17.49%) compared with the background (all common SNVs), six phenotypes were significantly enriched for start or stop codon or missense SNVs (χ2 test P < 0.05): Lifelines protein diet score, on-a-diet behaviour during the past month, thrombocyte count, waist circumference, β-blocker intake and sex (Extended Data Fig. 4). SNVs in the non-coding region may affect gene expression through upstream regulators. For example, variants located approximately 10 bp upstream of the start codon may affect the ribosome-binding site or other elements involved in translation initiation, thereby altering bacterial protein expression22. We further examined the distribution patterns of common and phenotype-associated SNVs in gene upstream regions. The common SNV count showed a drop in −10 bp regions (Fig. 3b), and the ratio of SNVs with at least one association showed an uneven distribution, with a drop at −11 bp and two peaks at −55 bp and −83 bp (Fig. 3c).

As SNVs can be correlated due to linkage disequilibrium in the genomes, we conducted a grouping analysis to select the most significant SNVs within each linkage disequilibrium block as representative tags of the independent signals (between-SNV r2 < 0.01; Methods). We then identified 940 independent SNV-MWAS signals (Fig. 3d,e and Supplementary Table 10) and 13,198 SNVs with a high probability of contribution to phenotypic variation (posterior inclusion probability > 0.8) (Supplementary Note 5 and Supplementary Fig. 6). Power assessment found that 70.5% of signals have more than 0.80 power to be detected given the observed effect size, sample size, and MAF (Supplementary Note 6 and Supplementary Fig. 7) and showed a negative correlation between MAF and effect size (Fig. 3f, R = −0.29, P = 6.06 × 10−20). We also assessed replication across cohorts of different ancestries. Among the 940 signals, 215 had both SNVs and phenotypes available in the Dutch and Tanzanian cohorts, with 161 (74.9%) signals involving 8 different phenotypes supported by both cohorts. For example, 48 association signals of 23 species with age are supported by Dutch and Tanzanian cohorts (Extended Data Fig. 5).

Notably, among the 940 SNV–phenotype association signals, 65.74% showed no significant associations at the abundance level (linear regression, Bonferroni-corrected meta-analysis P > 0.05; Fig. 3d,e). To illustrate the added value of SNV associations, we systematically assessed the phenotypic associations with the gut microbiome at the species abundance, SNV and structural variant levels. Among the 62,464 species–phenotype pairs (Methods), 533 showed associations at SNV level, 460 (86.30%) showed associations only at SNV level, and just 5 (0.9%) showed associations at all 3 levels (Extended Data Fig. 6 and Supplementary Tables 11–13). These results suggest that SNV-based analyses provide complementary information to structural variant- and abundance-based analyses when investigating host–microbiome associations4,5,23.

Among 940 signals, 810 were linked with intrinsic factors and 130 with exposure factors (Supplementary Note 7). We found 152 pairwise signal combinations involving 26 intrinsic phenotypes (excluding age, sex and height), in which the same tag SNVs were associated with 1 or more exposure factors (Fig. 3g and Supplementary Table 14). To assess whether exposure factors confounded the association signals of the intrinsic factors, we included the exposure factors as covariates in a robust association test using LMM-based permutation tests (999 permutations) for the association signals shared between intrinsic phenotypes and exposure factors. Owing to data completeness requirements (phenotype, exposure and SNV all had to be observed in at least 100 samples), we could evaluate 66 signals. Of these, 54 (81.8%) remained significant in at least 2 cohorts after controlling for the exposure factors (permutation P < 0.05), suggesting that the exposure factors did not confound the majority of the SNV associations with intrinsic phenotypes.

Age showed the highest number of association signals (99 signals) involving 8,117 SNVs across 42 species (meta-analysis P < 5.42 × 10−11) (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Table 10). We next assessed how well microbial SNVs could predict host age (Methods). To this end, we trained a machine learning model in the DMP cohort and evaluated its predictive performance in the other cohorts. The model explained 12.8–42.0% of the variation in age (R2) in the test datasets (Supplementary Notes 8 and 9, Supplementary Figs. 8–10 and Supplementary Tables 15 and 16), suggesting the predictive potential of gut microbial genetics for host age.

The most robust signal was supported by four independent cohorts (meta P < 5.42 × 10−11; Fig. 4a, Extended Data Fig. 7 and Supplementary Table 10). This signal contains five SNVs in the genome of F. prausnitzii_I (species ID: 102274), and their associations were not confounded by other microbial features, including bacterial lineage, species abundance and structural variants (Extended Data Fig. 8 and Supplementary Note 10). Notably, all five age-associated SNVs are missense variants located in the sarA_2 gene (gene ID: 102274_01471). The most significant SNV was 102274_1617247 (effect allele: T, effect allele frequency = 17.38%, β = 4.93, meta-analysis P = 1.00 × 10−17), showing that individuals carrying the T allele were 4.9 ± 0.6 years older (mean ± s.d.) than those without the T allele (Supplementary Table 10). The linkage disequilibrium analysis showed that the lead SNV 102274_1617247 is linked with the other four missense SNVs (R2 > 0.2; Fig. 4a,b) in sarA_2, and significant signals were detected in all cohorts except 300OB (Fig. 4c,d). Notably, all 300OB participants are older than 50 years and show a higher frequency of age-associated alleles compared with the other four Dutch cohorts, which have younger average ages (Extended Data Fig. 9). In other words, the age-associated allele in the sarA_2 gene of F. prausnitzii_I was enriched in an older population. Moreover, replication of the association across the Dutch and Tanzanian cohorts (Fig. 4d) suggests convergent genetic changes during host ageing in different ethnic groups.

The sarA_2 gene is a homologue of the oppA gene, which encodes an oligopeptide-binding lipoprotein with a Tat pathway signal sequence in its N terminus. The protein product of sarA_2 also forms an outer-membrane unit of an ATP-binding cassette (ABC)-type transporter system responsible for the uptake of oligopeptides—the oligopeptide permease (OPP) complex (Fig. 4b). We thus hypothesized that the age-associated missense SNVs may influence the function of the SarA_2 protein (also known as OppA). To test this, we assembled the OPP complex based on the AlphaFold3 prediction, including the five subunits encoded by sarA, oppB_4, oppC_4, oppD_4 and oppF_4 (Fig. 4e). This structural comparative analysis revealed that the predicted OPP structure is similar to the substrate-binding protein-dependent ABC transporter systems of Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv (Protein Data Bank (PDB): 8JA7)24 and E. coli (PDB: 6CVL)25, supporting the plausibility of the predicted ABC transporter architecture. The sectional view of the predicted OPP complex structure revealed a tunnel-like cavity, with the OppA subunit acting as a gate for the transportation tunnel (Fig. 4e). Notably, the age-associated SNVs we identify are located in the cavity of OppA that relates to the tunnel (Fig. 4f), which suggests that these SNVs may affect the transportation function of the protein complex.

To infer the potential ligand of the OPP complex and better understand the underlying age-related changes in transport function, we examined the functional annotations of each subunit of the complex in detail. The OppF_4 subunit, encoded by the gene 102274_01467, was annotated as a GsiA subunit of the transporter for glutathione, an antioxidant that can prevent the damage caused by oxidative stress for both eukaryotes and prokaryotes. We then compared the protein sequences of OppA, OppB_4, OppC_4, OppD_4 and OppF_4 with 3,239 existing protein sequences of the ABC-type glutathione transport system and found that all 5 subunits match existing protein sequences (E-value < 1 × 10−10; Methods), indicating that the OPP complex may function as a glutathione transport system. In silico molecular docking analysis further revealed that glutathione can bind to the pocket region of the OppA protein (Fig. 4g and Extended Data Fig. 10). This suggests that age-associated mutations may affect glutathione uptake efficiency and help F. prausnitzii_I better resist ageing-related oxidative stress in the intestinal environment.

Motivated by the structural characterization of age-associated SNVs in sarA_2, we further systematically depicted the effect of associated SNVs in relation to protein structures. To this end, we focused on 6,799 associated missense SNVs, which are related to 3,724 proteins. We retrieved high-confidence three-dimensional structures of 2,141 (57.49%) proteins with 3,705 associated missense SNVs from the ESM Metagenomic Atlas26 and AlphaFoldDB27. We then systematically characterized these SNVs in relation to structural properties, including relative solvent accessibility (RSA, how exposed a residue is to a solvent), distance to ligand (DTL, distance from the residue to the nearest predicted pocket centre) and distance to protein–protein interaction interface (DTPPI, distance to the closest residue within a predicted protein–protein interface region) (Methods). We designated SNVs in low-DTPPI regions (DTPPI < 10 Å) or low-DTL regions (DTL < 15 Å) as structurally important28,29,30,31,32. Out of 3,705 SNVs, 752 (20.3%) were structurally important by these criteria, including 246 and 528 SNVs affecting amino acid residues in low-DTL and low-DTPPI regions, respectively (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Table 17). These SNVs were associated with 40 different phenotypes (Fig. 5b,c).
