#1305. Portuguese Journalist Makes Bombshell Claim About Cristiano Ronaldo’s Retirement

The farewell Cristiano Ronaldo had envisioned for when he finally waved goodbye to international football with Portugal hasn't quite gone like the fairytale many expected.

Having hoped to hang up his international boots with a World Cup under his belt, things instead ended in tears for the 41-year-old, who spent the final month of his international career at loggerheads with new manager Jorge Jesus, received a fine for his public outburst and was subsequently handed a ban.

The Euro 2016 winner seemingly left it too late to call time on his international career, finding it increasingly difficult to accept that he was no longer the same player who had claimed five Ballon d'Or titles during his spells at Real Madrid and Manchester United.

But now, his farewell could be set for an even more sorrowful twist, should the bombshell claims made by a Portuguese journalist about plans for his send-off prove to be true.

Journalist Pedro Sepulveda told talkSPORT that Jesus had intended to call-up Ronaldo during the next international break, in an attempt to rebuild bridges, after the Al-Nassr superstar was left fuming over a decision that saw him benched during a 2-1 win against Norway and did not come on.

Sepulveda now claims that Ronaldo is still so caught up in that drama that the then-captain will be blocked from having a farewell match, though it might be because he doesn't want to either. He said:

“I can guarantee you that Ronaldo won't dress officially, let's say like that, in the Portuguese jersey again. I can guarantee you that until Jorge Jesus leaves the national team of Portugal that last friendly game for everyone to say goodbye to Cristiano Ronaldo won't happen.”

Ronaldo's exit comes after he dramatically fell out with Portugal boss Jorge Jesus.

He added: “The thing is, Ronaldo feels that he wanted to retire after the World Cup. He made that decision and then Pedro Proenca, the new president of the federation, with Jorge Jesus, they both convinced him to stay. In the head of Ronaldo, after they convinced him, they took the decision to make this to Ronaldo without defending him.”

That would be in stark contrast to his Argentine adversary, Lionel Messi, who played his 208th and final international match in Buenos Aires in October.

Interestingly, the journalist's comments seem to contradict the Portugal FA's initial statement, which concludes: “Cristiano Ronaldo has elevated Portugal’s name and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps, being, for many of us, the best player of all time!

“Therefore, the Portuguese Football Federation refuses to let this farewell take place without due tribute. It is our firm and immense desire to organise, plan, participate and actively collaborate in what will always be a fitting tribute to Cristiano Ronaldo’s immense career, in which fans and the country can applaud and celebrate, once again, the player who has given us so much.”

A date, time, and official agreement has not yet been reached as rumours of Ronaldo's desire not to take part in another game continuing to flutter. But as Portugal's greatest-ever player, and up there among the best players in world football, it would surely be inconceivable that CR7 doesn't get a proper goodbye.

#1304. Newcastle jeers tell Matthias Jaissle his ‘vertical’ football is not working

Newcastle United look like a poor team playing badly. The evidence is increasingly damning after Matthias Jaissle’s side were loudly booed off at the end of this limp defeat.

This has all the makings of a long, hard season. Anger is already rising to the surface, even though Jaissle claimed Newcastle deserved more from a game they “controlled” in the first half and “dominated” in the second. Those comments jarred with what we had just seen.

After four years of enjoying an upward trajectory under Eddie Howe, the team faded last season, sold their best players in the summer, lost the manager and there is no evidence yet they have replaced anything with better.

This was supposed to be a reaction to the embarrassing 4-1 thrashing at Coventry City, but it led to another loss and, in the first half at least, another abject display. Aston Villa were always the more fluent and more threatening. They should have won by more than just Johan Manzambi’s first-half header.

Johan Manzambi heads Aston Villa in front! 🟣 https://t.co/jxZf2568Sl

It is getting hard to comprehend what Jaissle wants his team to do. The much-hyped “vertical” style looks like an ugly incarnation of the long ball football of yesteryear. They did not like it at Newcastle in the 1980s and 1990s and some fashions should never return. It is in danger of resembling a shell suit that has emerged from the back of the wardrobe for a Saturday night out.

There is so much confidence in the German in the Newcastle boardroom that they believe improvement is inevitable, but that is far from assured. Newcastle are not getting better; they are making all the same mistakes and, if anything, as an attacking force, they are looking increasingly stale and predictable. They did not have a shot on target in the first half and, other than one fantastic save in the second, Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki had nothing to do.

"If he doesn't slip Harvey Barnes in, he's got to hit the target" Shay Given discusses Newcastle's decision-making in the final third 🔲 https://t.co/wh4kCAEbxV

It is time for a sharp dose of medicine on Tyneside. Expectations need to be adjusted, especially as none of the new signings have impressed. This was always the fear and the risk when you put all your faith in young players from abroad.

For Jaissle’s vertical football to work, Newcastle need to be able to win the ball high up the pitch, whether that is with a high press or competing for second balls from long passes. They do not do either well. More worryingly, they look so vulnerable, so easy to play through.

Villa did it to them all afternoon. Nicolas Jackson should have scored in the first half, Ibrahim Mbaye should have hit the target in the second.

#1303. Official: Latest Italy U21 squad includes Inacio, Mane, Lulli and Bartesaghi

Silvio Baldini has named a squad of 26 Italy U21 players including the likes of Samuele Inacio, Filippo Mane, Emanuele Lulli and Davide Bartesaghi for a pair of international friendlies against France and Belgium in November, as the Azzurrini prepare for the European Championships coming up this summer.

Like the senior Italy squad, the U21s will also be in action against France and Belgium in November, although the Azzurrini will face France away and Belgium at home: The opposite of the senior Azzurri squad.

These will both be friendly matches, following the completion of U21 European Championship qualifying last month.

The Italy U21s beat Armenia 1-0 last month, before an important 6-2 victory over Poland, which saw the Azzurrini leapfrog their opponents into first place in their qualifying group, earning them a guaranteed spot at the final tournament in the process.

The latest Italy U21 squad features several players who have returned after being named in the senior squad last month: Massimo Pessina, Eddy Kouadio and Inacio.

The squad also features a handful of players who had been considered for the senior squad this time around, but have been left with the U21s for another camp, including Milan’s Bartesaghi and Roma’s Lulli. Cher Ndour has also stayed with the U21s.

Regular centre-forward Antonio Raimondo is unavailable through injury. There are still several other Frosinone representatives, though, namely Lorenzo Palmisani, Gabriele Calvani, Matteo Cichella and Seydou Fini.

Luca Koleosho, a regular fixture of the U21 side during their European Championship qualifying campaign, has been promoted to the senior squad for November.

#1302. Ex-Man Utd Ace Apologises For Mason Greenwood Comments

Former Manchester United defender Clayton Blackmore has issued a public apology after sparking a backlash with comments about Mason Greenwood. The 25-year-old scored for Fenerbahce against Liverpool this week.

The Turkish giants beat their English opposition 3-2 in the Champions League, with Greenwood deflected equaliser levelling the scores after Trey Nyoni had opened the scoring. Alexander Isak then put Liverpool ahead in the 69th minute, but goals from Archie Brown and Vedat Muriqi saw Fenerbahce come away with all three points.

Greenwood joined the Istanbul-based club this summer, having spent the past two seasons in France with Marseille. He came through the Man Utd academy but left in 2024, two years after being arrested on suspicion of sexual assault.

Despite the circumstances around Greenwood's move away from the Premier League, former Wales and Man Utd defender Blackmore seemed desperate for the English winger to make a return to Old Trafford. He wrote on social media:

"Well done Mason Greenwood [for] beating Liverpool. Come home to us please."

The comments drew a lot of attention on social media as Blackmore – who played 241 times for the Red Devils, winning the Premier League and the FA Cup under Sir Alex Ferguson in the early 1990s – was widely criticised for his post. The 62-year-old then wrote a follow-up message, stating:

"Sorry I've offended anyone but I heard he had been cleared of any wrongdoing I apologise to everyone I've upset with my comments like I said I thought he had been cleared of everything and he’s had a baby with his girlfriend. Big sorry."

Perhaps Blackmore was confused by Greenwood, who claimed he had been 'cleared of all charges' in 2023. This wasn't quite the case. Rather, the charges were dropped by the Crown Prosecution Service when witnesses withdrew their involvement and new material came to light.

Ronaldo's exit comes after he dramatically fell out with Portugal boss Jorge Jesus.

It's little wonder many fans felt uneasy with Blackmore calling for Greenwood to come back to Man Utd. Although once the most talented prospect emerging at the Carrington academy, the winger's career was derailed in 2022 amid allegations of attempted rape, controlling and coercive behaviour, and assault, per Goal.

The Crown Prosecution Service ultimately dropped all charges in early 2023, citing the withdrawal of key witnesses as new material that also came to light. After separately conducting a lengthy internal investigation, however, Man Utd decided it was best for both parties if he continued his career elsewhere. That call came amid significant pressure from fans.

Greenwood scored 35 goals in 129 games for Man Utd. He was then loaned out to Getafe in 2023/24, before being sold to Marseille. With 48 goals in 81 games for the French club, Fenerbahce spent £33.27m to sign the Englishman in July 2026. He has eight goals in his first 19 games for the Turkish team.

#1301. 18 Most Decorated Players in Football History Ranked by Trophies Won

Every football player dreams of lifting as much silverware as they can possibly get their hands on. However, some of the best players to have played the beautiful game have curiously bare-looking trophy cabinets, proving how difficult it is to win any honour in the sport.

Players such as Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi have made it look easy for many years, as the duo have led their respective teams to an unbelievable number of trophies over their long and storied careers for club and country.

Then there are players like Zlatan Ibrahimovic who, while also brilliant footballers in their own right, move around the most historically successful clubs in the world to chase silverware at will.

We've listed the most successful players in football history, based on the number of trophies they have amassed throughout their playing careers.

There's even a chance for a couple of these players to add further to their already sensational hauls.

A man who doesn't need any introduction at all. Zlatan Ibrahimovic was a serial winner wherever he went during his journeyman football career. He won trophies in five different countries: in the Netherlands with Ajax, in Italy with Inter Milan and AC Milan, in Spain with Barcelona, in France with Paris Saint-Germain, and in England with Manchester United.

The Swedish maverick won almost every trophy there was to win during his time as a footballer, apart from the ever-elusive Champions League. He would be further up this list had Juventus' Serie A titles in 2004/05 and 2005/06 not been revoked. There will be no more opportunities to add further silverware for the Swede, as he announced his retirement in 2023. A sad day for the sport, though he continues to be in and around the game as one of 10 legendary ex-footballers who now own a club.

5x (2006–07, 2007–08, 2008–09, 2010–11, 2021–22)

From England's Manchester United to Italian giants AC Milan, ChatGPT has ranked the biggest clubs in world football - in order.

A tremendous footballer, Xavi was a key cog for a Barcelona side that dominated football at the back end of the 2000s and the first half of the 2010s. He won 25 trophies during his illustrious 17-year stint in Barcelona's first team, including four Champions League titles, with his tiki-taka brilliance alongside Andres Iniesta not going unnoticed.

He also guided Spain to success in back-to-back European Championships (2008 and 2012) as well as the 2010 World Cup. Xavi became a manager after hanging up his boots and led Barcelona to a La Liga title from the dugout rather than in the middle of the park, before being replaced by Hansi Flick. In his twilight years, he moved to Al Saad in Qatar and added four more trophies to his tally, and has recently taken on a new role in international football as the Netherlands' helmsman.

8x (1998–99, 2004–05, 2005–06, 2008–09, 2009–10, 2010–11, 2012–13, 2014–15)

Winning trophies isn’t for everyone, but to do it with such poise and know-how as Luka Modric has done over the years is commendable. Between 2005/06 and 2007/08, the Croat won everything there was to win domestically with Dinamo Zagreb before enduring a trophy-less four-year stint with Tottenham Hotspur.

A move to Real Madrid beckoned - and the rest is history, as they say. Having picked up a handful of trophies since arriving in 2012, the one-time Ballon d’Or winner has won the Champions League six times, La Liga on four occasions and is a five-time Spanish Super Cup winner. Poised to collect more before hanging up his boots, the 41-year-old is a bona fide winner – and will hope to lift more silverware now at AC Milan.

5x (2012–13, 2017–18, 2019–20, 2021–22, 2023–24)

5x (2014–15, 2016–17, 2017–18, 2022–23, 2024-25)

6x (2013–14, 2015–16, 2016–17, 2017–18, 2021–22, 2023–24)

A cool and collected figure in the Real Madrid engine room, Toni Kroos waltzed himself onto the list with 34 trophies to boot. Impressively, six of those are Champions Leagues - five of which have been secured in Spain. Even while at Bayern Munich, the midfielder was somewhat of a serial winner.

GIVEMESPORT Key Statistic: Toni Kroos is one of five players to have won six Champions League titles, joining Luka Modric, Nacho Fernandez, Dani Carvajal and Paco Gento.

He collected three Bundesliga titles in six years, alongside a UEFA Super Cup and three German Cups. Unlike many players on this list, Griefswald-born Kroos is also a World Cup winner with Germany. Fittingly, in his final game for Los Blancos, the German midfielder won yet another Champions League title. What a fantastic player.

5x (2013–14, 2014–15, 2016–17, 2017–18, 2022–23)

6x (2012–13, 2015–16, 2016–17, 2017–18, 2021–22, 2023–24)

The 10 footballers who have claimed the most individual awards during their illustrious careers

Maxwell’s legacy is a curious one. That he has won 35 titles in his career is fascinating. That he barely registers as one of football’s all-time greats is even more so. But perhaps that's down to the fact the clubs he played for often flattered him, with stints at Paris Saint-Germain, Barcelona, Inter Milan, and Ajax seeing him stay in cruise control while mopping up almost every honour available to him.

With just 10 Brazil caps to his name, he was never the star of any show. But with a remarkable 11 league titles and a Champions League to his name, the retired left-back probably won't care that much.

Mr. Bayern Munich himself, Thomas Muller made 756 appearances for Die Roten, scoring 250 goals, providing 285 assists, and playing a pivotal role in 13 Bundesliga titles and two Champions League triumphs. He also ranks among the top for most assists in World Cup history, having helped Germany secure the 2014 World Cup.

What's more, the understated workhorse is in the top 20 all-time Champions League goal scorers, while he also has the same number of assists in Europe’s leading club competition as Xavi. Taking those goals and assists into consideration, Muller is definitely one of the most underrated players in football history. But what he lacks in individual accolades, he most certainly makes up for in team honours. Indeed, Muller won his 35th title in October 2025, as he helped new club Vancouver Whitecaps to the Canadian Championship.

13x (2009-10, 2010-11, 2011-12, 2012-13, 2014-15, 2015-16, 2016-17, 2017-18, 2019-20, 2020-21, 2021-22, 2022-23, 2024-25)

8x (2010–11, 2012–13, 2016–17, 2017–18, 2018-19, 2020-21, 2021-22, 2022-23)

6x (2009–10, 2012–13, 2013–14, 2015-16, 2018-19, 2019-20)

Ryan Giggs' longevity was something else, and it will perhaps never be seen again in the rough and tuble of English football. The Welshman started off as a tricky winger with electric pace and then transitioned into a playmaker in his latter years, allowing him to play a key role for Manchester United until he hung up his boots at the age of 40.

Giggs spent his whole 24-year professional career at the Red Devils, where he won 35 trophies. His 13 Premier League titles is a record that may never be beaten. A large part of the winger's success at Old Trafford came through the trust shown in him by Sir Alex Ferguson for so many years. That faith certainly paid off, and he was a key figure under the guise of his manager's reign of terror.

13x (1992–93, 1993–94, 1995–96, 1996–97, 1998–99, 1999–2000, 2000–01, 2002–03, 2006–07, 2007–08, 2008–09, 2010–11, 2012–13)

9x (1993, 1994, 1996, 1997, 2003, 2007, 2008, 2010, 2013)

'King Kenny' established himself as a Celtic and Liverpool legend during his career as a professional footballer. After winning 11 trophies in Scotland, Kenny Dalglish moved to Liverpool where he won everything there was to win, including six First Division titles and three European Cup trophies.

Modern fans may know him better as the man who guided Blackburn Rovers to the Premier League title in 1994/95, but Dalglish was a serial winner during his playing days. To this day, he is regarded as one of Liverpool's greatest-ever players, which is quite a compliment with the wealth of talent to have performed and lifted trophies in front of the Anfield faithful, and he also became a pretty successful manager after that as well, winning a further four league titles (though they are not counted in the glorious table below).

6x (1978–79, 1979–80, 1981–82, 1982–83, 1983–84, 1985–86)

When you think of the greatest midfielders in the past 30 years, Andres Iniesta is a name that immediately springs to mind. The midfield maestro won everything there was to win during a 16-year spell in Barcelona's first-team, including nine La Liga titles and four Champions Leagues. His greatest moment came in the 2010 World Cup final when he scored a dramatic 116th-minute winner for Spain against the Netherlands.

Iniesta announced his retirement in October 2024, describing his decision as "the most difficult of my life". What's next for him remains to be seen, but it's possible that we'll see him involved in coaching in some capacity in the near future, like many of his Catalan teammates.

9x (2004–05, 2005–06, 2008–09, 2009–10, 2010–11, 2012–13, 2014–15, 2015–16, 2017–18)

6x (2008–09, 2011–12, 2014–15, 2015–16, 2016–17, 2017–18)

Cristiano Ronaldo moved further up the list after securing his second UEFA Nations League title with Portugal. The Al-Nassr forward scored Portugal's all-important equaliser against Spain before being substituted through injury. However, his teammates won the penalty shootout, and helped to deliver Ronaldo his third piece of international silverware.

The five-time Champions League winner has an incredible appetite to succeed and that has not waned despite now being 41 years old. The Portuguese footballer is still going strong despite his advancing years, and you wouldn't bet against him moving even further up this list at some point in the next couple of seasons as his longevity continues to shock the world, even after having decided to hang up hbis boots for the final time with Portugal.

5x (2007–08, 2013–14, 2015–16, 2016–17, 2017–18)

#1300. 'It's not a concern': Why Enzo Maresca will stick with 'awe-inspiring' Gianluigi Donnarumma despite Leipzig horror show, growing catalogue of errors and a worrying downward trend

Published: 12:00 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 12:00 EDT, 5 November 2026

There was a Manchester City fan on Thursday’s Ryanair flight back home from Leipzig wearing a Gianluigi Donnarumma sticker on his coat, portraying the Italian as Don Vito Corleone. The sticker, a bit worn and a bit crumpled, was peeling off. A metaphor exists within that somewhere.

Tough times for Donnarumma, a calamitous night in the Champions League – beaten at his near post by Ridle Baku's cross for one goal, fumbling another routine effort at the feet of a striker and allowing a straightforward shot to squirm through his fingers – just adding to the feeling that the past few weeks have not reflected kindly on him.

Question marks around Donnarumma’s suitability between the sticks are becoming more pronounced after a catalogue of mistakes this season. One against Paris Saint-Germain when Maghnes Akliouche’s shot was too hot (some would argue two after neglecting his near post for Desire Doue’s opener) and then Nicolas Jackson shooting through him at Aston Villa last month.

Each time, Enzo Maresca has publicly recognised the errors and intimated that nobody needs to rake over them in detail with his No1, who is experienced enough to know he must do better.

Now Leipzig. ‘It’s not a concern,’ Maresca said of the latest gaffe. The manager’s defences of Donnarumma are racking up and what City are witnessing is fundamental problems from somebody described as the best the world has to offer.

Maresca has rejected the idea that summer signing Geronimo Rulli, a 34-year-old Argentina international, could take over the gloves, claiming that City line-ups are always ‘Gigio plus 10’. Rulli understood his lot when joining from Marseille, to feature in domestic cup competitions, and was happy with that.

Gianluigi Donnarumma had a night to forget in Leipzig this week, making at least three individual errors

But Man City boss Enzo Maresca will stand by his goalkeeper, claiming that City line-ups are always ‘Gigio plus 10’

Happy in a way that James Trafford was not, after making it clear that one season as Donnarumma’s understudy was not palatable.

He has flourished at Leeds United so far this season, leading to some observers criticising Hugo Viana for letting him go, only to blunder for a goal at Bournemouth last weekend. Worth remembering that it does happen to all of them at some point.

Trafford did not appear ready for the big time last year when starting the season ahead of the wantaway Ederson and City had their eyes on Donnarumma months before landing him – a £26million deal struck just as Ederson left for Fenerbahce.

Trafford will be ready soon and is pushing Jordan Pickford hard to be England's No1, but definitely wasn’t back then.

With Trafford gone and Maresca seemingly ruling out his No2 taking over – while also making a vague reference to taking stock over the international break – it appears that City would have no option but to stick with Donnarumma if they did actually want to bring about a change. January signings seem remote in the current climate of guilty verdicts and appeals.

But there is something outstanding that Donnarumma does offer, one that does set him apart. Maresca categorised the stunning one-handed save from Leipzig’s Christoph Baumgartner as one nobody else could make.

And while some hyperbole might be at play there, very few could lay claim to producing that kind of moment on a semi-regular basis.

Repelling Baumgartner is up there with Donnarumma’s instinctive save from Bryan Mbeumo at a crucial juncture on debut last year and thwarting Alexis Mac Allister in a victory at Anfield. The sort of awe-inspiring saves thousands pay money to witness.

Very few goalkeepers can claim to make wonder-saves as regularly as Donnarumma does

Donnarumma's impressive shot-stopping in the Premier League is evidenced by this graphic of every shot he has faced since joining City (red circles = goals, blank circles = saves)

Nobody across the Premier League has a higher save percentage than Donnarumma’s 71.5 since his arrival from PSG. More scientifically, only Bart Verbruggen and Senne Lammens have prevented more goals in that time – a metric measured by the xG of shots compared to how many goals were conceded.

Donnarumma has prevented seven goals (1.4 this season), with Brighton’s Verbruggen at 9.7 and Manchester United's Lammens at 8.1 across the same period. These are broadly encouraging numbers for City, despite Donnarumma's save percentage dipping to 69.7 this season – eighth among his peers, with Trafford way out in front on 79.5.

City will need to keep a careful eye on that downward trend from a 27-year-old who they brought to the club to act as the anchor, to bail them out in a way that Ederson struggled. That was the trade-off for his limited footwork, being incapable of playing through the opposition lines in a way the Brazilian could.

The wonder saves cancel all of that out. Donnarumma has been the goalkeeper’s goalkeeper for those alone. But were the certainty around that aspect of his game to waver on a longer-term basis, City should have decisions to make.

#1299. Italy confirm Cassano and Lontani will not earn debuts in November despite first call-ups

Roberto Mancini has named Como and Parma teenagers Riccardo Cassano and Simone Lontani in his Italy national team squad for November’s Nations League fixtures, but the FIGC has confirmed that they will both be with the senior side for a few days before returning to the U18s and U19s squads.

Mancini announced his squad of 31 Italy national team players on Thursday evening: The Azzurri will be in action against France in San Siro next Thursday, November 12, and away against Belgium on Sunday, November 15.

As things stand, Italy sit in second place in their Nations League group on seven points after four matches. France lead the way on 10, Belgium are in third on six and Turkiye are bottom on zero.

Among the surprise selections were 17-year-old Cassano, who has not yet featured competitively at club level for Como, and 18-year-old Lontani, who has just 10 Serie A appearances, but three league goals to his name with Parma.

The FIGC has confirmed that both players have been called up so that Mancini can have an up-close look at them for the first few days of the training camp. However, Cassano will then return to the U18s squad and Lontani to the U19s after the first few days.

“As for Cassano and Lontani, Mancini wanted to call them up to have the opportunity to observe them closely and to give them a valuable opportunity to impress: They will not remain attached to the group for the duration of the camp.” the FIGC confirmed in their statement announcing the latest Italy squad.

“Instead, they will join the U18 and U19 teams, engaged respectively in the World Cup starting on November 19 in Qatar and the second phase of European Championship qualifiers scheduled for November 11 until November 17.”

Peter Young is a Senior Reporter with Football Italia.

#1298. Pierre Sage fears for his Crystal Palace future after Brighton humiliation

Pierre Sage has admitted that he fears for his future at Crystal Palace, adding that he felt “shame” after his side slumped to their joint-heaviest defeat by rivals Brighton and Hove Albion.

Sage replaced Oliver Glasner as manager in June but since then Palace have won just two league matches with him in at the helm. The south London club have taken seven points from seven Premier League games and have already conceded 17 goals, the most of any team in the league.

“I don’t know,” Sage said when asked if he will get enough time to rectify Palace’s slump. He admitted that his shame was about how Palace were overwhelmed, leaking three goals within the first nine minutes of the game before eventually losing 5-0.

“We are not at the level we expected, and I’m really sorry for that,” the 47-year-old said. “I just want to apologise to the fans because it’s not normal to show this face.”

The Frenchman said that he took full responsibility for the 5-0 defeat, and understood why hundreds of Palace fans left well before the final whistle.

“I cannot blame anybody because we didn’t do the job in a good way,” he said. “I’m responsible for this team, and when the team play as today, it’s not normal. It’s my fault. I understand them.

“Another feeling is about shame because that’s my feeling after the game and from the beginning. It’s not normal to not respect the necessary of this kind of game.”

Sage admitted that he will be assessing how Palace need to rethink their approach in the coming fixtures, beginning with Thursday’s trip to Besiktas in the Europa League.

“The first work to do is on me,” he said. “I’m responsible for what’s happened on the pitch, and I have a lot of work to do because I have to change this kind of thing.

“It’s maybe in the preparation, in the way we give them the motivation to start the game just before in the locker room in the warm-up. We have to analyse that because it’s not normal. And today it was really at the highest level we cannot expect, and that’s the moment to change the thing.”

For all the scrutiny on his back three, Sage urged his entire side to take greater defensive responsibility, highlighting how the team were too passive in pressing Brighton. Palace have struggled to regain the solidity that long characterised the side since the departures of Marc Guéhi in January and Maxence Lacroix this summer.

“The way of defending is not only on the back three; it is for every player, and there are some things to do collectively, too,” Sage said. “When we defend low we struggle a lot.”

Sage joined Palace after a fine campaign with Lens. He led the club to second place in Ligue 1, just six points off Paris St-Germain, and victory in the Coupe de France. Yet, despite Sage’s reputation when he moved to Selhurst Park, his suitability for the Palace job is increasingly being questioned.

Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Sage could suffer the same fate, with doubts growing that he will still be in charge for Thursday’s trip to Besiktas.

“It’s not my decision,” Sage said. “I don’t want to accept the level of the moment if we are able to do better. And today the work is really important to do, and I will do it. It’s my job, and I’d like to change this.”

With only Manchester City and Arsenal above them, Brighton and Hove Albion are entitled to dream of making history. Yet, whatever happens between now and May, one accolade is already surely their own: the goal of the season award.

Diego Gómez’s 56-yard strike will instantly become the stuff of Brighton lore. The Paraguayan’s audacity will be even more cherished for coming against Crystal Palace, who were pummelled 5-0 in the M23 derby.

All Premier League defeats are equal but some are more equal than others. Three years ago, Patrick Vieira lost his job after a defeat by Brighton. Now, Pierre Sage is at grave risk of suffering the same fate. Naturally, Brighton fans revelled in reminding him of this threat as the final whistle approached.Palace were so ragged that their performance felt like a defeat that marks the end of a managerial reign. Even stand-in captain Adam Wharton was guilty of dawdling and losing the ball in possession. Hundreds of away supporters left well before the full-time whistle and those who remained booed all players bar Jefferson Lerma.

With less venom in attack, especially with Ismaïla Sarr being an unused substitute, Palace’s sole chance lay in counter-attacking. This strategy disintegrated in the fourth minute, when Jaydee Canvot headed Pascal Gross’s free-kick into his own net.

But the hint of self-immolation in Palace’s display should not obscure the swagger of Brighton’s performance. Despite losing Danny Welbeck, last year’s top scorer, Brighton have scored 23 goals already this Premier League campaign, the most in the league. This tally includes one of the most extraordinary goals in Premier League history.

Most simply, Gómez’s goal, which put Brighton 2-0 up in the seventh minute, was a triumph of the imagination. Receiving a short pass from Olivier Boscagli just inside his own half, Gómez could have sought to pick out a team-mate. Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the M23 derby – or El Gatwicko, as the kids call it these days – as high-flying Brighton and Hove Albion host Crystal Palace at the Amex Stadium. Being frank, this is neither the fiercest nor the most storied Premier League rivalry, but few would have imagined when these sides faced off in the Third Division in the mid-1970s that this would ever become a top-flight match-up sandwiched between European games.

Brighton have been outstanding this season and took their league form into the Conference League, thrashing Lithuanian champions Kauno Zalgiris on Thursday night. Fabian Hürzeler was delighted by his fringe players’ performances on Thursday night and may have some selection questions to answer with Jack Hinshelwood and Georginio Rutter finding the net. Brighton are third in the Premier League and were the division’s heaviest scorers after the last round of matches.

Yet the Palace nut has been a tough one to crack for Hürzeler, having not yet registered a win in four attempts. When asked what he enjoyed most about the rivalry, the German said: “Nothing yet, because I didn’t win any games so far. Hopefully on Sunday this changes… I like these games because they’re derbies, more emotions, it’s a rivalry, it’s [us] against Crystal Palace.”

In his pre-match interview Hürzeler admitted to being an admirer of Pierre Sage, and while the Frenchman’s side have failed to match Brighton’s fast start, they rallied impressively to defeat rivals Nottingham Forest last weekend and fought back valiantly away at Lyon, albeit in a losing effort, in midweek. The return of Ismaïla Sarr from injury is a significant boost.

Elsewhere Bournemouth host Sunderland hoping to secure their first Premier League victory of the season. Marco Rose’s side and Tottenham are the only teams still without a win, but Bournemouth have been perfect in the Europa League and will look to transfer some of that momentum into the league. Sunderland scored late to win away at Portuguese side Torreense.

You can also follow the latest updates from Manchester United’s crucial trip to Elland Road in our sister blog here.

#1297. Allan Saint-Maximin Leads Very Different Life Away From Football

In England, Premier League fans will best remember Allan Saint-Maximin for his time at Newcastle United between 2019 and 2023. These days, the French winger plays for MLS club Charlotte FC, but – away from football – he has a very different life going on at the same time.

Saint-Maximin scored 13 goals and claimed 21 assists in 124 games for Newcastle. More than his stats, though, the winger caught the eye with his electric style of play. This helped him earn a £23m move Al-Ahli in 2023, but he's career since then has been that of a journeyman.

He was loaned out to Turkish side Fenerbahce after just one season in Saudi, and then joined Club América in Mexico one summer later. By February, he was sold to Lens, but only months later joined Charlotte in the United States.

With two goals and four assists in his first 15 games for the MLS club, he's settling in steadily enough, but the 29-year-old had reasons away from football to be content with his prospects right now anyway.

The 28-year-old has issued a statement following his sudden exit on Saturday.

As revealed in an interview with The Athletic, Saint-Maximin recently had the chance to make millions from his venture outside of football. The business in question is known as Helios, which is a Greek mythology-inspired card game created by the former Newcastle man.

The MLS star has claimed that he received a £22m (€26m) offer for the business, but turned it down as he wants to continue growing his free-to-play game. He explained:

“The journey is not about money. It’s to create something, to create jobs for people, to create opportunities.”

Saint-Maximin added that, despite rejecting the offer, he would prefer to bring in others to work alongside him, each taking a stake in the company in return for their investment.

It's not the first time he's spoken about Helios, named after the sun god. In 2022, he explained how he grew up with an interest in Greek mythology. This inspired him to combine his love for board games with the topic and create the game. He would even take it on team buses when travelling to away games.

"When I was young, I learned about Zeus and Athena and saw a lot of films and anime movies with them in," he said. "When you start to understand it, you really love it.”

According to Helios' official rulebook, the aim of the game is to win by earning coins or stealing them from your opponent. Saint-Maximin explained how he developed it, adding: “There was a lot of work, a lot of nights, because you need to come up with a new idea.

"I tested it with friends. We started to play small tournaments at home. It took two and a half years — but I am really happy that I didn’t stop.”

These days, his company appears to be going from strength to strength, and could even one day put him among footballers who have become successful businessmen

The Rossoneri had their confidence restored by Saturday’s 3-1 Derby della Madonnina victory, but were trailing in Europe after losing two of the first three games. Mike Maignan was sent off in the 3-0 defeat at Bournemouth, so was suspended here and third choice Lorenzo Torriani stepped in, with Pietro Terracciano, Fikayo Tomori, Matteo Gabbia, Samuel Chukwueze, Ruben Loftus-Cheek and Alexis Saelemaekers injured, plus Strahinja Pavlovic rested after playing almost every minute this season.

Ferencvaros had a perfect Europa League record after beating Celtic, Viktoria Plzen and Torreense, but missed Krisztian Lisztes, Franko Kovacevic and Daniel Radnoti, with Gergo Szecsi, Bence Otvos, Barnabas Nagy and Isaac Pappoe ineligible.

The Hungarians started the better team and tested Torriani with a Kristoffer Zachariassen angled drive, but Ardon Jashari almost gifted them the opener with a misplaced back-pass to send Lenny Joseph clear, the striker scuffing the finish one-on-one with Torriani.

Milan’s first chance was on 39 minutes with Alphadjo Cisse unable to keep the half-volley down on a Goncalo Ramos knockdown from 12 yards, but Joseph tested Torriani at the near post after blazing past Sankhoun Diawara.

Torriani was again forced into a tough save on the Joseph angled drive from 10 yards at the end of a very sluggish first half performance.

Ruben Amorim was as unimpressed as the fans, so made a triple substitution at the break, introducing Christian Pulisic, Diego Moreira and Mario Gila.

They seemed immediately brighter, Omari Hutchinson hitting the side-netting from a tricky angle and Goncalo Ramos with an effort deflected wide.

However, it was Ferencvaros who broke the deadlock when Torriani had a heavy touch, Zachariassen tried to pounce and was perhaps fouled by the goalkeeper, but Joseph turned the loose ball into the empty net to resolve the situation. The defending was again sluggish with nobody warning Torriani that he was under pressure.

Hutchinson’s angled drive shaved a coat of paint off the far post, while Diego Moreira caused problems with a couple of cross-shots and a curler over the bar.

Just as they were pouring forward, they left huge gaps in defence and were caught out on another rapid counter-attack. Zachariasson sprinted from his own half and drew out Torriani, laying it off for the simple Joseph tap-in.

Francesco Camarda came on and turned wide of the near post on a Diego Moreira roll across from the left.

Zachariasson was a constant danger, forcing a great one-handed Torriani save at the near post, and the Gomez free header inches over on the resulting corner.

Ferencvaros went down to 10 men, as Bamidele Yusuf foolishly raised an elbow to Mario Gila’s face in an off the ball incident that was spotted by VAR.

Milan tried to take advantage, but Denes Dibusz stuck out a boot to parry the Hutchinson low drive.

Down to 10 men, Ferencvaros nearly scored a third in stoppages with Madarasz unable to make the most of another defensive error, hitting the side-netting.

#1295. Can Portugal Retire Cristiano Ronaldo’s No.7 Shirt

Many wondered if this news would ever come, but yes, Cristiano Ronaldo has finally retired from international football. Now 41, the veteran forward has played his final game for Portugal.

The Al-Nassr star bows out with 146 goals in 234 caps for his country, having also won Euro 2016. In his departing message, he said: "To the Portuguese people, the day has come to return the number 7 jersey of our national team. I never felt it was exclusively mine. But for 23 years I had the privilege and responsibility of wearing it, defending it, and taking it with me to stadiums all over the world. Today the moment has come to hand it over to the future. It wasn't an easy decision, because there are decisions that aren't made only with the head. They are also made with the heart."

For club and country, the number seven shirt has become synonymous with Ronaldo. As such, despite his claims that it's 'time to return the jersey,' some are wondering if Portugal will instead retire the number as an acknowledgement of his special career.

However, it might not be quite so simple as just making one decision.

The 41-year-old has retired from international football, havign scored a record 146 goals in 234 Portugal caps.

A little-known FIFA rule stops international shirt numbers from being retired. Ronaldo actually started out wearing No.16 when he made his debut in 2003, but was handed the No.7 shirt in 2008. He wore it as he lifted Euro 2016 and two Nations League titles, while also becoming the all-time men’s international top goalscorer.

Had he achieved that level of success at a club team, maybe he would have seen the shirt number retired. Johan Cruyff (14 at Ajax), Paolo Maldini (3 at AC Milan), and Franco Baresi (6 also at Milan) are all among the legendary footballers to have had their shirt numbers retired, while Liverpool paid respect to Diogo Jota by retiring his No.20 jersey after his tragic passing in 2025.

Ronaldo, though, will have to pass on the number seven shirt to another Portuguese star. This is because national teams are required to designate consecutive numbers for every player in the squad for FIFA and FIFA confederation tournaments. At the 2026 World Cup, for example, sides were made up of 26 players, meaning squad numbers had to go from 1 to 26. As such, it would be a breach of rules to skip past the number seven on a tournament-going squad list.

Perhaps this isn't the worst rule in the world. After all, Argentina once tried to retire the No.10 shirt in honour of World Cup-winning great Diego Maradona. They had a request denied by FIFA ahead of the 2002 World Cup, but the number was fittingly later won by Lionel Messi, who would win the 2022 World Cup and match his predecessor's legacy.

Despite also having many past greats, Portugal have never requested to retire a number before. Ballon d'Or winner Luis Figo used to wear No.7, while the likes of Nani and Ricardo Quaresma even donned it while Ronaldo was absent.

It's worth noting that when Ronaldo quit the Portugal camp early in September, Rafael Leao took on the vacant No.7 shirt for the two remaining Nations League fixtures. It remains to be seen if he will wear that number in the upcoming break later this month.

#1294. Venousization enables angiogenesis in the absence of VEGFR signalling

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) ligand and its main receptor VEGFR2 are considered to be essential for endothelial differentiation, proliferation, sprouting and survival1. Blood vessels cannot form in growing embryos or tissues when VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling is compromised in all cells2,3. The anti-VEGF antibody, which can block angiogenesis in cancer, wound healing or ischaemic diseases, is among the most widely used antibodies in the clinic. However, vascular resistance to anti-VEGF therapy has been reported4,5. Here we used iFlpMosaics and iSuRe–HadCre to induce and track genetic mosaics of endothelial cells (ECs) lacking VEGFR2 during the entire embryonic and postnatal development. These Vegfr2-knockout (Vegfr2KO) ECs adapted, proliferated normally and competed with wild-type cells over time, eventually forming a substantial portion of the vascular network in most organs. Vegfr2KO ECs could not sprout during the first wave of angiogenesis in most tissues, because this process is highly VEGF-dependent and favours growth and mobilization of wild-type ECs. However, owing to their inability to respond to VEGF, Vegfr2KO ECs became dominant in veins, which represented a long-term and continuous source of ECs for subsequent waves of VEGF-independent angiogenesis. Comparative single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of ECs with acute and long-term loss of VEGFR2 identified both common and organ-specific molecular mechanisms of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss. These included significant endothelial venousization and upregulation of ligands for VEGFR1 and VEGFR3. VEGFR1 only partially compensated for VEGFR2 loss in capillary ECs, whereas VEGFR3 compensated only in arterial ECs. Loss of the three VEGF receptors did not compromise venous growth. Notably, loss of the master regulator of venous development, NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), significantly compromised expansion of Vegfr2KO ECs. This work has implications for our understanding of the role of VEGF receptors in angiogenesis and demonstrates venousization as a mechanism of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss during angiogenesis.

VEGF is frequently targeted in clinical settings to suppress tumour angiogenesis, metastasis and retina disease6. However, resistance to VEGF-blocking antibodies arises over time, which limits the effectiveness of such treatments4,5,7,8. By contrast, resistance to loss of VEGF signalling has not been reported during physiological vascular development.

Embryos or postnatal tissues lacking activity of the VEGF signalling pathway in all cells fail to develop vessels3. VEGFR2 (encoded by the Kdr (also known as Vegfr2) gene in mice) is the most important VEGF receptor and has been shown to be essential for angiogenesis in all vascular development contexts studied so far1,9. Germline mutants for this gene completely lack blood vessels and die very early during embryonic development2, and mouse embryos chimeras formed by wild-type and Vegfr2-knockout (Vegfr2KO) progenitor cells cannot form endothelial cells (ECs)10. Conditional deletion of Vegfr2 with Tie2–Cre after endothelial differentiation11, or in postnatal tissues with Cdh5–CreERT2, also strongly impairs angiogenesis12, without any evidence of genetic compensation or resistance.

Despite a large body of literature showing that VEGFR2 is essential for endothelial differentiation, proliferation, migration and survival, previous studies involving deletion of Vegfr2 in all ECs (Vegfr2iDEC) during embryonic or postnatal organ development could only analyse its effect on angiogenesis for a relatively short period of time. Its essential role in vascular development and hence in tissue development and organ function causes severe impairment of angiogenesis and premature lethality of Vegfr2iDEC embryos and postnatal animals; thus, such studies have been unable to determine whether ECs can adapt to loss of VEGFR2 over time or make certain organ vascular beds in the complete absence of VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling.

Here we used iFlpMosaics13 and iSuRe–HadCre14 to mosaically induce and longitudinally track Vegfr2KO ECs, enabling us to assess the role of this gene during the entire embryonic and postnatal vascular development of different organs. We found that despite its essential role during the initial wave of embryonic and postnatal angiogenesis, VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling is dispensable for many subsequent angiogenic processes originating from veins. Vegfr2KO ECs expand and out-compete wild-type ECs in venous vessels, which serve as a continuous source of these mutant cells for angiogenesis in most organs. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) showed that Vegfr2KO ECs adapt over time through upregulation of ligands for other VEGF receptors and through increased expression of venous-specific genes, particularly Nr2f2. Targeting these adaptive and resistance-associated molecular mechanisms prevents expansion of ECs following prolonged loss of VEGFR2 signalling.

Given the essential role of VEGFR2 in early angiogenesis and embryonic development, we induced mosaic loss of VEGFR2 with iFlpMosaics13 to investigate whether mutant cells could adapt and form new vessels over time. This technology enables FlpO-dependent ratiometric induction and tracking over long periods of time of cells expressing MTomato-2A-Cre (knockout for any floxed gene) or MYFP (wild type). To induce these mosaics, we used the Apln-FlpO allele, which is expressed in the first angiogenic and sprouting ECs at embryonic day 8.5 (E8.5) and throughout vascular development. In female embryos, the X-chromosome-located Apln–FlpO allele is mosaically silenced15 and expressed only in a fraction (23–50%) of ECs, generating relatively few mutant and wild-type cells, which we found to be compatible with embryonic development (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1a). Analysis of major organs of Apln-FlpO iFlpMosaic mice showed that ECs with full loss of VEGFR2 (Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7) were able to survive and proliferate during embryonic development and until postnatal day 7 (P7), with only a relatively minor competitive disadvantage (2–7-fold) compared with wild-type cells (Fig. 1b). This competitive disadvantage was more pronounced in the lung and kidney endothelium and less so in brain ECs (Fig. 1b,c and Extended Data Fig. 1a–c). As Apln-FlpO is constitutively active and can drive recombination at later stages of embryonic development, we also induced Vegfr2 deletion using 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4-OHT) at E10.5 and E12.5 in embryos carrying Cdh5-CreERT2, iSuRe-HadCre and an iMb2-Mosaic16 control reporter that recombines independently of Vegfr2 deletion (Extended Data Fig. 2a–c). This resulted in a maximum of 1–6% recombined ECs, as opposed to 23–50% with Apln-FlpO. However, this recapitulated the trend in which brain ECs were least affected by VEGFR2 loss, followed by those in the heart, liver, lung and kidney (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c).

a, Schematic of iFlpMosaics induced by Apln-FlpO from E8.5 to P7. b, log2 ratio of MTomato+/MYFP+ within CD31+CD45− cells detected by FACS for the indicated organs. The absolute fold change of the ratio of Vegfr2KO ECs versus the ratio of control Tomato+ cells is indicated in red. c, Representative gating scheme for the ratiometric analysis (see also Extended Data Fig. 1a). d, Representative confocal micrographs of control and Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 retinas immunostained for Tomato, YFP and ERG (which labels EC nuclei). Heatmap, XY dot plot and charts showing the zonal distribution and percentage of Tomato+Cre+ cells when equal numbers of randomly selected YFP+ and Tomato+ cells were plotted (see method in Extended Data Fig. 3a). Right, log2 ratio of Tomato+/YFP+ cells detected in whole-mount retina immunostainings, showing an overall competitive disadvantage of Vegfr2KO cells in the mapped retinas. e, Representative confocal micrographs of retinas immunostained for ERG at P7, from pups injected with 4-OHT at P1. Heatmap, XY dot plot and charts showing distribution of MTomato+ERG+ (wild-type, Vegfr2HET or Vegfr2KO) cells in space in relation to MTomato−ERG+ (wild-type) cells. f, Bar plot contrasting the relative frequency of the indicated cells in the indicated areas and genotypes. g, log2 fold change of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 and Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 cells relative to the respective control wild-type cells. Numbers indicate fold change (×) between the two groups. Data are presented as the mean ± s.d. Scale bars, 100 μm. A, arteries; AF, angiogenic front; dist., distance; freq., frequency; IntCap, intermediate capillaries; LE, leading edge; MA, mature area; V, veins; WT, wild type.

VEGFR2 activity is essential for NOTCH activation and the development of arteries17,18,19. Arteries are formed by tip ECs20, which have the highest level of VEGF–VEGFR2 signalling and guide vascular growth. Our high-resolution spatial zonation data with long-term iFlpMosaics showed that Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs were significantly enriched in veins and surrounding capillaries, and avoided angiogenic front capillaries or tip ECs, but were able to form arteries (Fig. 1d; see also Extended Data Fig. 3a for the heatmapping method).

To complement these results, we intercrossed the Vegfr2 floxed allele with Cdh5-CreERT2 and iSuRe-HadCre14 alleles to ensure fast (24 h; Extended Data Fig. 3b,c) and effective mosaic genetic deletion and full loss of VEGFR2 protein and downstream targets in ECs (Cdh5 expressing), after a single injection of 4-OHT. Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 ECs were located mainly in veins and surrounding capillaries, as well as in the more proximal and mature segments of retina arteries (Fig. 1e). This indicates that when Vegfr2KO ECs are induced in the initial retina sprouting plexus at P1, they can make arteries forming from P1 to P3. However, owing to their inability to continue to sprout and form tip cells at the leading edge, they cannot participate in the subsequent arterial development process occurring from P3 to P7, which in the retina is dependent on incorporation of new tip cells21.

Notably, compared with Vegfr2IECKO-P1−P7 ECs, Vegfr2KO-E8.5−P7 ECs were more frequent at the leading edge and angiogenic front capillaries (Fig. 1f,g) and were still able to make arteries. This suggests that embryonic Vegfr2KO-E8.5−P7 ECs can adapt to long-term loss of VEGFR2 and contribute to venous vascular growth, tip cells and arteries at postnatal stages.

We next investigated how Vegfr2KO ECs could compete with wild-type cells and contribute to growing vascular networks over long periods of time, given the proposed important role of this pathway in EC proliferation1,22. During angiogenesis, there are two main locations for EC proliferation: the capillary angiogenic front and veins (Fig. 2a). We found that the surviving Vegfr2KO-E8.5−P7 ECs proliferated (as determined by Ki-67 detection) as well as wild-type cells in postnatal brain, heart and lung vessels (Fig. 2b).

a, Representative confocal micrograph of a control P7 retina immunostained for the proliferation marker Ki-67 and the EC nuclear marker ERG. The chart shows the frequency of Ki-67+ERG+ (pink pseudocolored) nuclei in different vascular zones. b, Representative confocal micrographs of the indicated organs of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 mice at P7, immunostained for YFP, Tomato, ERG and Ki-67. Yellow arrows indicate YFP+Ki-67+ cells and magenta arrows Tomato+Ki-67+ ECs. c, Representative confocal micrographs of control and Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P20 retinas induced at P1 and analysed at P20. Heatmap, XY dot plot and chart showing that Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P20 ECs grow in veins and surrounding capillaries. d,e, Representative confocal micrographs of retinas immunostained for cleaved caspase 3 and respective quantification charts, showing increased apoptosis of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 but not Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 ECs. f, Representative confocal micrographs of the indicated organs of control and Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 mice induced at P4 and analysed at P7. Arrows indicate recombined ECs (Tomato+) that are Ki-67+ (yellow) and Ki-67− (white), respectively. Chart shows the percentage of Tomato+ ECs positive for Ki-67. Data are presented as mean ± s.d. Scale bars, 100 μm (a,c–e), 50 μm (b,f). Cap., capillaries; CC3, cleaved caspase 3; Ctrl, control; DCap, distal capillaries; IntCap, intermediate capillaries; PCap, proximal capillaries. *Adjusted P < 0.05.

Venous ECs provide a continuous source of ECs for angiogenesis and these migrate against the blood flow to capillaries and then towards arterial vessels20,23,24. When we induced Vegfr2KO ECs for longer periods of time, from P1 to P20 (Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P20), we observed that mutant cells stayed in the vein stem, where they proliferated and gradually outcompeted wild-type cells, which moved outwards towards the VEGF-rich leading edge and adjacent capillaries (Fig. 2c). This preferential occupation of the venous stem niche by Vegfr2KO ECs allowed them to continue proliferating for longer periods of time and later to form most of the perivenous capillary vessels and the deeper vascular plexus that developed during a second wave of VEGF-independent angiogenesis from P7 to P20 (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). This was consistent with previous findings showing that the tip cells that dive to form the deeper vascular plexus in the retina lack expression of the VEGFR2 signalling target gene Esm1; instead, their migration is dependent on other pathways such as Alk or TGFβ and WNT signalling25,26,27.

Together, these data show that VEGFR2 function is essential for the initial sprouting angiogenesis driven by high VEGF levels in hypoxic embryos and organs but not for the development of veins and perivenous capillaries or the subsequent steps of capillary angiogenesis and remodelling that occur after the first vascular plexus is formed in various organs. Thus, by forming veins, which are known to provide a continuous source of ECs for angiogenesis23, Vegfr2KO ECs can continue to proliferate and participate in subsequent steps of vascular development for long periods of time.

We previously observed that the distribution of Vegfr2KO ECs in the retina plexus at P7 differed between animals with long-term (Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7) and short-term (Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7) mosaic deletion of Vegfr2. Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs were more frequent at the leading edge and angiogenic front than Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 ECs (Fig. 1f,g). Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs also proliferated normally (Fig. 2b). Therefore, we hypothesized that Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs might be genetically rewired and adapt over time to loss of the most important receptor for VEGF.

To assess the early response of ECs to loss of VEGFR2, we first analysed apoptosis markers in growing retina vessels, as VEGFR2 has been shown to regulate EC survival. Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 mice showed a very significant increase in the number of apoptotic (cleaved caspase 3 positive) ECs (Fig. 2d). This apoptosis was a reaction to the acute loss of VEGFR2, as Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 or even Vegfr2IECKO-P1–P7 mice did not show any apoptotic ECs (Fig. 2e), suggesting adaptation of the surviving cells over time. When the acute loss of Vegfr2 was induced in all ECs, we observed an immediate depletion of Vegfr2KO ECs from the VEGF-high angiogenic front, but not from veins or more mature vessels (Extended Data Fig. 4c). Therefore, even though many ECs in the retina plexus showed upregulation of the apoptosis marker in the first days after Vegfr2 loss (Fig. 2d), only the angiogenic ECs that were exposed to high VEGF levels at the time of Vegfr2 deletion died (Extended Data Fig. 4c).

We also found that Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs were significantly less proliferative than control cells only in the heart and kidney (Fig. 2f), whereas the proliferation of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs was similar to that of controls (Fig. 2b). This suggests that Vegfr2KO ECs adapt over time and are later able to proliferate in these organs. In the newborn retina, deletion of Vegfr2 did not affect the proliferation of surviving ECs in any segment (Extended Data Fig. 4d), indicating that in this organ VEGFR2 mainly controls EC migration and survival, not proliferation.

Together, our data suggest that ECs lacking VEGF signalling during active angiogenesis suffer an acute VEGFR2 withdrawal effect, followed by a period of adaptation to the loss, after which they can form new vessels. ECs that are more distant from the VEGF source, and therefore have less VEGF signalling, adapt better to the loss and can expand over time, particularly in veins and perivenous vessels.

To further confirm the insensitivity of more mature ECs to loss of VEGFR2 signalling, we deleted Vegfr2 in several adult quiescent vascular beds for 2 weeks. Only the quiescent sinusoidal liver endothelium showed a strong sensitivity and loss of Vegfr2KO ECs, whereas only the kidney endothelium showed significantly lower proliferation (Extended Data Fig. 5), suggesting that only fenestrated or discontinuous mature endothelial vessels present in these organs remain sensitive to VEGFR2 loss.

Given the observed differences in the biology of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 and Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs, we performed scRNA-seq of these cells and respective control Tomato+ cells to identify possible differences in their transcriptional profiles and potential mechanisms of adaptation to loss of VEGFR2 signalling in distinct organ vascular beds.

Although VEGFR2 is a central regulator of angiogenesis and widely regarded as essential for EC biology, Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs showed only modest changes in their transcriptome (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 6), even though VEGFR2 protein and downstream signalling were lost already within the first 24 h following 4-OHT administration (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). In general, the expression of genes related to sprouting or tip cell biology was decreased, whereas that of genes related to apoptosis and vascular permeability was increased in all organs analysed (Fig. 3a,b). However, considerable differences were observed among organs.

In the brain, clusters of proliferating (S–G2–M) ECs expressing venous capillaries markers were increased after Vegfr2 deletion for 3 days (Fig. 3c–f). This was consistent with higher clonal expansion of Vegfr2KO ECs from P1 to P20 in this organ (Extended Data Fig. 7a). Clusters comprising capillary and activated or angiogenic ECs (with high expression of Apln, Adm, Mcam, Lamb1 and Angpt2) were decreased (Fig. 3d–f). In total, only 569 genes were significantly deregulated (Fig. 3g). Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed an increase in the expression of E2F and MYC target genes, as well as G2M, DNA repair and mitotic spindle genes, confirming the increase in EC proliferation (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 7a). The expression of most tip cell marker genes was decreased in Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 brain ECs (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 6a–f).

In contrast to those in the brain, Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 capillary ECs in the heart were significantly less proliferative (Fig. 3j–m and Extended Data Fig. 7b), matching the 54% decrease in Ki-67 percentage observed in sections (Fig. 2f). The proportion of mutant ECs found in bigger vessels (arteries and veins) was increased 2- to 4-fold (Fig. 3k–m), suggesting a proportional fast depletion of Vegfr2KO capillary ECs in only 3 days. Unlike in the brain, GSEA of Vegfr2KO heart ECs showed the expected decrease in expression of E2F and MYC target genes, as well as decreases in expression of G2M, mitotic spindle and tip cell genes (Fig. 3n–p), in accordance with the decrease in proliferation and sprouting of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 heart ECs. Vegfr2KO heart ECs also showed upregulation of genes related to apoptosis and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (Fig. 3n–p), as has been shown previously for ECs losing ERK signalling28.

In contrast to the results for brain and heart, we found no significant difference in the proportions of proliferating cells among control and Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs in lung (Extended Data Fig. 6g–j), as shown by immunostaining for Ki-67 and clonal analysis (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 7c). The proportion of the vein cluster was only slightly increased, and the capillary cluster was slightly decreased. Despite the lack of significant changes in cluster proportions, GSEA showed increased TNF signalling through NF-κB, hypoxia and reactive oxygen species signalling and a decrease in the interferon response (Extended Data Fig. 6k,l). In lung, there was only a small trend of decreased expression of tip cell marker genes (Extended Data Fig. 6m), and several genes related to apoptosis were upregulated (Extended Data Fig. 6l,m).

In the kidney, similar to the heart, Vegfr2 deletion for 3 days led to an increase in the relative proportion of ECs of bigger vessels (arteries and veins), suggesting fast depletion of a fraction of capillary ECs in only 3 days (Extended Data Fig. 6n–q). Proliferation and clonal expansion of kidney capillary ECs were also reduced (Extended Data Figs. 6o,q and 7d), as shown by immunostaining for Ki-67 (Fig. 2f). GSEA showed the expected decrease in expression of E2F, G2M and mitotic spindle genes and an increase in the expression of genes related to p53, xenobiotic metabolism and apoptosis (Extended Data Fig. 6r,s), indicative of cellular stress in kidney ECs after short-term Vegfr2 deletion from P4 to P7. Similar to brain and heart ECs, the expression of tip cell marker genes was also decreased in kidney Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs (Extended Data Fig. 6t).

Following our analysis of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, we performed scRNA-seq of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs of distinct organs to identify potential differences in gene expression related to long-term adaptation of cells to loss of VEGFR2 (Extended Data Fig. 8a). In contrast to Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs exhibited predominantly upregulation rather than downregulation of genes, including marked upregulation of several venous-enriched genes (compare Figs. 3a,b and 4a).

In contrast to brain Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, brain Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs had increased frequencies of venous capillaries (Extended Data Fig. 8b–d) and marked upregulation of the key regulator of vein specification Nr2f2 (Extended Data Fig. 8e). Similarly to Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, brain Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs had decreased frequencies of activated and sprouting ECs and lower expression levels of several tip cell genes (Extended Data Fig. 8c–e). The number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs), particularly upregulated genes, was much higher (1,621 versus 569 DEGs) in Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs; this is likely to represent a long-term adaptation response to loss of VEGFR2 function (compare Extended Data Fig. 8e with Fig. 3g). Whereas in Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 brain ECs, genetic pathways related to EC proliferation and cellular activity (E2F targets, MYC, oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis) were paradoxically increased, in Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs they were decreased (compare Extended Data Fig. 8e,f with Fig. 3g,h). This suggests that brain Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs adapt to the long-term loss of VEGFR2 signalling through a decrease in cellular activity and upregulation of Nr2f2, which probably decreases their dependence on VEGF signalling for growth and survival.

In the heart, we confirmed previous histological analysis showing that heart Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs proliferated at levels similar to those of control cells and markedly higher than those of Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs (compare Fig. 3k,m with Fig. 4b–d). They also had many more DEGs (1,750 DEGs versus 242 DEGs), particularly upregulated genes (compare Fig. 3n with Fig. 4e). GSEA showed increased epithelial–mesenchymal transition, KRAS signalling and angiogenesis, and less expression of metabolic-pathway-related genes (Fig. 4e,f), as seen in the brain. Expression of tip or activated EC genes was not as compromised in Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs compared with Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs (Fig. 4g), suggesting some adaptation over time to the loss of VEGFR2. Notably, Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs were four times more frequent in veins (Fig. 4c,d), similar to our observations in the retina (Fig. 1d–f), confirming that mosaic loss of Vegfr2 causes mutant ECs to expand more in veins. In comparison with Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs, Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs showed strong upregulation of most venous-specific genes, including Nr2f2, Fbln2, Igf1 and Vwf (Fig. 4e). This was not caused only by the increased proportion of venous ECs in these mutants; capillary and angiogenic ECs also showed much higher expression of these venous marker genes, indicating venousization of mutant Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 capillary ECs over time (Fig. 4h,p).

In the lung, the same adaptation and venousization of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs was observed. Mutant cells were four times more frequent in veins (Fig. 4i–k), and even capillary or CAR4+ ECs showed significantly upregulated expression of lung venous genes including Vegfc, Nr2f2, Vwf and Fbln2 (Fig. 4l,m and Extended Data Fig. 9a,b). Similar to findings in the other organs, lung Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs had significantly more DEGs than lung Vegfr2IECKO-P4–P7 ECs (3,116 vs 502), particularly upregulated genes (compare Extended Data Fig. 6k with Fig. 4m). Volcano plots and GSEA revealed upregulation of many venous-enriched and epithelial–mesenchymal transition genes, as well as oestrogen response genes. Lung Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs had lower expression of E2F targets and metabolism genes, as seen in the other organs (Fig. 4m,n).

Notably, deletion of Vegfr2 for 2 weeks in adult organ blood vessels did not induce venousization of adult Vegfr2KO ECs; instead, it decreased expression of venous genes (Extended Data Fig. 8g–u), indicating that upregulation of Nr2f2 and venousization may represent a long-term adaptative response to VEGFR2 loss that occurs only during active angiogenesis.

The scRNA-seq data indicating venousization of Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs over time were confirmed by immunostaining for the master regulator of venous development NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII) (Fig. 4o,p and Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). To understand the venousization requirement for long-term adaptation of Vegfr2KO ECs, we also analysed Apln-FlpO iFlpMosaic Vegfr2Flox/Flox, Nr2f2Flox/Flox mice. When ECs lacked both VEGFR2 and NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), their capacity to expand was significantly reduced, particularly in veins (Fig. 4q,r and Extended Data Fig. 9e). This suggests that endothelial venousization is a key mechanism of adaptation to long-term loss of VEGFR2 signalling during angiogenesis that enables mutant cells to expand in veins and derived vessels over time.

In addition to analysing embryonic and postnatal angiogenesis, we tested the capacity of Vegfr2KO ECs to form tumour vessels over a period of 2 weeks. When Vegfr2 deletion was induced a few days before tumour implantation, Vegfr2IECKO-day-3–adult ECs formed tumour vessels mainly at the tumour border and failed to penetrate deeper into the tumour, where they were 5.2-fold less frequent than control ECs (Extended Data Fig. 10a). By contrast, Vegfr2KO-E8.5–adult ECs, which had undergone venousization throughout embryonic and postnatal development, could better reach inside the tumour and were only 2.6-fold less frequent than control ECs (Extended Data Fig. 10b). These data show that although VEGFR2 signalling promotes tumour angiogenesis, ECs can progressively adapt to its absence and sustain tumour angiogenesis.

In addition to our findings with respect to venousization, we observed significant upregulation of expression of other VEGF receptor ligands in Vegfr2KO-E8.5–P7 ECs (Extended Data Fig. 11a), including PGF and VEGFC, which bind and activate VEGFR1 and VEGFR3, respectively1. In the absence of VEGFR2, VEGFR1 is the only other receptor that can bind VEGFA. However, all studies so far have shown that VEGFR1 kinase activity is too weak29,30, whereas its extracellular soluble form (sVEGFR1 or sFLT1) acts as a strong VEGF decoy receptor31. Therefore, when VEGFR2 is present, VEGFR1 is considered to mainly antagonize VEGFA–VEGFR2 signalling and angiogenesis. However, we found that Vegfr1 expression was much higher in ECs in the brain, the organ least sensitive to VEGFR2 loss (Extended Data Fig. 11b). We also found that during postnatal angiogenesis, sVegfr1 showed 2–5-fold lower expression than the membrane full-length Vegfr1 (flVegfr1) mRNA form, except in brain ECs (Extended Data Fig. 11c), suggesting a potential signalling role for flVEGFR1.

To evaluate whether VEGFR1 could compensate for loss of VEGFR2, we induced mosaic codeletion of Vegfr1 and Vegfr2 in ECs with iSuRe-HadCre from P1 to P7 (Vegfr1/2IECKO-P1–P7). Compared with Vegfr2KO ECs, Vegfr1/2KO ECs showed a further decrease in ability to migrate and form retina capillaries, but not veins or arteries (Fig. 5a). In veins, Vegfr1/2KO ECs could clonally expand (Extended Data Fig. 11d). Brain and heart Vegfr1/2KO ECs proliferated less than Vegfr2KO ECs at P7 (Extended Data Fig. 11e,f). Deletion of both Vegfr2 and Vegfr1 had a stronger effect on endothelial and pup survival (Extended Data Fig. 11g–i), confirming the requirement for VEGFR1 signalling when VEGFR2 is absent in capillaries. Mosaic deletion of Vegfr1 alone also led to a decrease in EC migration towards the VEGF-rich front (Extended Data Fig. 11j). In contrast to deletion of Vegfr1 in all ECs, mosaic loss of Vegfr1 in single ECs did not increase VEGF signalling (as assessed by ESM1 expression), probably owing to normal levels of sFLT1 present in the mostly wild-type microenvironment (Extended Data Fig. 11k).
