In addition to VEGFR1 and VEGFR2, ECs express VEGFR3. Previous studies have shown that VEGFR3 is strongly expressed by capillary and venous ECs; however, this receptor cannot bind VEGF (VEGFA), only VEGFC and VEGFD, which are key molecules for lymphangiogenesis but less relevant to blood vessel angiogenesis. Vegfr2IECKO-E8.5–P7 ECs showed very strong upregulation of VEGFC (Extended Data Fig. 11a), which could signal to VEGFR3 in the absence of VEGFR2. Loss of VEGFR3 in growing retina ECs has been shown to induce angiogenesis, suggesting that VEGFR3 negatively regulates VEGFR2 signalling32. However, single Vegfr3IECKO-P1–P7 ECs also had decreased ability to migrate and reach the leading edge (Extended Data Fig. 11l–n). Arterial ECs and smooth muscle cells express high levels of VEGFC33,34,35 a ligand that can bind both VEGFR2 and VEGFR3. Compared with Vegfr2IECKO-P1-P7 ECs, Vegfr2/3IECKO-P1-P7 ECs had a very similar zonal distribution in capillaries and veins (Fig. 5b) but a 3.4-fold lower frequency in arteries (Fig. 5c); this suggests an important role for VEGFC to VEGFR3 signalling in arterial mobilization or survival, but only when VEGFR2 signalling is absent. Loss of both VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 did not compromise the proliferation of surviving ECs in any vascular segments (Fig. 5d).

We also observed that Vegfr2KO ECs had decreased VEGFR3 expression only at the angiogenic front, where VEGFA levels are highest. By contrast Vegfr1/2KO ECs showed strong downregulation of VEGFR3 in all vascular segments, except in arteries (Fig. 5e). Vegfr1/2/3IECKO-P1-P7 ECs behaved similarly to Vegfr1/2IECKO-P1-P7 ECs, except for a pronounced decrease in formation of arterial vessels (Fig. 5f–h). Taken together, our findings show that in the absence of VEGFR2 signalling, VEGFR1 is required to sustain VEGFR3 expression and growth and migration of capillary ECs. In arteries, VEGFR3 continues to be expressed after loss of VEGFR1 and VEGFR2 and regulates development of arteries when the other VEGFA receptors are missing. Notably, vein ECs can survive and clonally expand in the complete absence of all VEGF receptor signalling (Fig. 5i).

Our study challenges the longstanding view that VEGFR2 signalling is indispensable for endothelial proliferation, migration and sprouting during angiogenesis1,22. By using iFlpMosaics to induce ratiometric genetic mosaics of wild-type and Vegfr2KO ECs, we demonstrated that these mutant cells are capable of surviving, proliferating and competing with wild-type ECs during the entire embryonic and postnatal organ growth period (Extended Data Fig. 12). Contrary to previous studies suggesting that VEGFR2 is required for all forms of vascular differentiation and development10,12,36, our findings indicate that VEGFR2-independent mechanisms support angiogenesis in certain vascular beds, particularly the long-term development of venous and perivenous capillaries.

We identified significant organ-specific differences in adaptation to acute loss of VEGFR2 signalling (Extended Data Fig. 12a), thereby extending previous findings37,38. Whereas angiogenic retina ECs were strongly affected, brain ECs were the least affected, retaining high angiogenic potential, partially because of VEGFR1 compensation (Extended Data Fig. 12b). By contrast, postnatal heart, kidney and liver ECs were more sensitive to acute withdrawal of VEGFR2, showing partial depletion of Vegfr2KO ECs in capillaries, as well as a partial reduction in proliferation. The postnatal lung showed a distinct response, with no major changes in EC proliferation or cluster composition but instead a shift in transcriptional programs towards inflammation and metabolic adaptations. These findings highlight the heterogeneity of endothelial responses across different vascular beds and suggest that organ-specific factors influence EC resilience to perturbations in VEGF signalling.

The long-term adaptation of Vegfr2KO ECs was a notable observation. Although these cells initially had a competitive disadvantage during early embryonic and postnatal sprouting angiogenesis stages, they ultimately expanded and outcompeted wild-type cells in venous and perivenous regions, indicating that alternative pathways support their survival and proliferation in this niche. Veins are known to provide a continuous source of ECs for capillary angiogenesis and later arterialization20,23, and this venous dominance of Vegfr2KO ECs allows them to compete with wild-type cells over time. Our scRNA-seq analysis of different vascular beds further showed that ECs with prolonged loss of VEGFR2 exhibited a significant shift towards a venous transcriptional signature (venousization), marked by upregulation of many venous genes, including Nr2f2, a master regulator of veins development24,39. Vegfr2KONr2f2KO ECs were significantly less able to expand, particularly in veins, showing that venousization is a key adaptation mechanism that enables Vegfr2KO ECs to persist and contribute to vascular development (Extended Data Fig. 12c,d).

In addition to venousization, our findings demonstrate the compensatory roles of VEGFR1 and VEGFR3 in supporting survival and growth signalling when VEGFR2 is absent (Extended Data Fig. 12b). Previously, VEGFR1 has mainly been reported to negatively regulate VEGFR2 signalling during angiogenesis, because its soluble secreted version sFLT1 or VEGFR1 is a decoy receptor of VEGF1,22. In our mosaic Vegfr1KO and Vegfr1/2KO experiments, sFLT1 levels in the microenvironment were normal; this led us to find that membrane or full-length VEGFR1 acted as a positive regulator of angiogenesis and partially compensated for VEGFR2 loss, supporting both EC survival and migration. The mosaic single loss of VEGFR3 also showed that this receptor was a positive regulator of EC migration towards the leading edge. This was consistent with results obtained using VEGFR3-blocking antibodies40; however, our findings were contrary to results from pan-endothelial Vegfr3KO genetics experiments32 in which the receptor was lost from all ECs. In this case, VEGFC and/or VEGFD bioavailability in the whole body increases, thereby increasing VEGFC–VEGFR2 signalling, whereas in low-frequency Vegfr3KO mosaics this does not occur. In addition, Vegfr2/3KO ECs mobilized less to the angiogenic front and had decreased arterialization when compared with Vegfr2KO ECs. The ability of these alternative VEGF receptors to sustain EC survival, migration and proliferation at the single-cell level indicates potential functional plasticity and compensation within the VEGF signalling network, as suggested previously by studies using classical full-tissue conditional genetics12,32,37.

An important implication of our study is that EC sensitivity to VEGFR2 loss varies depending on the vascular context and the time since the loss. We found that acute loss of VEGFR2 during active angiogenesis resulted in significant EC depletion in the first 3 days, particularly depletion of tip cells and other ECs at the angiogenic front, where VEGF signalling is highest. However, Vegfr2KO ECs in VEGF-low areas and those that had undergone long-term adaptation were able to persist and even contribute to a substantial portion of capillary vessels, particularly those around veins. This suggests that ECs experiencing prolonged VEGFR2 deficiency undergo venousization in VEGF-low areas, enabling them to survive and then grow in the absence of canonical VEGF signalling. Our tumour models showed that Vegfr2KO ECs could form tumour vessels, particularly if they had previously undergone venousization during embryonic angiogenesis. The use of ratiometric and trackable iFlpMosaics was key to obtaining these findings.

Our work may also provide biomarkers and insights into resistance mechanisms to anti-VEGF therapies5,41,42,43. Adaptation of ECs to VEGFR2 loss by engaging alternative venous-related angiogenic pathways may also occur in tumours. If this is confirmed, therapeutic strategies that simultaneously block the compensatory and venous-related pathways identified here may be necessary to overcome resistance to anti-VEGF treatments.

In conclusion, our study reshapes our understanding of VEGFR2-dependent angiogenesis by demonstrating that ECs possess intrinsic mechanisms to adapt to long-term absence of VEGFR2 signalling. The discovery of endothelial venousization and compensatory VEGF receptor signalling provides a new framework for investigation of alternative modes of vascular development and resistance to anti-VEGF therapies.

All mouse husbandry and experiments were conducted using protocols approved by local animal ethics committees and authorities (Comunidad Autónoma de Madrid and Universidad Autónoma de Madrid CAM-PROEX 164.8/20, PROEX 293.1/22 and PROEX-288.7/24). The mouse colonies were maintained in racked individual ventilation cages according to current national legislation. The mice had dust- and pathogen-free bedding and sufficient nesting and environmental enrichment material for development of species-specific behaviour. All mice had ad libitum access to food and water in environmental conditions of 45–65% relative humidity, temperatures of 21–24 °C and a 12 h/12 h light–dark cycle. For preservation of animal welfare, mouse health was monitored with an animal health surveillance programme that followed the recommendations of the Federation of European Laboratory Animal Science Associations for specific-pathogen-free facilities

We used Mus musculus lines mostly on the C57BL6 genetic background, with some having a fraction of 129SV, or B6CBAF1 or DBA genetic backgrounds. Mice were backcrossed to C57Bl6 for several generations. To generate mice for analysis, we intercrossed mice aged between 7 weeks and 30 weeks. We did not anticipate any influence of mouse sex on our data, and both female and male mice were analysed. The initial sample size was determined taking into account the ‘3 Rs’ for animal experimentation and the expected experimental variability based on protocols (published and our own; refs. 13 and 14). The final sample size was defined a posteriori after statistical analysis of the data. Sample size and related statistical analysis methods are indicated in the figure legends or source data. No randomization or blinding was used, and the animals or tissues were selected for analysis on the basis of their genotype, the detected Cre- or FlpO-dependent recombination frequency and the quality of multiplex immunostaining.

The following mouse lines were used and intercrossed: Tg(Cdh5–CreERT2)44, Tg(iSuRe–HadCre)14, Vegfr2flox (ref. 45), Vegfr1flox (ref. 46), Vegfr3flox (ref. 47) (for this work, we also generated a new Vegfr3flox allele in the Vegfr1/2flox background, as indicated below), Nr2f2flox (ref. 48), iMb2–Mosaic16, Apln–FlpO15 and the iFlpMosaic lines13 (R26-iFlpMTomato-2A-Cre/MYFP and Tg-iFlpChromatin–Mosaic).

To generate a new Vegfr3flox allele combined with Vegfr1/2flox we injected Cas9, donor DNAs containing LoxP sites and guide RNAs (TGTTAAAGACACGCATACCT/AGG and AGATGGGGTGAATAGCTCCG/TGG) into mouse eggs of the Vegfr1/2flox iSuRe–HadCre Cdh5–CreERT2 line. Founders containing LoxP sites flanking exon 1 in the same chromosome were screened by PCR, and inducible Vegfr3 deletion was confirmed by PCR and immunostaining for the VEGFR3 protein (Extended Data Fig. 11l,m).

For induction of CreERT2 activity in adult mice, 1 g tamoxifen (Sigma-Aldrich, P5648_1G) was dissolved in 50 ml corn oil (stock tamoxifen concentration, 20 mg m−1), and aliquots were stored at −20 °C. Animals received intraperitoneal injections of 100 µl of this stock solution (total dose: 2 mg tamoxifen per animal at 80 mg kg−1), as indicated in the figures. To activate recombination in pups, we injected 4-OHT at the indicated stages at a dose of 40 mg kg−1. For double (VEGFR1/2, VEGFR2/3) or triple (VEGFR1/2/3) mutants, 4-OHT was administered to pups at 15 mg kg−1. For activation of recombination during embryogenesis, pregnant dams were induced with 0.25 mg 4-OHT supplemented with 0.125 mg progesterone at E10.5 and E12.5. All mouse lines and primer sequences required for genotyping are provided in Supplementary Table 1.

Lewis carcinoma cells were obtained from ATCC and cultured in DMEM (Gibco) containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 1× penicillin–streptomycin and 2 mM glutamine at 37 °C, 5% CO2. The cell medium was changed every other day, and cells were passaged every 3–4 days. Cells were routinely screened for mycoplasma contamination. Cells were used for tumour inoculation when they were at 75–80% confluency. Cells were trypsinized and resuspended in Matrigel solution (Biosciences). Age-matched (15–20 weeks) and sex-matched mice were injected subcutaneously with 5 × 105 tumour cells suspended in Matrigel (Corning, 354234). Mice were euthanized after 15 days, and tumours (less than 2 cm3) were extracted, fixed and processed for immunostaining.

For immunostaining of mouse retinas, eyes were dissected from mouse pups and fixed by incubation with agitation for 20 min in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) (diluted from a stock of 16% PFA; EMS 15710). After two washes in PBS (5 min each), retinas were microdissected from the eyes; 4 incisions were made to enable later flat mounting, and the retinas were refixed in 4% PFA for 45 min with agitation. After two washes in PBS, retinas were blocked and permeabilized by incubation for 1 h in PBST (0.3% Triton X-100, 3% FBS and 3% donkey serum in PBS). Samples were then incubated with primary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) diluted in PBST overnight at 4 °C with agitation. The next day, retinas were washed 5 times for 20 min in PBST diluted 1:2. Then, they were incubated in the same solution for 2 h at room temperature with Alexa-conjugated secondary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2). After washing (3 × 15 min) in PBS containing 0.15% Triton X-100, retinas were washed (2 × 15 min) in PBS and flat mounted in Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech). For combination of rabbit anti-ERG-647 with other antibodies produced in rabbit, retinas were incubated with the Alexa 594 AffiniPure Fab Fragment Donkey Anti-Rabbit secondary antibody, then with 5% rabbit serum for 30 min at room temperature, and finally with rabbit anti-ERG-647.

For collection of organs and histological analysis, mice were euthanized in CO2 chambers, and 10 ml of PBS was injected into the left ventricles, followed by perfusion with 3.7–4% formaldehyde (ITW Reagents, 252931) at pH 7. The explanted organs were postfixed for 2 h in 4% PFA (Thermo Scientific, 043368.9M) in PBS at 4 °C with gentle rotation. After three washes in PBS for 10 min each, the organs were stored overnight in 30% sucrose (Sigma) in PBS. The organs were then embedded in optimal cutting temperature compound (Sakura) and frozen at −80 °C. Cryosections of 30 µm were cut on a cryostat (Leica), washed three times for 10 min each time in PBS, and blocked and permeabilized in PBS containing 10% donkey serum (Millipore), 10% FBS and 1% Triton X-100. The primary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) were diluted in the same buffer and incubated with sections overnight at 4 °C. This step was followed by three 10-min washes in PBS and incubation for 2 h with conjugated secondary antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) and 4,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) in PBS at room temperature. After three washes in PBS, the sections were mounted with Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech). For combination of rabbit anti-ERG-647 with other antibodies produced in rabbit, retinas were incubated first with the other primary rabbit antibodies, followed by Alexa 594 AffiniPure Fab Fragment Donkey Anti-Rabbit secondary antibody, then rabbit epitopes blocked with 5% rabbit serum for 30 min at room temperature, and finally incubated with rabbit anti-ERG-647.

For confocal scanning, immunostained organ sections or whole-mount retinas were imaged at high resolution with a Leica SP8 Navigator confocal microscope fitted with a ×10 or ×40 objective. Individual fields or tiles of large areas were acquired. All images shown are representative of the results obtained for each group and experiment. Animals were dissected and processed under identical conditions. Phenotypes or signal intensities were compared using images obtained with the same laser excitation and confocal scanner detection settings. We used ImageJ/Fiji v.1.54f to threshold, select and quantify the objects in confocal micrographs.

For arteriovenous mapping of ERG-labelled control and mutant ECs (Extended Data Fig. 3a), a semiautomatic Fiji script (available at https://github.com/RuiBenedito/Benedito_Lab) was developed. First, six regions of interest were manually defined by the user: artery, vein, mature capillaries between the established arteries and veins, intermediate capillaries, angiogenic front and leading edge. ERG labelling was used to segment endothelial nuclei and classify each nucleus according to reporter or marker positivity (determined by the percentage of pixels within each nucleus above a given intensity threshold level), and the XY coordinates of nuclei were extracted. Then, arterial, venous, distal and proximal arteriovenous boundaries were defined by the user to determine the relative position of each segmented nucleus to each arteriovenous field boundary; this enabled compilation of data extracted from different arteriovenous fields into a single XY dot plot or heatmap.

The data collected in Fiji were post-analysed in R (v.4.5.2) for generation of graphs representing the spatial distribution of the cells of interest. For the XY plots and heatmaps, samples were randomly subsetted to enable us to display equal numbers of control and mutant cells (MYFP+ versus MTomato+ in the Apln–FlpO, iFlpMosaic background, and MTomato− versus MTomato+ in the Cdh5–CreERT2, iSuRe–HadCre background); this was to make clear the zonation differences between control and mutant cells. For visualization with XY dot plots, 2,000 randomly selected cells of each group were plotted; for the heatmap generation, the maximal number of cells (determined by the cell type (control or mutant) with fewer cells) was used. The percentage of each cell type in each arteriovenous region was calculated given its spatial distribution per field (Extended Data Fig. 3a).

We generated Fiji macro Script_Reporter_MarkerDetection_Mapping.ijm for spatial mapping of ERG and/or quantification of EC colocalization with reporters (MYFP or MTomato) and other markers (Ki-67) as in Figs. 1, 2, 5. R scripts were used for data quantification and heatmapping (Script_Spatial Heatmap; Figs. 1, 2, 5 and Extended Data Figs. 3, 4, 11) and are available at GitHub (https://github.com/RuiBenedito/Benedito_Lab). Fiji, Adobe Photoshop CC 24.1.0 and Adobe Illustrator CC v.27.1.1 were used for downstream image processing, analysis and illustration.

To quantify the clonal expansion of single ECs expressing the iSuRe–HadCre and the Tg-iFlpChromatin–Mosaic alleles, we segmented and analysed images with MTomato+H2B-Cherry+, MTomato+H2B-EGFP+ or MTomato+HA-H2B-Cerulean+ signals with the Clone_Identification_Quantification script, deposited at GitHub (https://github.com/RuiBenedito/Benedito_Lab/).

Postnatal and adult tissues were dissociated before fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS). Enzymatic digestion was carried out at 37 °C for 20 min using a solution containing 2.5 mg ml−1 collagenase type I (Thermo Fisher), 2.5 mg ml−1 dispase II (Thermo Fisher) and 50 μg ml−1 DNase I (Roche). Following dissociation, samples were pelleted by centrifugation (450g, 4 °C, 5 min). Pellets were gently resuspended in 1× blood lysis buffer (BioLegend, 420301) and incubated on ice for 5 min for lysis of erythroid cells. After lysis, cells were passed through a 70-μm cell strainer and centrifuged again (450g, 4 °C, 5 min). Cells were resuspended in antibody incubation solution (PBS without Ca2+ or Mg2+, supplemented with 2% dialysed FBS; Biowest, X0515), with primary antibodies (APC rat anti-mouse CD31 and APC-Cy7 anti-CD45; Supplementary Table 2) only or with the addition of Hashtag oligo (HTO) antibodies (Supplementary Table 2) when scRNA-seq was performed. Samples were then incubated at 4 °C with gentle agitation for 20 min.

After immunolabelling, cells were centrifuged (450g, 4 °C, 5 min), washed with antibody incubation solution, centrifuged again and resuspended in sorting buffer (10% FBS in PBS without Ca2+ or Mg2+). Stained cells were maintained on ice until acquisition. DAPI (5 mg ml−1) was added immediately before FACS analysis. Cells were analysed using an LSRFortessa cell analyser or sorted using a FACS Aria Cell Sorter (BD Biosciences). For an example of the FACS gating strategy, see Extended Data Fig. 1a. BD FACSDiva v.8.0.1 and FlowJo v.10 were used for data acquisition and analysis.

For RNA-seq analysis, APC rat anti-mouse CD31 (which labels ECs), APC-Cy7 rat anti-CD45 (which labels blood cells) and HTO antibodies (BD Biosciences) (Supplementary Table 2) were used together to hashtag and distinguish the different organ Tomato+CD31+ ECs when loaded on the same 10x Genomics port (Extended Data Figs. 6a and 8a). After antibody incubation, samples were washed twice with antibody incubation solution, centrifuged (450g, 5 min, 4 °C) and resuspended in sorting buffer (10% FBS in PBS without Ca2+ or Mg2+). Stained cells were maintained on ice until acquisition. Immediately before FACS analysis, DAPI (5 mg ml−1) was added, and the cell suspension was passed slowly through a 70-µm cell strainer attached to a 1-ml syringe for removal of aggregates. Live, DAPI-negative, CD31+CD45− and endogenous-reporter-positive cells were sorted into cold 1.5-ml microcentrifuge tubes containing 300 µl of sorting buffer. Cells were collected using a 100-µm nozzle at 20 PSI in high-purity mode with a flow rate of fewer than 3,000 events per second to preserve cell viability and minimize contamination. After sorting, cells were pelleted at 500g for 5 min at 4 °C and resuspended in 30–40 µl cell-capture buffer (Ca2+- and Mg2+-free PBS supplemented with 0.04% ultrapure bovine serum albumin; Thermo Fisher, AM2616). Viability and cell concentration were determined using a Countess 3 Automated Cell Counter (Thermo Fisher Scientific) before loading of the 10x Genomics port.

Single-cell suspensions were loaded on to the 10x Genomics Chromium Controller system for encapsulation into emulsion droplets. The 10x Genomics Chromium single-cell 3′ RNA-seq library preparation and sequencing were carried out at the CNIC Genomics Unit according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Each port was loaded with 20,000 to 50,000 cells. Final libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NextSeq 2000 platform, with software v.1.7.2.

scRNA-seq data were aligned and quality controlled by the CNIC Bioinformatics Unit using Cell Ranger (v.8 and v.9). Clustering, cell type identification and downstream analysis were performed by I.G.-G. The following pipeline was applied for transcript alignment, quantification, quality control and cell type classification.

Reference transcriptomes were generated using the Ensembl GRCm38 mouse genome, build version 98 (sep2019.archive.ensembl.org). Genes metadata were obtained from the corresponding Ensembl BioMart archive. To enable downstream analysis of gene deletion efficiency and soluble versus full-length isoform abundance, we appended Vegfr2 (also known as Kdr) exon 3, Kdr exon 30, Vegfr1 (also known as Flt1) exon 13b and Flt1 exon 30 to the reference transcriptome as custom metadata features. Gene annotations were obtained from the corresponding Ensembl BioMart archive. Raw sequencing reads from gene expression libraries, hashtag oligonucleotides and targeted transcript sequences were aligned and quantified using Cell Ranger (v.8 and v.9).

Downstream analyses were performed using R (v.4.5.0) and the Seurat package (v.5.5.1; https://satijalab.org/seurat/)49. Cells were filtered for removal of low-quality profiles and technical artifacts using the following criteria: 2,000–30,000 total unique molecular identifiers (UMIs), 800–6,000 detected genes, mitochondrial transcript content less than 25%, fewer than 65% of reads mapping to the top 50 expressed genes and fewer than 0.1% haemoglobin transcripts. Cells with fewer than 15 hashtag UMIs were excluded to improve sample assignment accuracy. To enrich for endothelial populations and exclude hematopoietic contamination, we also required cells to express Cdh5 (normalized expression greater than 0.1) and no or very low expression of Ptprc (normalized expression less than 0.1). Cells identified as doublets on the basis of hashtag antibody signals were removed. Demultiplexing by organ was performed using sample-specific hashtag oligonucleotide signals (Supplementary Table 2) and after confirmed by organ-specific EC markers, and all downstream analyses were conducted separately for each organ ECs.

Mitochondrial genes, haemoglobin genes and transgenes were removed before clustering to avoid biasing of normalization and dimensionality reduction. Filtered count data were log-normalized and scaled before analysis. Dimensionality reduction was performed using principal component analysis, and batch effects across independent ports were corrected with the Harmony algorithm50.

We clustered cells by constructing a shared nearest neighbour graph and applying the Louvain community detection algorithm to identify distinct cell populations. The optimal number of principal components for dimensionality reduction was determined using an elbow plot, and clustering resolution parameters were selected on the basis of the EC complexity observed in each organ.

Clusters and cells were classified using the SingleR function from the SingleR package v.2.10.0 (ref. 51). Putative doublets were identified as cell clusters that had high total UMI or gene counts or unusual gene coexpression or were located in principal component analysis outliers. Cells classified as singlets were retained and reclustered. Final cluster identities were manually curated on the basis of known EC subtypes and literature-based markers. The FUNCTION_Dotplot_Markers custom function in R was used to find and plot top marker genes per cluster to determine cell identities.

To assess the rate of exon deletion in Vegfr2flox/flox samples, we computed the number of UMI reads aligned to each exon, including the floxed region and the terminal 3′ exon or untranslated region (which is typically overrepresented in 10x Genomics 3′ libraries). Only reads with valid barcodes, UMIs and matching strand orientation were retained.

Read counts for floxed exons were normalized to total UMI counts per cell. These values were added to the Seurat metadata. Deletion efficiency was visualized using dot plots and violin plots, comparing expression of the whole transcript (including the 3′ untranslated region). These visualizations were generated using the custom R function FUNCTION_violin_dotplot_deletion_FC.R, which combines violin plots of single-cell expression distributions with dot plots displaying total average expression numbers and signed fold change between conditions.

To obtain the ratio between the soluble (sVegfr1) and full-length (flVegfr1) isoforms, the normalized reads from exon 13b (the last exon in the soluble form) were divided by the normalized reads of exon 30 (the last exon in the full-length version).

We quantified differences in cell type composition between control and mutant samples for each organ by comparing relative proportions across conditions. For UMAP visualizations (both split and integrated), equal downsampling of the two conditions was performed to ensure identical cell numbers, thereby avoiding sampling bias in visual comparisons.

Differential gene expression between conditions was visualized using volcano plots. These were generated using R functions (FUNCTION_VolcanoPlot) developed in-house that built on the EnhancedVolcano package (v.1.26.0)52. For volcano plots and heatmaps, statistical analyses were performed using Seurat’s FindMarkers function, with Wilcoxon rank-sum test and Bonferroni correction for multiple testing. GSEA was performed using FGSEA with a custom wrapper function (FUNCTION_Fgsea_TableFgsea) based on the FGSEA package. For hallmark pathways, statistical analyses were performed using the multilevel Monte Carlo approach implemented in fgseaMultilevel (R package fgsea v.1.34.2)53 and Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction for multiple testing.

Genes used for differential gene expression analysis were prefiltered using FUNCTION_FilterLowExpressionGenes_onlyTable; this removes genes with low and highly heterogeneous expression patterns across cells, which are often inconsistently detected between datasets and potentially reflect technical artefacts such as ambient RNA contamination. The function acts as an empirical, distribution-based filter to improve robustness of downstream differential expression analysis. Differential expression heatmaps were generated using a custom function (FUNCTION_Find_PlotGenesHeatmap_FC_Metadata), implemented in-house and based on the pheatmap package.

Most numerical data shown in charts were first compiled and processed with Microsoft Excel 2019 and 2024 and then analysed and plotted with GraphPad Prism v.10.1.0. All bar graphs show mean ± s.d. Experiments were repeated with independent animals, as stated in the source data file or figure legends. Comparisons between two sample groups with a Gaussian distribution were performed using unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests. Comparisons among more than two groups were made by one-way or two-way analysis of variance followed by multiple comparison tests. Data points were analysed and plotted with GraphPad Prism. No randomization or blinding was used, and the animals or tissues were selected for analysis on the basis of their genotype, the detected Cre- or FlpO-dependent recombination frequency and the quality of multiplex immunostaining. For mosaic analysis, only samples with less than 50% recombination were selected. The sample sizes were chosen according to the observed statistical variation and published protocols.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

RNA-seq data can be viewed at the Gene Expression Omnibus under accession code GSE331295. Unprocessed FACS raw data files and original microscopy images of the data are available upon request. All other data supporting the findings in this study are included in the main article and associated files. Source data are provided with this paper.

a, Single cell RNAseq and histological analysis of Vegfr2KO-P4-P7 ECs (gene deletion induced at P4 and analysis at P7) in distinct organs revealed common but also distinct transcriptional programs and functions for VEGFR2. b, Loss of VEGFR2 affects the migration of ECs towards VEGF produced by hypoxic tissues, during the first wave of angiogenesis. This leads to the accumulation of Vegfr2KO ECs in more mature vessels and veins, which provides for a continuous source of mutant ECs during subsequent waves of angiogenesis derived from veins. The additional loss of VEGFR1 compromises capillary angiogenesis, whereas the additional loss of VEGFR3 compromises arterialization. c, The comparison of scRNAseq data from ECs with short-term (P4 to P7) and long-term (embryonic to P7) deletion of Vegfr2 revealed that over time Vegfr2KO ECs undergo significant transcriptional changes and upregulate the expression of many venous genes (venousization), particularly Nr2f2. d, The upregulation of Nr2f2, and venousization, enables Vegfr2KO-E8.5-P7 ECs to compete with wildtype ECs over time, and form veins and many other venous-derived vessels, such as capillaries, tip cells and even arteries. Note that these cells adapt over time to the loss of VEGFR2 and become more capable of angiogenesis than Vegfr2KO-P1-P7 ECs. The additional loss of the master regulator of vein specification Nr2f2, prevents the venousization and growth of Vegfr2KO ECs.

#1293. UECL | Atalanta 1-1 Kairat Almaty: Dea crisis drags on with meagre point

The Atalanta wait for a victory drags on to seven matches, as they scraped a 1-1 draw with Kairat Almaty in the Conference League thanks to Nikola Krstovic.

La Dea were in crisis after scraping two draws from six competitive games, culminating in a humiliating 3-0 home defeat to Parma on Monday, so went into a three-day training retreat to prepare for this match. Thomas Kristensen, Gianluca Gaetano, Raoul Bellanova, Franck Kessie, Sead Kolasinac, Isak Hien, Giacomo Raspadori and Odilon Kossounou were injured, so youth team defender Javison Idele made his first start. They beat Pafos 3-1, but then lost 2-0 away to Ajax in this tournament.

Kairat Almaty dropped out of the Champions League and Europa League preliminary rounds after winning the Kazakhstan title, drawing at Riga and losing 5-1 to Panathinaikos in the Conference League.  Striker Jorginho had been out since July with a torn ACL, but this was only their second game under caretaker manager Zhora Arutyunyan.

Jonathan Rowe stung the goalkeeper’s gloves from the edge of the area, then nodded over as the move continued.

Kairat almost scored a comical own goal when Damir Kassabulat didn’t look at his goalkeeper for a back pass, dribbling it wide of an open goal after 11 minutes.

A ferocious Rowe strike from outside the box was acrobatically palmed out from under the bar, while Marco Carnesecchi needed a double save on Alexandr Mrynskiy and the Gustavo Mendonca follow-up.

Atalanta should’ve taken the lead on the half-hour with a well-worked passing move, but Mario Pasalic only grazed the outside of the near post from close range.

La Dea were caught out on a classic counter-attack with an Edmilson pass from the centre-circle to send Marc Gual running against two defenders, beating the on-rushing Carnesecchi.

Idele couldn’t keep the volley down from seven yards on the Nicola Zalewski cross, while when Eljif Elmas did have the ball in the net on 65 minutes, he was offside to redirect the wayward Zalewski strike.

Elmas put real power behind his curling attempt from the edge of the box, forcing a flying save from the Kairat Almaty goalkeeper.

There was another tough save on the Ederson half-volley from close range and Atalanta equalised on the resulting flapped corner, as it was knocked back from the by-line by Relja Obric for Nikola Krstovic to bundle over the line from six yards.

Atalanta pushed to the bitter end and had a huge chance to win it in stoppages, but Mario Pasalic couldn’t keep the finish on target.

Scraped? Atalanta played better and managed to come back from going behind after being hit on the break, yet again. The stats show a different story.

#1292. Long balls are NOT banned at Newcastle! Matthias Jaissle insists his criticism after Everton defeat was lost in translation - having said stars were failing to follow tactics

Published: 11:50 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 12:02 EDT, 5 November 2026

Matthias Jaissle says his criticism of Newcastle’s players was lost in translation and has clarified that long balls are not forbidden under his management.

The head coach also believes that his squad understands what is being asked of them, although he says his door remains open to any player seeking clarity over his instructions.

In the wake of Monday’s 1-0 home defeat by Everton, Jaissle said that the players had failed to follow his instruction and bemoaned their use of long balls when the plan was to keep it on the floor.

Asked if those comments had been addressed with the squad this week, Jaissle said: ‘I don't know if it's a misinterpretation or a language barrier, but there is an element of that when I explained that in the press conference.

‘But it is indeed (something) we address, because we talked sometimes about the no-risk zone, where we had previously critical-ball losses leading to goals. Of course, if there is a clear risk for ball loss, then I prefer playing a long ball to our striker and protecting the ball and develop the game from there.

‘It (my comments) are not to point any fingers, not at all. Sometimes you are willing to do something, but on that day it just did not work and you make the wrong decisions. It comes also with confidence.

Matthias Jaissle, pictured giving instructions during Newcastle's defeat by Everton, has insisted long balls are not banned

'If you have scenarios where you can find easily your team-mate on the ground and we build up from there with our patterns, then you should for sure also prefer that.

‘But it's not easy, it's easier said from outside. If the confidence is missing, then you prefer to be really safe and shooting maybe even more the long ball.’

Daily Mail Sport was told this week that some players are ‘confused’ by exactly what it is Jaissle wants from them, but the head coach said: ‘The fundamental thing is that we can count on unity and togetherness.

'The door is always open if ever there is anything unclear. If you see the training then I’m pretty sure everyone understands and is fully committed. There was never a question, at least I’m not aware of it.

‘It’s important we listen to the players. If there is anything unclear, they will drop in.’

Meanwhile, Jaissle says he retains the support of the club’s hierarchy after a run of four defeats in five matches.

‘The nice part is that I got even more the feeling from within the club how committed they are (this week),’ he said.

‘That just shows me that everyone believes in the long-term project and that everyone is also aware and realistic about the journey and where we are right now.’

#1291. Slow and dull Man Utd are just not good enough

Manchester United are like John Toshack’s duvet. You fix one problem – being far too vulnerable to conceding goals – only to create another – lacking the threat to score. It is all very Meh United not Man United. The indisputable fact is they are just not very entertaining to watch. They are slow and dull.

In the end it also points to another thing. The thing highlighted in midweek by Lisandro Martínez after the Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid: they do not have the strength in depth to compete.

What they do have appears to not be fit for purpose. Certainly Michael Carrick, the under-pressure manager, is struggling to get the best out of the resources he has.

“It’s like a duvet,” Toshack, the former Real Madrid and Wales manager, famously said of football. “If you pull it up, your feet get cold. If you pull it down, your shoulders get cold.”

There will have been times in the last few days, with the intense criticism and scrutiny over his future, when Carrick will have simply felt like dragging that duvet up over his head and keeping it there.

Defeat by Leeds United would have been unthinkable. It would have put Carrick under potentially intolerable pressure in what appears to be a pivotal week, with Como away in the Champions League and a home Premier League fixture against Bournemouth in the coming days.

Was this a lifeline or the tightening of the noose for Carrick? Time will soon tell. The relief of avoiding defeat was tempered by the reality of it now being just one win in their opening seven league games – at home to newly promoted Ipswich Town – and they are down in 13th place. It is six games without a win in all competitions.

That is unacceptable and is their fewest number of league victories in a top-flight campaign since 1986-87. Back then they sacked their manager in November and brought in a certain Alex Ferguson.

The hard truth is Carrick needs to start collecting some “Ws” in those results columns. United are already 14 points behind leaders Manchester City and five outside the probable Champions League places. Qualifying again for that tournament must be the minimum expectation.

Ruben Amorim, Carrick’s predecessor, lost his job within 24 hours of the same 1-1 scoreline at Elland Road last season – dismissed after Martínez-like explosive comments again aimed at director of football Jason Wilcox. Carrick will not suffer the same fate after this, but the ice is becoming increasingly thin.

We have seen this movie before at United. A slow start to the season, a period of drift, falling out of contention, no reaction on the pitch, backing from the hierarchy that becomes increasingly unconvincing. And then a change.

Can Carrick, who genuinely does still retain support at the highest level, alter that pattern? Does he have it in him? Is he too passive like his team? Carrick said this draw felt like a “fresh start”, but on this evidence that comment can be classified as wildly optimistic.

Having directed his criticism at the United hierarchy, and specifically Wilcox, the former Leeds winger who was here, over a lack of summer signings, Martínez apologised and was named in the starting XI. But the Argentine only lasted to half-time, withdrawn injured with a tight thigh, and sat watching the second half with his hood up over his head.

What United did sign in the last window was three midfielders – at a cost of £155m – and all three started: Carlos Baleba alongside Andrey Santos with Youri Tielemans in the No 10 role, which meant Bruno Fernandes was pushed out to the left, from where he constantly wanted to come in-field, with Amad Diallo on the right.

Carrick talked of having a “fresh spine” as well as that fresh start. But it did not make for a potent combination even if, further forward, Bryan Mbeumo played through the middle and scored one. He should have scored another.

Bryan Mbeumo finds the net this time to put Manchester United 1-0 up at Leeds! 🔴 https://t.co/NKDIhlUND1

But beyond that United created little. “It was a dominant performance against Man United,” Daniel Farke, the Leeds manager, claimed. He was right. If one team deserved to win it was his. They had the chances but snatched at them with Anton Stach, in injury time, having a weak shot cleared off the line by Martínez’s replacement Noussair Mazraoui after a mistake by goalkeeper Senne Lammens. Stach had to score.

United were ahead at half-time. Mbeumo had headed wastefully wide when unmarked but did well to force his way past James Justin and meet a low cross from Tielemans to poke the ball home. The way the usually undemonstrative Carrick punched the air in his technical area showed the pressure he felt. It was something to build on. To gain control.

Leeds had started well but did not really pose much of a threat – beyond forcing Lammens to save well from Nico Elvedi’s downward header – and maybe the earlier kick-off subdued the crowd. This was far from a bear pit.

But after the break, Leeds were comfortably the better side. The nature of their equalising goal, with Dominic Calvert-Lewin too strong and alert for first Baleba and then Mbeumo to fire in from a corner, exposed the enduring softness at the heart of United.

And that must be addressed by Carrick, especially as he appeared to sacrifice attacking intent by shoring up defensively. But that duvet is looking far too inadequate right now. Or Carrick is making it appear so.

Michael Carrick says he has put on “the headphones” this week in an effort to drown out the noise, but admitted Manchester United have to stop their struggles from snowballing.

United sit just two points above the relegation zone after a 1-1 draw at Leeds left them with just one win from their opening seven Premier League matches.

Carrick claimed the result felt like a “fresh start” after a week in which Lisandro Martínez publicly apologised for criticising Jason Wilcox, the United director of football, and the Old Trafford board.

But the United manager acknowledged their position “doesn’t look too good” and that they must start winning soon to stop the club from entering another doom cycle.

“Listen, we’re not accepting it as everything’s great by any stretch, so I’m realistic with that,” said the United manager, who claimed “the headphones have been on this week”.

“But sometimes you do struggle, sometimes there’s a bit of it where you have to find a way through it. We haven’t really had to go through that yet [before now] and we have to find a way through it.

“There has been a cycle at times here over a period of time when it can go in different directions. We’ve got to be stable enough to keep doing the right things for the right reasons as a group, and we’re more than capable of winning football matches.

“I understand the situation doesn’t look too good if you look at it from a certain way, but I’ve no doubts we can go on a good run.”

United face Como in the Champions League in Italy on Wednesday before Bournemouth visit Old Trafford four days later.

Carrick said he remains convinced United can still have a strong campaign, despite their worst start to a season for 40 years. I know what we’ve got in the changing room, where we want to get to, how we want to get there,” he said. “We know we can do it.

“We’ve done it for some time, and we feel we’re a better group now, and I do feel that. Sometimes it doesn’t always show, but you get a feeling and I’m encouraged by a lot of things. And if we keep doing the right things, I think we can still have a really good season.”

Asked if he would be putting the headphones back on this week ahead of two more pivotal games, Carrick added: “Nah, it’s always quiet for me.”

Martínez was substituted at half-time at Elland Road with a tight thigh just days after his tirade at club executives and Marcus Rashford was left out for “purely tactical” reasons. “Nothing personal, the front players were doing a good job on and off the ball,” Carrick said. “Everyone is ready for Wednesday.”

The Leeds boss told Sky Sports: “We are slightly disappointed it is just a point. Overall, I felt it was not necessary to be losing at half time but it is still Manchester United. Second half, we got the equaliser, we should have kept up the dominance, too many strikes went over the crossbar but it was overall a solid performance. We should have won the game but we move on.

“We took it as a compliment that we have done many things right over the last month if we were seen as favourites against Manchester Untiedbut we have earned this. We wanted to prove the comments right.

“We were the dominant side but we couldn’t capitalise as we lacked quality in and around the box.

“It says a lot about how much respect we have earned. Overall, this is where we are at the moment and overall, it is a good place to be.

“It is still difficult in this league to win points. You have to be clinical and be very, very effective but we have to keep going.”

Speaking to Sky Sports, he said: “I think we could’ve played with a bit more quality in the final third, particularly in the first half. We were getting good quality in the box but just not enough numbers.

“We made sure in the second half we came out with more confidence going forward. I think we were unlucky not to win the game.

“They tried to [match us up formation-wise]. Not surprised given what happened last season. They were probably looking at our physical output and the way we liked to play and tried to go man-for-man.

“It took us a little bit to adjust to it, but I don’t think it was too difficult to adjust. It was more down to us and maybe a lack of quality in the final third.”

Lisandro Martínez delivered a strong and powerful message to his Manchester United team-mates: if you’re playing terribly, use the director of football as a punchbag and you might become a hero.

It is a popular play in a world in which certain players have become as adept at scapegoat-hunting as man-marking. Passionately speak about what someone else at your football club is doing wrong – particularly the unloved executives – and cast yourself as a whistleblower, selflessly exposing the truth that the long-suffering supporters deserve.

Such internal fights make for great drama, unless your own club is caught in the middle of it.

That’s why in the immediate aftermath of Martínez’s scathing comments about Jason Wilcox following the Champions League defeat by Atlético Madrid, there was a division between those who celebrated the Argentine speaking out and those who felt it was self-serving, a convenient deflection by an out-of-form player in the final year of his contract.

Just 10 months on from Ruben Amorim’s final game in charge of Manchester United, the club return to Elland Road on Sunday afternoon with another manager under pressure and the director of football again in the spotlight.

The difference is Michael Carrick still has a chance to determine the course of his United future whereas Amorim had already sealed his fate after a furious bust-up with Jason Wilcox 48 hours before his last game ended in a 1-1 draw with Leeds and post-match fireworks.

But even for a club never far from a crisis, it seems remarkable to think they are back in a tailspin so soon after Amorim’s sacking in early January.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this mouthwatering Premier League fixture between Manchester United and Leeds United at Elland Road.

Quiet week in the world of Man Utd? Don’t be silly. Following a 2-0 defeat in the Champions League against Atlético Madrid in Spain on Wednesday, defender Lisandro Martinez launched an extraordinary attack on Man Utd’s director of football Jason Wilcox and the club’s hierarchy because of a dreadful start to the campaign, which has yielded two victories in nine games across all competitions.

The Argentine criticised Man Utd’s recruitment and said he expected more, but didn’t suggest Carrick was to blame. Martinez has since apologised for his outburst and met with Wilcox, Man Utd chief executive Omar Berrada and Michael Carrick, with Telegraph Sport understanding that he’s free to play today, although his role remains unclear as we all eagerly await the team news.

Carrick is under immense pressure to get a result here in Yorkshire, with last weekend’s 1-1 draw with 10-man Tottenham at Old Trafford condemning Man Utd to their worst league start for 40 years.

With all eyes on the visitors, Leeds will be licking their lips at the prospect of piling further misery on their beleaguered opponents. Daniel Farke’s side suffered their first Premier League loss last weekend, falling 2-1 to Arsenal at the Emirates after going a goal up, but the mood remains positive after a solid start to the campaign.

Leeds are eighth and the club will be harbouring ambitions of a top-half finish in the Premier League for the first time since the 2019/20 season, with the prospect of qualifying for European football not out of the realm of possibility.

Unlike Man Utd, Leeds have a settled, reliable system that clearly suits their current squad. Elland Road will also be a cauldron of hostility and noise, given the fierce backdrop between these two bitter rivals.

This has all the ingredients to be a thrilling and fascinating watch as we bring you the latest updates, information and drama. Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news coming shortly.

#1290. Spalletti: ‘Juventus must build on positive signs, otherwise back to square one’

Luciano Spalletti insists Juventus ‘showed positive signs’ when beating Napoli, but they must build on those in the Europa League with AZ Alkmaar ‘otherwise we go back to square one.’

It kicks off in Alkmaar at 20.00 GMT (21.00 CET).

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens on the Liveblog.

The Bianconeri got back on track domestically with their 2-0 victory against Napoli on Sunday, and are unbeaten so far in the Europa League with two wins and a 2-2 draw with Stade Rennais.

However, injuries rule out Weston McKennie, Kenan Yildiz, Manuel Locatelli, Nico Gonzalez, Francisco Conceicao, Zeki Celik, Khephren Thuram and Kamil Grabara.

“Alajbegovic works well with the rest of the team, he can pass the ball and cut inside, creating a moment out of nowhere to shock the opposition, as we saw against Napoli,” Spalletti told Sky Sport Italia.

“There is also an opportunity for us to rotate ahead of the trip to Fiorentina. We changed four this evening, but what becomes fundamental is to repeat the kind of performance we saw with Napoli.

“That match showed clear signals, it is important to recognise their power and repeat them with more emphasis and consistency in future, otherwise we go straight back to square one. From here on is the opportunity for real growth.”

McKennie is left out due to a fitness issue, although he should be back this weekend in Serie A, so Pape Matar Sarr steps into the starting XI.

“McKennie is someone who knows how to encapsulate the mentality of a strong team, he fights everywhere all over the pitch to help out, he is convinced of his own strength,” explained Spalletti.

“Pape Sarr plays this evening and we want to see how he can repeat what he did at Tottenham in important matches. I want the best out of my players, just like we did in the last game.

“We’ve got Juan Cabal and Lloyd Kelly back to fitness, we trust these lads, but they too need to prove they’ve got the right attitude.”

AZ Alkmaar are unbeaten at home in 17 UEFA matches going back to October 2023, so are a tough prospect here.

“They haven’t lost here in a long time, so we need a great performance,” warned Spalletti.

“We can’t come here and think of controlling the match, we need to raise the level, recognise the importance of the gestures made during the game, and repeat them more consistently, even constantly.

“I did see positive signs from the team, and it is essential we repeat them tonight. AZ Alkmaar have a clear identity, they know what they want to do, they all know what they need to play there. Juventus still need to fully understand that.”

#1289. Amorim: ‘No explanation for Milan performance, we are not ready to play’

Ruben Amorim was furious and bemused by Milan’s 2-0 Europa League defeat to Ferencvaros. ‘There is no explanation. We were not prepared to play football. We are not ready to play every three days.’

The Rossoneri cannot seem to find any consistency, as they can follow up the 3-1 Derby della Madonnina triumph against rivals Inter with this remarkably sluggish performance in the same stadium.

Lenny Joseph pounced on two defensive and goalkeeping errors to beat 21-year-old Lorenzo Torriani, deputising for suspended Mike Maignan and injured Pietro Terracciano, to give Ferencvaros a 2-0 victory at San Siro.

“There is no explanation. There is nothing I can say, especially about the first half,” confessed a visibly shaken Amorim to Sky Sport Italia.

“I don’t remember us playing any other first half performances like that. This is about ambition, concentration. We gifted opportunities, made stupid errors. We were not prepared to play football tonight.”

How does the coach think this can be the same team that ran riot against Inter at the weekend in Serie A, yet had such a totally different approach?

“It is difficult to explain,” added Amorim.

“Quite simply, we were not ready to go from the derby to this competition. When you play with the Milan jersey, you have a responsibility, and you cannot turn up like this.

“Probably I didn’t do enough to make sure the team was ready.”

There are quite a few injuries that reduce the options, but after three defeats in the opening four Europa League matches, it is evident they struggle on a Thursday evening.

“We are not ready to be competitive on two fronts. We’ve got to work on our approach and the way we view football. There are no excuses tonight, there is nothing that I can say.

“I usually have a lot to say to defend my team, but tonight I really don’t. We must be humble and try to understand what happened.”

It is not the first time that Milan have stepped up several gears in the big games, only to crumble when they seem to take things for granted, so what can Amorim do about this situation that goes back long before his arrival?

“Perhaps I did something wrong over the last two days, but I saw the team had similar problems last season. We have to find a solution. We were not ready tonight, we showed no courage. If we don’t win, we should at least do everything we can to turn the situation around, but we didn’t see that tonight.”

It was the first match where Strahinja Pavlovic was allowed rest after playing almost every minute of the season so far, and Amorim admits the defender was missed.

“Everyone ought to train like Pavlovic. He is ready to die in training, he sets a good example. At times, players struggle when they do not start matches, but there are no excuses, we ought to have won with those who started too.

“We have to fix it! We cannot think that this is just how it goes. We should’ve done so many things better this evening,” said an increasingly agitated Amorim.

“Just being better on the second balls would’ve helped. We were just not in the game.”

At this stage, losing three of the opening four, it is likely Milan won’t be able to turn this around and stay in the Europa League beyond January.

“I have to think about Serie A, obviously, but we do need to do well in the Europa League too. We can and must win games despite squad rotation. We have to be ready, and right now we are not, to play and win every three days.

“I will not give up on this competition, though, so as long as it is mathematically possible, we will fight in this competition just like the others.”

How long will Italy have four places in CL? They are garbage and doesn’t seem interested to play in Europe where they play at a higher pace than Serie A. Their stadiums are worse than elsewhere and they loose out on coefficient points again and again. The coaches in Italy are too defensive. Only Como play well.

lame excuses! what a shame to Italian football, the teams are sluggish and not ready to play,they deserve early elimination

We have a team that can bsat Inter but we are not good enoug to beat Farencavos? The earlier they get rid of this one the better for everybody.

#1288. Liverpool Confidential: Billionaires' investment set to beat deadline, new deal for Trey Nyoni, the academy kids who shone in Istanbul and Mor Talla Ndiaye's visa issues

Published: 12:00 EDT, 5 November 2026 | Updated: 12:04 EDT, 5 November 2026

The deal for a group of billionaires to buy a minority stake in Liverpool remains on track to pass a deadline set by the new independent football regulator.

The consortium led by Amit Bhatia, known as 1892 Holdings, agreed to purchase a 38 per cent stake in Fenway Sports Group’s controlling interest in the club earlier this season. And despite some anxieties externally and in the fanbase about a lack of updates, I have been told this week that everything is moving in the right direction.

Sources close to Bhatia and his consortium insist the process takes time but there are no hitches and it is still expected to beat the deadline. It is understood the date in question is in December and in accordance with the new regulator, who must take within 90 days to issue a final suitability determination for prospective new owners or senior executives.

Indeed, this week brought the news that FSG are in exploratory talks to buy a significant stake in Formula One team Cadillac. Both FSG and Cadillac were contacted for comment around that story – and insisted it is an ongoing process.

One source pointed to the fact that FSG clearly expect to have some ‘spare pennies lying around’ – hinting the Liverpool investment will go through.

Senior FSG staff have constantly stressed that selling 38 per cent of the club does not mean they are losing interest and that they are as committed as ever, though the potential for the buy-in to become a full-scale takeover at some point in the future remains.

Bhatia is backed by his billionaire father-in-law Lakshmi Mittal, plus Jeff Bezos and Eduardo Saverin.

Amit Bhatia (second left) is heading up a consortium to buy a stake in Liverpool from John Henry (second right) and his Fenway Sports Group

Liverpool supporters hope the deal will transform the club's fortunes on the pitch

Jeremie Frimpong has had rotten luck with injuries since he joined Liverpool – and Andoni Iraola ruled him out for more than a month with a problem he suffered at Brentford on October 17.

I understand the Dutch international is now all-but fit and could play this weekend if needed – however, given his high number of injuries, a decision has been made to delay his return.

Liverpool were recently punished for bringing back Dominik Szoboszlai too quickly as the Hungarian pulled up shortly after his first start upon his return, which set him back a fortnight.

Frimpong missed only seven Bayer Leverkusen games through injury in four years at the club according to Transfermarkt, but has already sat out nearly 30 Liverpool matches. Most of those absences have been hamstring related, so Frimpong is not being rushed back and will be given the international break to continue working on his recovery.

Jeremie Frimpong has had rotten luck with injuries since he joined Liverpool and went down again against Brentford last month. However, the Dutch international is now close to a return

Trey Nyoni has been offered a bumper new contract to reward him for his fine progress.

The 19-year-old, who scored his first Liverpool goal in the defeat in Istanbul against Fenerbahce on Wednesday night, has had a stellar rise since Iraola took over at Liverpool.

Nyoni, signed from Leicester City in 2023, was in many matchday squads and featured sparingly last season but has come of age this campaign and has already doubled his first-team minutes – with three quarters of the season still to play.

Nottingham Forest made a £30million bid in the summer but Iraola identified him as a key asset and he will be rewarded handsomely for his progress.

Trey Nyoni scored his first Liverpool goal on Wednesday night in the Champions League loss against Fenerbahce

Your question answered: What's the January priority?

One topic fans have asked me about this week is which position is a priority in the January and summer transfer windows.

The first area to mention is midfield. I have reported in the past how Chelsea are currently ahead of Liverpool in the race for Bournemouth's Alex Scott, so let’s keep an eye on that – and the situation of Lamine Camara of Monaco. But I think the priority has to be a left-back.

Are Milos Kerkez and Kostas Tsimikas good enough? Neither have performed at the required level so far this season and bringing Tsimikas back from a loan at Roma – where he barely played – felt like a bit of a cop-out. It has to be a priority position in the next 12 months.

Liverpool flew straight home from Istanbul after the loss to Fenerbahce and did not land on Merseyside until past 2am. It is a departure from last season, when Arne Slot would often have his squad stay for two nights on European away days.

Players are said to be big fans of the extra night at home with most preferring to sleep in their own beds.

Iraola did not hold a post-match team talk after Fenerbahce but will debrief the squad when back in training, having branded the defeat ‘cheap’ and ‘messy’.

Another UEFA Youth League game, another hat-trick for Will Wright.

I was in place on the outskirts of Istanbul on Wednesday afternoon to watch the 18-year-old bag his second treble in four European matches this term, making it 13 goals for the season in all competitions.

Wright had a heated exchange with Josh Sonni-Lambie over who would take a penalty but the pair have smoothed things over now after Wright took it and scored. The striker’s assist for Finn Inglethorpe was also a notable moment that showed he is a team player and not a greedy No9.

Liverpool's Will Wright scored another hat-trick in the UEFA Youth League on Wednesday, against Fenerbahce Under 19s

I was also impressed by right back Oliver O’Connor, who looks like a real athlete. He aced every physical pre-season test for the academy and is versatile, with a quality delivery into the penalty area.

The Scouser joined the club aged six and has been a midfielder for most of his career. Boss Rob Page does not necessarily see him as a right back long-term but he caught the eye up and down that flank.

Those who did watch the academy game – and the first-team later on – would have been wondering where defender Mor Talla Ndiaye was. He is a mainstay in the Youth League XI and has been on the seniors’ bench several times.

It is believed the Senegalese defender had a visa issue and could not feature in the game in Turkey, though next month’s away match in Bruges is not expected to pose the same problem.

Liverpool's Mor Talla Ndiaye (centre) was nowhere to be seen in Istanbul due to visa issues

Also in academy news, young midfielder Michael Laffey has signed with the OmniSports agency who represent the likes of Wright and Crystal Palace midfielder Adam Wharton. Under 21s captain Laffey, whose dad owns the Glenbuck pub in Anfield, made the first-team bench a fortnight ago.

Liverpool supporters have drawn the short straw and will pay more than any of their English counterparts for a pint while following their team in Europe this season.

That’s according to data from LiveScore, who have worked out that Reds will pay an average of £4.91 per pint on their travels.

Still, £4.91 for a pint? Better than most places at home. You might need one after watching Liverpool’s defending this week!

#1287. Europa League Liveblog: Milan-Ferencvaros, AZ Alkmaar-Juventus, Atalanta-Kairat

Atalanta have just two draws in five competitive matches, so cannot slip up against Kairat Almaty.

AZ Alkmaar are unbeaten at home in Europe for 3 years…

Kelly robbed at the touchline by Oufkir, it doesn’t look like it rolled out of play, sent down the right for Dijkstra, who pulled back for the Meerdink tap-in!
