Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of this Europa League tie between Bournemouth and AC Milan at the Vitality Stadium.

Back in 2008, Bournemouth’s prospect of a European meeting with Milan seemed impossible. After entering administration with crippling debts of around £4m, Bournemouth were handed a 10-point deduction and relegated from League One. To make matters worse, a hefty 17-point deduction was given to the club ahead of the 2008-09 League Two season, with relegation to non-league seeming inevitable. However, midway through the campaign, the transformative Eddie Howe was parachuted in as Bournemouth’s saviour, eventually guiding the club to safety.

Fast forward to October 2026 in an extraordinary rise and Bournemouth are competing in their first-ever European campaign in the club’s 127-year existence. They welcome Milan to Dorset, having earned back-to-back victories over Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz to kick off their inaugural Europa League adventure in style.

Now, they host the second most successful side in the European Cup history. In terms of heritage and silverware, these clubs could not be further apart, but on the pitch, it’s incredibly tough to call.

On Sunday, Marco Rose’s Bournemouth picked up their first Premier League win of the season, beating 10-man Sunderland 2-0 at the Vitality thanks to goals from Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson to move out of the relegation zone.

Meanwhile, Ruben Amorim is in charge at Milan and returns to England after a tumultuous 14-month reign at Manchester United, where he was sacked in January. Milan lost their opening Europa League fixture 2-0 at home to Benfica, before battering Salzburg 4-0 in Austria, with Alphadjo Cisse netting a stunning hat-trick.

Crystal Palace are also in the Europa League tonight and face an incredibly daunting away trip to Turkish side Besiktas. Pressure is firmly on manager Pierre Sage following the 5-0 humiliation against Brighton last weekend and a shaky start to the season. Palace lost 3-2 to Sage’s former employers Lyon in their previous Europa League outing, with a positive performance and result needed to restore the fans’ faith.

Both games kick-off at 20:00, with team news coming imminently.

#1248. Simeone equals Luis Aragonés’s LaLiga wins record as Atlético Madrid beat Levante 2-0

Atlético Madrid won 2-0 at Levante on Saturday, making it a milestone afternoon for Diego Simeone. Barcelona are next up in the league, and one more victory would give him the coaching record on his own.

Atlético Madrid’s trip to Valencia ended with a milestone for their coach. It took the Argentine 565 LaLiga matches in charge to reach the mark, according to Club Atlético de Madrid.

The visitors went in at the interval a goal up. Álex Baena supplied the pass for their second. Earlier, Morten Hjulmand had a goal ruled out by VAR in the 17th minute. Levante coach Luís Castro was shown a yellow card for dissent a minute later.

The scoreline did not reflect the balance of chances. Levante shot 14 times from inside the box, while Atlético managed 3. The hosts’ expected goals reached 1.33, against 0.63 for the visitors.

Jan Oblak was the difference. Around the tenth minute, he made a crucial one-handed save to deny Dani Requena, Infobae (EFE) reported. The goalkeeper finished with a rating of 8.08.

Atlético had more of the ball, with 54% possession and 560 passes to Levante’s 450. Simeone made two double changes. Jonathan David and Sørloth replaced Lee Kang-In and Julián Álvarez in the 67th minute. Le Normand and Lookman came on for Barrios and Baena in the 76th.

The result was Atlético’s seventh league win in a row. It briefly took them top of the table. The teams’ last meeting, on 31 January 2026, had ended 0-0 in Valencia.

Simeone already leads Aragonés on wider measures at the club. Across all official competitions with Atlético, he has 479 wins from 813 games. Aragonés managed 308 wins from 612 games there. The club credits Simeone with eight trophies as coach, two more than Aragonés’s six.

The coming weeks carry real weight. From 11 games, Atlético have nine wins, one draw and one defeat. Real Madrid sit third on 24 points from 10 games.

Three big points in Valencia 💪 pic.twitter.com/W1JUeW8Uqh

— Atlético de Madrid (@atletienglish) October 31, 2026

Levante are 17th on 10 points after their second straight defeat. They travel to Tarancón in the Copa del Rey on Thursday 5 November. Their next league game is away to Celta de Vigo at 18:30 on Sunday 8 November.

Atlético host Bayern München in the Champions League on Tuesday 3 November. Their meeting with Barcelona is the last match of matchday 12, kicking off at 21:00 on Sunday 8 November. The Riyadh Air Metropolitano will stage the game.

#1247. Manchester City might decry the 'Red Cartel' of Arsenal, Liverpool, and Manchester United, but is it real?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

As two of their number face off at Anfield on Sunday afternoon, this would seem to be a good time to find yourself one of the so-called Red Cartel. Manchester City are facing the prospect of sanctions that would cast them out from the Premier League's inner circle, while those other big-six clubs that play in white and blue have spent half a decade retreating from the title race (as, it should be noted, have Manchester United).

If City's sanctions land this season, it could be that Liverpool are the nearest rivals to Arsenal in the title race, another domestic crown carved up by the grand old dukes of the English game. Believe City's defenders and this triopoly is just what Abu Dhabi protected the Premier League from. "A conspiracy by the Red Cartel to keep clubs like Manchester City out of sitting at the top table," was how one supporter described the finding that City had breached 114 of the Premier League's rules over a nine-season period. When their chief executive Ferran Soriano talks about a "Premier League conspiracy theory," well, no one thinks the shadowy cabal is being led by Brentford and Bournemouth.

A version of this framing has gathered pace beyond the realms of the Etihad Stadium, intermingling with burgeoning dissatisfaction over financial rules from both the Premier League and UEFA, that have resulted in sanctions for grand old clubs such as Everton, Nottingham Forest and Aston Villa. It was best articulated by ex-Chelsea midfielder Joe Cole earlier this month, who insisted that the game's financial settlement was locking out ambitious clubs in a way that his former club was not when it was bought by Roman Abramovich.

"The regulations that are in place are not doing the job they're supposed to do," he said. Of course, there is one crucial caveat to any assessment of the Premier League's profit and sustainability regulations (PSR) and the squad cost ratio that has replaced it. When one team is found to have flouted them through "sham" contracts that inflated its revenue to the tune of over $1 billion, it is quite hard to know how this sport might operate on a level playing field. Under Pep Guardiola, City's domestic achievements were unprecedented. No English side had sustained a four-year spell of domestic preeminence, won all three domestic trophies or delivered a 100-point season.

Anyone who argues that, were it not for City, this would have been a Premier League dominated by the big boys in red must accept that they are engaged in historical counterfactuals. What actually happened was a record-breaking spell of dominance by a team that, it was found, "systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade."

Then again, if you were to journey through the what-ifs, maybes and never-weres of the last 18 years, you would struggle to immediately and convincingly argue that it was City and City alone who stood against the LaLiga-fication of the Premier League. Indeed, there was never really a period when all three of Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United were in the chasing pack. The last season in which these teams all finished in the Premier League top four was 2008-09, the campaign whose defining moment was the unheralded sale of City to Sheikh Mansour on Sept. 1. Indeed, 2026-27 should be considered a banner year in the smoke-filled, oak-clad boardrooms of the cartel. For the first time since 2009-10, all three of their teams are playing in the Champions League. The intervening 17 years had their ups and downs for all three: a pair of eighth-placed finishes each for Arsenal and Liverpool, that 15th place for Manchester United and whatever they have themselves on course for this time out. One or two have generally been there or thereabouts, but all three at once just has not happened. Nor did it really happen before the Manchester City takeover.

The period between 1996 and 2009 is the exception to the rule, containing 10 of the 11 seasons in which Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United have all occupied top-four positions. Either side of that, you have broad similarities. The late 1950s and early 1960s is the only period in English footballing history when none of the triumvirate was in the top four, and the turn of the millennium the only one when all three were.

The mid-2000s was also perhaps the era when the Premier League's most successful sides had the most meaningful financial heft when compared to the rest of the English game. In the year before the takeover at what was then the City of Manchester Stadium, Manchester United posted revenues of €324.8 million, making them the second-richest club in Europe behind Real Madrid.

At that time, the seventh-richest club in England was, ironically, Manchester City. Their €104 million in earnings was barely enough to place them in the Deloitte Money League outright. In 20th place, they were being out-earned not only by the boys in red but also by the likes of Fenerbahce, VfB Stuttgart and Olympique de Marseille. The gap between them and England's monied elite was vast, United raking in more than three times the revenue of their noisy neighbors.

Move on to the most recent Money League and the picture has changed more significantly than it might initially appear. In 2024-25, the richest club in England still played in red, Liverpool taking in €836.1 million in their title-winning season. This time, however, the seventh-richest English side, Aston Villa, had earned €450.2 million.

In absolute terms, of course, the gap is far greater, but what matters more is the proportions. In 2008, the seventh-richest team in England earned less than a third of what the richest did. Seventeen years later, the richest earns less than double. Meanwhile, the comparative purchasing power of any Premier League side has risen. Nine of the 20 richest clubs in the game are English, as are half of the top 30. Two decades ago, it would have been unimaginable that a club like Brentford might snare Mamadou Sangare from the runners-up in Ligue 1, that Bournemouth might pick up future stars like Junior Kroupi and Antonio Silva, and that a newly promoted side like Ipswich might have the finances to land a Bundesliga champion in Exequiel Palacios.

As football finance expert Kieran Maguire puts it, "the Premier League is the Super League." Scarcely a week goes by without it being impressed on Manchester United that they cannot spend their way out of their latest crisis. It is perhaps too early to be certain what this all means, but it is worth noting that in the past four seasons Bournemouth, Aston Villa, Newcastle (unable to turn on the money taps like City were when they were taken over by sovereign wealth) and Brighton have all broken into the top six. If the gravitational pull of talent to the Premier League remains as is, an era of relative competitiveness seems plausible. Meanwhile, supporters of West Ham, Villa and Crystal Palace are discovering that a domestic cup win or a strong Premier League campaign can be parlayed into the sorts of European nights they will never forget.

This is not the 1950s or 1960s anymore, when provincial clubs from across the land could take a big swing at a title, but imagine a world where the regulations that Cole and others bemoan were struck from the books. Nothing would stand in the way of those with sovereign-wealth money -- Newcastle United and Manchester City -- but themselves. Those other ambitious clubs that just want to spend their owners' cash could soon find themselves dicing with danger. PSR and UEFA's financial fair play regulations would appear to have entrenched the old powers, but in the last decade and a half no Premier League side with dreams of grandeur has taken the route to the precipice of oblivion that Leeds United and Portsmouth did.

The arc of the Premier League itself might be very slowly bending toward parity, but that does not mean that Manchester United, Liverpool and Arsenal are necessarily happy with the status quo. Indeed, if there is any justification for the conspiratorial thinking of City supporters, it comes in how their rivals have attempted to change the playing field to suit their needs.

In October 2020, the owners of Liverpool and Manchester United proposed Project Big Picture, offering the lower leagues a financial life raft in the form of an immediate $325 million payment and a 25% cut of future Premier League TV deals. That came with strings attached, the most notable being a shrinking of the calendar that would surely have suited those teams with lucrative Champions League fixtures and preseason tours. Nine clubs would also have been afforded special voting rights, Liverpool, Manchester United, Arsenal (and City) among them.

A little over six months later came proposals for a European Super League. Chelsea, Manchester City and Tottenham were in on this one, but it was notable that three of the league's five founders were Joel Glazer (co-owner of Manchester United), John W. Henry (owner of Liverpool) and Stan Kroenke (owner of Arsenal).

"There has been a broad attempt to change the landscape," says Maguire. "Kroenke, Henry and the Glazers are likely to have broadly similar views to each other. Conceptually there is no doubt that what they would like from football going forwards [is greater influence and revenue]. Spurs would like to be at the table with them. Chelsea under Clearlake Capital, the same. Under Abramovich, I'm not sure it would be the same.

"Manchester City were quite happy being Manchester City. They were quite prepared to achieve what they wanted to independently, as we now find, through sham contracts."

If that all sounds quite cartel-ish, Maguire would suggest otherwise. "A cartel stops everybody else from taking part. This is an interest group who have common interest. They're trying to hijack the legacy sport of football for their own ends."

Their past wheezes may have fallen foul of the English supporter, but Maguire predicts they will try again, pointing to the increasingly likely re-election of Gianni Infantino as FIFA president next March. That could mean a doubling down on the Club World Cup, for which a joint venture has been agreed with European Football Clubs. It is expected that the 2029 iteration of the competition will make room for more clubs per country, opening the door for at least some of the Premier League's red brigade (unfortunately for Manchester United, qualifying for any global competition on sporting merit seems a long shot).

"Those clubs will want to ensure that they're at the top [of the] table because Chelsea made £80 million from winning a competition last year that nobody watched," says Maguire. "They will watch if we've got four Spanish teams, four English teams and so on as opposed to the two of the latter. It would have helped if it had been Manchester United and Liverpool, as opposed to Chelsea and Manchester City. The media interest would have been there.

"It's Manchester United, Arsenal and Liverpool that drive viewing figures, that drive clicks, that drive interest, that drive engagement."

And that is the fundamental truth that drives so much frustration at Manchester United, Arsenal and Liverpool from City in particular, but also from those across the Premier League who share Cole's view. There may not be a Red Cartel, but it is hard to argue against the fact that those three teams are a bit different. Anyone who has worked in football media will be able to tell you that there is the web traffic generated by those teams and then, a chasm later, there is the rest of the league. You might not need that expertise either. Wherever in the world you are reading this, there is a fair chance you are more likely to cross paths with an Arsenal, Liverpool or Man United fan than a fan of any other team, with Chelsea as a potential exception.

That much is apparent in Brand Finance's most recent assessment of the value of the world's top 50 football clubs. One might reasonably assume that City's perceived value to non-UAE sponsors has taken something of a kicking over the course of the last month. If that is the case, quite the gap has emerged between England's premium brands and the rest.

Ultimately, these three clubs timed their ascent fortunately. Liverpool's success in the 1970s and 1980s was among the contributory factors in their popularity in continental Europe, particularly Scandinavia, as indeed it was among floating voters in the UK. The establishment of the Premier League as a global sporting mega league dovetailed with Arsene Wenger, Sir Alex Ferguson, Thierry Henry and David Beckham duking it out for titles. It's no wonder so many felt compelled to pick a side in that great rivalry. And once you've picked your team, you're probably stuck with it. This isn't a grocery store.

These teams aren't willing to settle for what they have. Kevin Demoff, president of team and media operations at Kroenke Sports & Entertainment, has suggested that "Arsenal can be the biggest global brand in the world." The Gunners, who have worked deliberately to situate themselves at the nexus of culture and creativity since being fully taken over by the Kroenkes in 2018, are the yardstick by which the rest of the KSE empire is assessed, Demoff added. That is a collection of sports teams that includes the Denver Nuggets, Los Angeles Rams and now the Los Angeles Angels. Against all those teams, many of them championship winners, it is the team from north London that is considered the most premium brand.

Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United have the weight of history in their favor. Sponsors want their reflected glow. Players dream of taking the field at the Emirates, Anfield and Old Trafford. Managers convince themselves they are the one to turn the project around. Can anything be done about that? The rest of the Premier League could drag them into a more balanced playing field in financial terms.

Maguire's pitch is a hard cap based on average player costs with a "super tax." "What the owner has to do is put the additional cash in an escrow account. If the owner walks away or if their business goes belly up then you've got three years' worth of physical cash to acclimatise to a different lifestyle." Even he acknowledges that it's a hard sell. "Liverpool aren't going to vote for it because it increases competition. Brighton aren't going to vote for it because [owner] Tony Bloom doesn't have enough money to compete with Newcastle and Aston Villa."

Proposals for an anchoring system, which would have limited spending on squad costs to five times the broadcast and prize money of the league's bottom club and might have included a salary cap, were summarily dismissed when put to a vote in November 2025. Seven clubs voted in favor of the proposals. Manchester City were among those to vote against.

Realistically, even balancing out the money only does so much. If the English top flight were to implement the sort of financial regulations more commonly associated with the NBA or NFL, Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United would still be the premium franchises. Their resonance, their location, their history would attract the best in much the same way as the Los Angeles Lakers or Miami Heat do. However you organize a competition, there is no escaping the fact that some teams are just bigger deals than others.

Given the opportunity to hamstring the richest teams, the Premier League, in which television revenue is still distributed more equitably than in many other major European leagues, continually chooses not to. That, of course, is the point. If ever the other 17 clubs deemed the imagined cabal to be over-mighty, they could bring it to heel swiftly under the "tyranny of the majority" that was Manchester City's issue when they were fighting the league over associated party transactions. It would seem quite a challenge to run the Premier League from the shadows when you have less than half the votes required to block any changes.

And so no, there is no Red Cartel. But then you, I and Manchester City probably knew that already.

If last season's visit to Anfield taught Arsenal anything, it was the need for a killer in the final third to break the game open. Fail to do so and they are vulnerable to the sort of magic that bamboozled them in August of last year, even if the man who scored that brilliant free-kick winner, Dominik Szoboszlai, is a doubt for Liverpool on Sunday.

And if this game is indeed one that will be decided by what Mikel Arteta terms the "moments players," then it could scarcely have come at a worse time for the Arsenal manager. Bukayo Saka -- the Gunners' top shot taker, goal scorer and expected goals compiler -- has more than a month left on the sidelines with the thigh injury he suffered in Munich. Noni Madueke could miss the trip with an ankle injury. Christos Tzolis has returned to training but has not played for his new club in more than a month. Max Dowman, the precocious youngster whom Arteta has already entrusted with turning the tide on Merseyside, will serve the first of a three-game ban for his controversial red card.

It speaks to the depth at Arteta's disposal that, even if none of the aforementioned quartet play, there will still be game changers in the side. Even so, this does feel like an occasion where a first-choice center forward in top form would be handy. Kai Havertz is not that. Twelve games in and this has been perhaps the weirdest season of all since this esoteric forward landed on English soil in 2020. At his best, he has blown his former club Chelsea away. His worst, meanwhile, includes a wasteful performance in the EFL Cup defeat at Fleetwood and a baffling new tendency to slip offside.

The obvious answer when a player slides from peak to trough in a matter of weeks is to consult his injury record. Havertz did return from the last international break early after straining a muscle and went straight back into the side, playing an hour against Leeds and featuring in every other game since. In those six games he has no goals and one assist. In most of the minutes he has played, he has struggled to link the Arsenal attack together the way he usually does, let alone to threaten the opposition goal. That is not, however, a hangover from his injury travails.

"There's nothing to do with that," said Arteta. "It's true that in terms of the numbers, we have dropped those numbers but he certainly had the chances as well to play."

That was the case against Fleetwood, seven shots for the German adding up to 0.72 expected goals. That sounds perfectly adequate on first pass, and there are certainly others in the Arsenal side who ought to have asked more of a League Two defense. And yet when chasing a game for 70 minutes, is it fair to ask for more than three-quarters of an xG from the senior attacker of the English champions, a man who has scored in two Champions League finals?

Wanting a bit more has been a familiar experience for both Chelsea and Arsenal during his time with them. For the Gunners, it has been over two and a half years since they discovered just how good Havertz could be for them. The shift to center forward in a 3-1 win over Sunday's opponents, Liverpool, was the start of a brilliant year leading the line. Across 37 Premier League games, the Germany international delivered 18 goals and nine assists, not Erling Haaland numbers but exceptional output for the center forward in Arteta's everyone-eats offense.

Even since that brilliant run, there have been flashes. For an hour in May's Champions League final, Havertz was as threatening an attacker as anyone in PSG colors. A few weeks earlier he had been excellent in defeat to Manchester City, not the first time he had bossed Arsenal's title rival. If Chelsea have the misfortune of running into their former star, they're probably going to get him in the mood to do some damage. Of all the attackers available to Arteta this week, Havertz is the nearest he has to a big-game hunter. Indeed, if you want to make the case against Arsenal "just signing a striker" in January (you shouldn't), a key component of your argument ought to be how few players suit this manager as well as a fully fit Havertz. It is just that, well, a fully fit Havertz has been an elusive creature. And yet if Arteta will not use injuries as justification for the current wobble, perhaps we shouldn't. And wobble this is. Through eight league games, Havertz is averaging fewer shots, goals and non-penalty xG than in any other season in his Arsenal career on a per-90 basis. The same is true when you adjust for the fact that the 27-year-old is touching the ball a bit less on average this season than last. There is one notable stat where Havertz's numbers have skyrocketed, though, and that is in offsides. In every Premier League season before this one, he was caught out behind the opposition defense on less than one occasion per 90 minutes. In most of them, he averaged around one offside per two full games played. This year, however, no one in the league matches Havertz's 10 offsides already, and the gap is not particularly close. Joint-second on seven are his teammate Bukayo Saka and Dominic Calvert-Lewin of Leeds.

Now, the sample size of minutes is still small and open to distortion. It might be that one explanation for Havertz's skyrocketing offsides is that he has played Aston Villa and their occasionally effective, invariably cavalier high line. Equally, not all of those 10 offsides are about what the defense did well or about a run that came at just the wrong moment from the center forward. Watch Havertz move a good moment too soon to collect a pass off his friend and captain Martin Odegaard before bending well wide from a promising shooting position against Villa, and you see what looks like a forward who is simply off color, nothing more and nothing less, really. Sometimes the easiest explanation is the correct one. Havertz is just a bit out of sync with both his game and that of his teammates, as his manager acknowledged on Friday.

"That kind of form and that kind of efficiency with the front players, it's very common," said Arteta. "Full trust on him and what he's doing."

The natural response, then, for Arteta would be to pick the next cab off the rank, as he did in the win over Everton where Viktor Gyokeres started. That was the Swede's best game of the season, but he still did not register a shot. Gyokeres scored against Fleetwood but took only two other shots. Per 90, he averages 0.92 shots, 16th on Arsenal, with both left backs ahead of him. The evidence of his past entanglements with elite opposition suggests that Gyokeres is not the player to turn to at Anfield.

Instead, it will be Havertz, in need of something of a jump-start to his season. While he retains the "full trust" of a manager who has never faltered in his support, there might be time enough to sniff out his best form.

#1245. Athletic end Real Sociedad’s four-game league run as visitors protest Berenguer penalty

Athletic Club beat Real Sociedad 2-1 at San Mamés on Sunday 1 November to end their rivals' run of four straight league wins. The visitors have formally disputed the first-half penalty that decided the derby, while Athletic lost another striker to injury.

Every goal in the Bilbao derby arrived before half-time.

Nico Williams provided the assist for the opening goal. Luka Sučić equalised on the half-hour. A crowd of 50,092 watched the game.

Before kick-off, Unai Simón presented his Yashin Trophy to the home crowd. A minute’s silence was also held for the victims of the Urda rail accident.

The visitors left Bilbao angry about the decisive spot-kick. In its official match report, Real Sociedad called it a penalty that never was and criticised VAR for not stepping in. The club statement added that the chip inside the match ball shows Jon Aramburu made contact with the ball in his challenge on Nico Williams.

Pellegrino Matarazzo said that for him it was clearly not a penalty. The Real Sociedad coach could not understand why VAR had not intervened to cancel it. He was booked for dissent in the 65th minute, a minute after Mamadou Sarr received a yellow card for the same offence. Referee Alejandro Hernandez showed Real Sociedad four yellow cards in total, against two for Athletic.

The statistics point in two directions. Real Sociedad dominated the ball, completing 514 accurate passes to Athletic’s 307. Terzić’s side created the clearer chances, however. Unai Simón made four saves, while Álex Remiro made one. Sučić was the highest-rated player on the pitch at 7.52.

The victory came at a cost. Maroan Sannadi felt his hamstring early in the game. Athletic will need one or two more days to know how long he will be out. His injury follows Gorka Guruzeta’s serious knee injury at Valencia on 17 October, which left the squad short of strikers.

With 83 minutes on the pitch, Navarro created four key passes and was rated 7.2.

The win was Athletic’s third in a row across all competitions, after a 6-1 victory over Prat and a 4-0 win against Getafe. They sit seventh, two points behind Sevilla. Real Betis are four points clear of Real Sociedad.

#1244. Matthias Jaissle throwing his players under the bus is a dangerous game. Newcastle have no identity, no direction and no patterns - and that's on the manager, writes CRAIG HOPE

Published: 05:50 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 04:25 EDT, 4 November 2026

There often comes a point in a manager’s reign when the blame for defeat shifts from the dugout to the dressing room, and it is invariably the point of no return. Rarely does it arrive after just nine matches.

So when Matthias Jaissle took aim at his players in the wake of Newcastle’s 1-0 defeat by Everton on Monday, it was arguably a more concerning display than the 90 minutes which had preceded it, as alarming as those had been.

Jaissle’s post-match reflections were not inaccurate. This was not a manager talking nonsense. He fronted up and gave what felt like honest answers.

The 38-year-old is bright and articulate and, with each defeat, has shown an increasing humility that was less visible during the optimism of his introductory days.

To show the players the underside of the bus so soon, however, is as baffling a tactic as the strategy enacted on the pitch, even if Jaissle insists that performance had no resemblance to what he had asked of his team.

Rather, says the German, he had wanted his players to keep the ball on the floor and get the wingers in one-on-one situations high up the pitch. What he saw was a collection of long balls and a heading-practice session for Everton’s centre backs. The wingers, meanwhile, were spectators.

When a manager blames the players for defeat - as Matthias Jaissle did after Newcastle lost to Everton on Monday night - it is often the beginning of the end for the man in the dugout

Newcastle winger Harvey Barnes struggled to get on the ball during the defeat by Everton

‘The plan was not to shoot the long balls,’ he said.

Nor was the plan to shoot at all, it seemed. It took until the 85th minute for Newcastle to trouble Jordan Pickford, and even then the goalkeeper wasn’t overly concerned.

Short ball? Long ball? Whatever pass Newcastle pick, it is invariably the wrong ball. They are a team without identity – no patterns, no partnerships and, certainly, no sign of progress. So while there is some sympathy with Jaissle if players are failing to follow his instructions, it always comes back on any manager to make sure they do.

I once wrote of Everton boss David Moyes, when in charge of Sunderland, that he had inherited a sinking ship, only to drill another hole. Moyes, for the record, is a very good manager, he just wasn’t at Sunderland.

And that is the danger with Jaissle. He, too, walked into a difficult situation post Eddie Howe and the loss of several star players. Their replacements have been bench-warners or cold starters.

But Jaissle has to be the solution, not another problem. At present, the fear is that a young manager with no major-league experience is held hostage by his ideals and refuses to bend to what his players want and need.

His continued use of a 4-2-3-1 system, with two midfielders who cannot really run and a revolving cast of No 10s who are not No 10s, feels with each passing week and each passing defeat like a blueprint for relegation.

Maybe the team ignoring their manager’s wishes on Monday night was a cry for change. A protest, even? Do they not believe in his methods or do they not understand them?

Newcastle's Yoane Wissa rues a missed chance against Everton in what was Newcastle's third loss in their last five Premier League games

Jaissle tries to get his message across to Joelinton and Harvey Barnes at St James' Park

Either way, Newcastle must try something different. The Everton loss, and the nature of a performance absent of direction or conviction, was not a surprise. This run of form – four defeats in five in all competitions – has been coming since the early weeks of the season, when results flattered performances and the underlying numbers told a more troubling story.

It is not the time to change manager, and nor do the club’s hierarchy think so. The change has to come from within – approach, attitude, execution. That is on Jaissle and the players, not one or the other.

That is why before the head coach addresses what happened on the pitch, he must clarify to his players what he said off it. To lose matches is one thing, but to risk losing your dressing room is quite another.

That would leave Jaissle facing the one situation from which his ‘vertical football’ could offer no way forward.

#1243. Carrick weighs up stripping Bruno Fernandes of Man Utd captaincy

A defiant Michael Carrick refused to rule out stripping Bruno Fernandes of the captaincy as the Manchester United manager told his players to cut out their public sniping and start doing their talking on the pitch.

Carrick struck a bullish tone as he came out fighting and moved to reassert his authority after a tumultuous past fortnight that has left him battling to save his job ahead of Sunday’s must-win game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

The United manager began his press conference on Friday afternoon with a stirring five-and-a-half-minute monologue in which he issued an emotional call to arms to his players to demonstrate the values of hard work, sacrifice, humility and resilience that define the club.

Referencing Sir Matt Busby, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Bobby Charlton, Ryan Giggs and Wayne Rooney, Carrick warned there could be no “entitlement” culture in echoes of complaints from his predecessor Ruben Amorim.

United are actively considering their options in the event Carrick cannot quickly arrest a shocking start to the season that hit a new low with Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation by Como. The likes of Julian Nagelsmann, Eddie Howe, Unai Emery, Fabian Hürzeler and Antonio Conte are in the frame.

But Carrick insisted he was “100 per cent” convinced he was the right man to take United forward and, while he claimed the dressing room was “not divided”, he has had to contend with first defender Lisandro Martínez and then Fernandes venting in public.

Martínez was fined and publicly apologised for an extraordinary tirade at Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and the Old Trafford board last week before Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics in the wake of the Como debacle.

Carrick responded at the time to having his set-up and approach questioned by suggesting tactics count for little if players are unprepared to run.

Asked if he would consider taking the captaincy off Fernandes, Carrick said: “I’m just saying I’ll always – whatever the situation is – do what’s best for the club.”

Pressed on whether Fernandes’s comments were all the more insidious and divisive at a time when the manager was trying to pull the squad together so soon after Martínez’s outburst, Carrick added: “Yeah, the most important thing for me is the team.

“First and foremost is the squad, the dynamics in the squad. And again, it’s about the club. And I’ll always do what’s best for the club.”

Carrick, Wilcox and United chief executive Omar Berrada held a meeting with Martínez in the wake of his criticism but the manager would not be drawn on whether he had spoken with Fernandes and it remains to be seen if he will be captain or start against Bournemouth.

“If I’ve spoken to him or haven’t spoken to him, I don’t think this is the time to go into too much detail,” he said.

Carrick agreed that United collectively needed to stop turning on each other in public. “We need to move forward in the right direction. We need to do things that enable us to do that. That’s pretty clear,” he said.

“It [the dressing room] is not divided, no. We just need to get back to doing what we do best and we will.”

Separately, Carrick expressed sympathy for Fernandes over the “awful” burglary at his home on Wednesday night when he was in Italy, and said the club “are doing a lot of work to support Bruno and his family”.

Carrick is under huge pressure heading into Bournemouth but said he was happy to take the heat if it enabled his players to perform.

“It is my responsibility whatever goes on the pitch, and what we are as a group, and what we look like, and what we feel like,” he said. “I’ll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and for everyone else to stay dry.”

Nonetheless, Carrick admitted he was “hurting an awful lot” and that the team had to get back to showing the values and qualities that have underpinned the club’s historic success after a “really unacceptable” performance against Como and wider struggles. United have won two of 11 matches this season.

“I’m not entitled to be here,” Carrick said. “We’re not entitled to win. We’ve won in the past, we’ve got an incredible history, but that doesn’t mean you’re entitled to just win.

“I’m fully aware of that. It takes hard work, a lot of sacrifice. You’ve got to invest yourself in the club and you’ve got to do a lot of things that maybe aren’t so nice, but you’ve got to do it for each other, and you’ve got to win.

“It’s important we live up to that, and it’s important for me to push those values, and for our supporters to feel that moving forward.

“We’ve kind of lost our way a bit if I’m honest, and we will get it back. I’m totally confident we’ll get it back. Respect this club, respect what it takes, because it’s very important to me.”

Carrick added that he was inspired by the values of “humility, hard work, resilience, sacrifice and pride” embodied by the likes of Busby, Ferguson, Charlton, Giggs and Rooney.

“We can never lose that, and I won’t let us lose that,” he said. “We’ve had it for a spell, I feel very strongly about that. It inspires me a lot to live up to that and keep driving that with the players.

“There’s a resilience about this club that’s been shown for a long time. Whether that’s bouncing back from adversity, comebacks, late goals, success, sustaining success, there’s a resilience in this club that runs very deep.”

Carrick was trailed by a camera crew from Amazon Prime as he entered the media auditorium at Manchester United’s Carrington training base at 1.30pm on Friday.

There have been plenty of dark moments at Old Trafford in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era. But the difference this season is that any internal drama will soon be available for public consumption after the decision to allow cameras into a once-sacrosanct dressing room.

Whether Carrick will see out the next week, let alone a season being captured by filmmakers from Amazon’s All Or Nothing series, who probably cannot believe their luck at the unfolding crisis, remains to be seen. He certainly needs a big reaction against Bournemouth at Old Trafford at the very least.

But it became clear as he began his press conference with an emotional 5½-minute monologue that he would not go down without a fight.

#1242. Manchester United stick with Michael Carrick ahead of Chelsea matchup as dressing-room discord fuels crisis

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

To the surprise of many, Michael Carrick will continue to be in the dugout for Manchester United as they face Chelsea on Saturday. During their eight-game winless run in all competitions, United have allowed 15 goals while scoring six, and off the pitch, everything is unraveling, with players and fans alike questioning the direction of the club. United have been in this position before, and it has usually led to a change of manager and a rebuild of the club from the ground up. But what's different is that during this rut, players are publicly speaking out. While things will sometimes leak via undisclosed sources, players saying the quiet part out loud about what's going on with the club is not a good look. Defender Lisandro Martinez spoke about the need for the club to have higher standards and claimed that it's lacking ambition after a poor loss to Atletico Madrid in Champions League play, but it went from bad to worse as captain Bruno Fernandes spoke out after a humbling loss to Como, questioning the team's tactics.

That led to Fernandes being benched and United failing yet again to pick up a victory. While the public view is that Fernandes will retain his captaincy, the episode has to strip away at least some of Carrick's authority within the club. "There is no decision to be made on [the captaincy]," Carrick said. "It will be Bruno. Listen, we're clear with the situation of the team and as a football club at the moment. He's an important player for this group. He has been and he will be." Ahead of a match where both teams are struggling, the slightest lack of balance could lead to yet another United loss. With no clear sign that authority lies with the manager rather than the captain, especially after Carrick held meetings about the future of his job, this could get worse before it gets better. What do you do if United concede an early goal and the match goes off the rails? On the evidence we've seen, it's tough to say Carrick will be able to get the club out of that spiral, and if he can't, there's no reason why he should be the manager. On paper, while too much money was invested in the midfield instead of defense, this isn't a bad squad, but United find themselves in the relegation race only one season after qualifying for Champions League play. Even their numbers scream midtable, not doomed to relegation.

That's where the mentality of the squad comes in. It's been a persistent issue since Sir Alex Ferguson left, and it's not an issue that seems to be going away anytime soon. At times, it will lie dormant for a season during which you think United are righting the ship, only to come back at the worst time possible. Carrick is only a symptom of a larger issue at Manchester United, and the club has gone through eight permanent managers since Ferguson without sustained success. It's not for lack of spending, and even though there are questions around who is recruited, for the most part, the squads have been fine. They just can never perform to the sum of their parts.

Since Jim Ratcliffe took over, the club has been more focused on profits off the pitch than actual success on it, and that's catching up with United. Turning that around is going to be quite a challenge. Fan protests have been seen, but they aren't igniting real change, and we may be in a situation where United need a sustained spell in the bottom half of the table to lead to anything different. In short, this is already dire, and every day with Carrick at the helm delays the start of that turnaround, even if that isn't his fault. United have become a club without a direction, and that's something Chelsea can take advantage of as the Xabi Alonso era at Stamford Bridge has signs of success but needs a result to get back on the right track.

#1241. Barcelona rout Alavés 6-1 to retake LaLiga lead before top-two clash with Atlético

Barcelona beat Alavés 6-1 at Spotify Camp Nou to go back to the top of LaLiga. The win came with a reshuffled defence and sets up a meeting of the top two at the Metropolitano.

Atlético Madrid had gone top of LaLiga earlier on 31 October by winning at Levante. Within hours, Barcelona took the place back. Hansi Flick’s side dismantled Alavés in front of their own fans. The result ended a two-game losing run after defeats to PSG and Real Madrid.

Barcelona have scored 46 goals and conceded 12, a goal difference of +34, according to the official LaLiga table. Atlético have scored 22 and conceded 8.

This was Barcelona’s first test since the Clásico. Real Madrid won that game 2-1 at Camp Nou on 25 October. Kylian Mbappé scored twice, the second in the 87th minute, after Raphinha had equalised on 61 minutes. That defeat ended a run of nine straight league wins at the start of the season.

Raphinha opened the scoring in the 8th minute. Fermín López added a second in the 23rd. Raphinha struck again in the 41st, and Lamine Yamal made it four in first-half stoppage time. Barcelona held 77% of the ball, in front of a crowd of 53,523.

Yamal’s second goal, in the 64th minute, was first ruled out for offside. A VAR review showed his run was onside. He was taken off to a standing ovation soon afterwards, with Gordon replacing him.

The former Newcastle winger scored in the 81st minute, his first league goal for the club. He ran on to a through ball from Rodri and chipped the goalkeeper. Mariano Díaz pulled one back for Alavés in the 84th minute.

Absences left Flick short at the back. Fariñas started at right-back and played the full 90 minutes. Frenkie de Jong moved to centre-back alongside Cubarsí. João Cancelo completed the back four at left-back. Gerard Martín replaced De Jong in the 82nd minute.

Fariñas is normally a midfielder. He is from the Valencian Community and joined Barcelona as an under-14 player in 2018. He had some experience of the role, spending almost half an hour at right-back in a 2-2 pre-season draw with Birmingham City on 31 July.

¡Un #AtletiBarça por todo lo alto en #LALIGAEASPORTS! 🤩 pic.twitter.com/IZy7xJkuad

Fariñas said Flick had asked whether he could play there, and that he felt nervous at first before settling into the game.

The schedule now tightens. Barcelona host Aston Villa in the fourth round of Champions League league-phase games at Spotify Camp Nou on Tuesday 3 November, kicking off at 21:00 local time.

#1240. Comprehensive mapping of essential-gene interactions in M. tuberculosis

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the causative agent of tuberculosis, remains the world’s deadliest pathogen1. Despite intensive study, many of its genes remain uncharacterized, which limits the insight that can be gained into tuberculosis biology and constrains drug development. Genetic interaction (GI) mapping is a powerful strategy to define functional relationships between genes by quantifying how the phenotypic effects of combined perturbations deviate from expectations based on single-gene perturbations2,3. Here we develop a dual-sgRNA CRISPR-interference platform that enables high-throughput GI mapping in mycobacteria. We address key technical challenges in library construction and data interpretation by incorporating unique barcodes for each sgRNA pair and implementing a robust statistical pipeline for GI detection. Focusing on essential genes, we generate comprehensive GI maps in the model mycobacterium Mycobacterium smegmatis and the pathogen M. tuberculosis. These maps recapitulate known biology, uncover thousands of previously unrecognized interactions and identify functional connections between essential genes and drug targets. By generating AlphaFold3-based protein–protein interaction predictions4 for all gene pairs in our GI maps, we show that a subset of GIs is likely to reflect underlying physical associations. Validation of selected GIs confirms both novel biological relationships and opportunities for synergistic targeting. Overall, this work establishes a generalizable framework for dual-gene perturbation and defines the architecture of essential-gene networks in mycobacteria, advancing both our understanding of tuberculosis biology and the rational design of combination therapies.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the world’s leading infectious cause of death1, is among the bacteria that have been most extensively sequenced, but the functions and interactions of many of its genes remain poorly understood. This knowledge gap limits our understanding of the genetic foundations of tuberculosis (TB) and hinders the development of effective therapies.

Genetic interaction (GI) mapping is a powerful approach for deciphering the functional relationships between genes2,3. It involves systematically assessing how perturbing one gene modifies the phenotype associated with perturbing a second gene. A GI is defined as a combined phenotype that deviates from the expectation based on single-gene perturbations. Positive interactions occur when dual perturbation produces a milder phenotype than expected, whereas negative interactions—including synthetic lethal effects—result in a more severe phenotype. Applied at scale, GI mapping yields quantitative interaction profiles that serve as high-resolution phenotypes3. These profiles can generate functional hypotheses for uncharacterized genes, reveal surprising roles for genes of known function and identify connections between distinct biological pathways3. Moreover, they can highlight potential synergistic and antagonistic drug–target relationships, informing combination therapies5.

GI mapping in Mtb has historically been constrained by biological and technical challenges, including slow growth, biosafety requirements and limited early genetic tools. The development of high-density transposon mutagenesis libraries combined with hybridization- or sequencing-based readouts (TnSeq)6,7 constituted a major advance, permitting genome-wide identification of conditionally essential genes8 and GI mapping in deletion mutants9. However, such approaches are typically restricted to non-essential genes, excluding most antibiotic targets. CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) has since emerged as a complementary technique10,11,12,13, enabling conditional and tunable knockdown of both essential and non-essential genes. In bacterial systems, dual-gene knockdowns have been used to identify GIs among small gene sets14, and larger-scale efforts have paired individual deletion or knockdown strains with genome-wide libraries15,16. Dual-CRISPRi and dual-TnSeq approaches for comprehensive GI mapping have been implemented in Bacillus subtilis and Streptococcus pneumoniae17,18,19. However, technical limitations have thus far precluded the development of a comparable system in Mtb.

To enable high-throughput GI mapping in Mtb, we developed a dual-single-guide RNA (sgRNA) CRISPRi platform for mycobacteria. Addressing key challenges in library construction and data analysis, we devised a robust experimental and statistical pipeline for high-confidence detection of GIs. Using this platform, we mapped GIs among nearly all essential genes in Mycobacterium smegmatis (Msm) and Mtb, prioritizing this technically demanding class of genes because of their centrality to cellular processes and importance as antibiotic targets. These maps recapitulate known biological relationships, validating the platform, and also uncover thousands of novel GIs. We further performed AlphaFold3 co-folding for all gene pairs (approximately 600,000) represented in the GI maps, identifying GIs that are likely to reflect physical associations and offering a basis for mechanistic hypotheses. Finally, we validated selected predictions from the maps, including drug–drug interactions and roles in the electron transport chain (ETC) for several genes of unknown function. Together, these maps constitute a powerful resource for elucidating Mtb biology and guiding the rational design of combination therapies.

To enable dual-sgRNA CRISPRi-based GI mapping in Mtb, we adapted the Combinatorial Genetics En Masse (CombiGEM) framework20 to the Mtb CRISPRi platform10, assigning each sgRNA a barcode, and using a cloning workflow that preserves sgRNA–barcode linkage and positions paired barcodes in close proximity (Extended Data Fig. 1a). This design permits accurate quantification of dual-sgRNA strain abundance by barcode sequencing, facilitating high-throughput GI mapping.

GI detection for essential genes requires sgRNAs that impose a precise fitness cost: sufficient to reveal interactions, yet not so severe as to mask additive or synergistic effects. Compounding this challenge, the combinatorial scale of dual-sgRNA libraries necessitates selecting only a small number of sgRNAs per gene. To define the optimal fitness cost for GI detection, we performed a pilot screen in Msm using a panel of 16 genes that are predicted to interact. We selected up to 24 sgRNAs per gene (Supplementary Methods and Supplementary Table 1) spanning a broad range of fitness costs, cloned a dual-sgRNA library containing all pairwise permutations and performed a GI screen using the workflow planned for larger-scale studies (Extended Data Fig. 1b). The resulting data allowed us to identify the sgRNA strength window that best supports GI detection under these conditions: an approximately 8% reduction in fitness per generation (Extended Data Fig. 1c–h and Supplementary Discussion).

To establish feasibility, we built a comprehensive essential-gene GI library in Msm. Guided by the pilot screen, we selected up to two sgRNAs per gene with reproducible, intermediate fitness costs (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1). The library contains 1,524 sgRNAs targeting 787 genes, plus 10 non-targeting (NT) controls, yielding about 2.3 million sgRNA permutations. Target genes included those that are essential for Msm fitness and those that are non-essential in Msm but essential in Mtb; the latter were targeted by the predicted strongest sgRNAs10. The library was cloned in Escherichia coli, validated by deep sequencing (Extended Data Fig. 2a) and transformed into an Msm strain containing a chromosomally encoded Streptococcus thermophilus (Sth1) dCas9 expression cassette. This yielded a pooled library in which each bacterium carries a single integrated guide plasmid expressing two sgRNAs. We subjected this library to competitive growth, tracking dual-sgRNA strain abundance over time by barcode sequencing. Strain depletion was modelled using a piecewise linear regression10, providing a quantitative readout of fitness.

a, Schematic of the screen. (1) Up to two sgRNAs per gene (log2-transformed fold change (L2FC) –1 to –5) were selected. (2) sgRNAs were assigned barcodes (BCs), and all pairwise permutations were generated. (3) The library was passaged with or without anhydrotetracycline (ATc), and L2FC trajectories were computed from barcode counts. (4) GI scores were calculated for each gene pair (see e,f), and genes were clustered by GI profile correlation. (5) Applications of GI data. b, Distribution of observed L2FC at generation 20 for dual non-targeting (NT), single-targeting (A + NT) and dual-targeting (A + B) constructs. c, Correlation of observed L2FC at generation 20 for single-targeting constructs differing only in sgRNA position (Pos1, position 1; Pos2, position 2). d, Multiplicative model of GIs for sgRNAs targeting genes A and B. Fitness outcomes greater or less than expected indicate positive or negative GIs, respectively. e, Example of GI quantification. Left: L2FC trajectories for a representative dnaJ1 + dnaJ2 dual-sgRNA construct. Right: ΔL2FC (observed − expected) trajectories for all eight dnaJ1 + dnaJ2 constructs. f, Expected versus observed L2FC at generation 25 for all dual-targeting constructs. Black line, x = y; red line, generalized additive model (GAM) fit. GI scores were computed as the median GAM residual per gene pair. g, Distribution of GI scores across all gene pairs. Shaded regions denote statistically significant (p > 0.5) interactions. h, Heat map of GI scores for all gene pairs, hierarchically clustered by Pearson correlation of GI profiles. Values beyond ±5 are clipped. i, Number of positive and negative GIs (p > 0.5) per gene. j, Distribution of pairwise GI profile correlations among all sgRNAs, and among sgRNAs targeting the same gene. k, GI scores for all genes paired with murA (left) or with cwlM (right). l, Left, dendrogram of all genes, clustered by GI profile correlation. Branches are coloured by nodes enriched (false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.005) for Gene Ontology (GO) terms by Fisher’s exact test. Right, representative clusters.

Growth phenotypes were highly reproducible across biological replicates (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). As expected, strains with two NT sgRNAs showed minimal depletion, single-targeting strains exhibited moderate depletion and dual-targeting strains showed the greatest depletion (Fig. 1b). sgRNA position within the plasmid had little effect on fitness, indicating consistent activity from both expression cassettes (Fig. 1c).

To identify GIs, we compared the observed fitness of each dual-targeting strain to the expected outcome under a null model of no interaction (Fig. 1d,e). Deviations from this expectation were quantified and corrected for floor effects (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 2d,e), and then aggregated at the gene-pair level to generate a GI score. Gene pairs with greater-than-expected depletion were assigned negative GI scores, and those with less-than-expected depletion yielded positive GI scores (Fig. 1d). To assess confidence, GI scores were modelled as a mixture of typical deviations (normal distribution) and deviations outside the norm (uniform distribution). Gene pairs with interaction probabilities of 0.5 < p ≤ 0.95 were designated likely interactions, and those with p > 0.95 confident interactions.

The Msm GI map revealed nearly 8,500 interactions (p > 0.5), with negative GIs outnumbering positive ones (Fig. 1g–i and Supplementary Table 2). This 2.7% hit rate across gene pairs aligns with previous GI studies3. Most genes interacted with fewer than 15 partners, but a subset exhibited high connectivity, consistent with hub-like behaviour that has been observed in other organisms, such as yeast3 (Fig. 1i). Out of 787 targeted genes, 64 (8.1%) showed no interactions under these conditions. Notably, GI strength did not correlate with gene vulnerability10, confirming that our fitness-based sgRNA selection accounts for gene vulnerability (Extended Data Fig. 2f). sgRNAs targeting the same gene exhibited highly correlated interaction profiles (Fig. 1j), underscoring the reproducibility of measured GIs.

Illustrative examples confirm that the map captures known or mechanistically plausible functional relationships. We observed a strong negative GI between the Hsp40 chaperones dnaJ1 and dnaJ2 (Fig. 1e), consistent with their known synthetic lethal relationship21. Another strong negative GI, between cwlM and murA (Fig. 1k), is consistent with the proposed role of CwlM in binding to MurA, stimulating its activity, and promoting peptidoglycan precursor synthesis22.

With individual GIs providing initial confidence in the dataset, we next sought a global assessment of the functional signal encoded in the map. To this end, we analysed correlations among GI profiles, because profile similarity often reflects similar gene function3.

Pairwise correlation and clustering revealed that genes with related biological functions tended to group together (Fig. 1l). We systematically annotated the tree, identifying 63 functionally coherent clusters containing 2 to 48 genes each. Representative clusters spanned functions including cell-wall synthesis, protein degradation, cell division, cofactor and nucleotide synthesis, the ETC, and protein folding and ribosome rescue (Fig. 1l, top to bottom, left to right). Several observations highlight the biological relevance of these clusters. First, cwlM and murA share not only a strong negative GI (Fig. 1k), but also highly correlated GI profiles22 (Fig. 1l). Second, the two genes most closely associated with the mycolic acid transporter mmpL3—pgfA and ttfA—were previously shown to interact physically with MmpL3 and support mycolic acid transport23,24. Third, the transcription factors whiA and whiB2, which are involved in cell division and act in a co-dependent manner in Streptomyces, clustered with each other and with ftsZ, consistent with their established roles25 as transcriptional activators of ftsZ. Many clusters also contained previously uncharacterized genes, as well as functionally annotated genes with unexpected correlations, suggesting unrecognized biological connections. Barring technical limitations (for example, polar effects), these clusters offer functional predictions by placing genes in the context of their network relationships.

Encouraged by the validity of the Msm map, we next extended our approach to Mtb. Following the same experimental blueprint, we constructed a dual-sgRNA library containing up to two sgRNAs per gene with reproducible, intermediate fitness costs (Supplementary Table 1). The library includes 1,483 sgRNAs targeting 762 genes, most of them essential for in vitro Mtb growth, plus 10 NT controls, yielding about 2.2 million sgRNA permutations. The library was cloned in E. coli, validated by deep sequencing (Extended Data Fig. 2a) and transformed into an H37Rv Mtb strain containing a chromosomally integrated Sth1 dCas9 cassette. Competitive growth and barcode sequencing were performed as in Msm.

As in Msm, growth phenotypes were highly reproducible across biological replicates (Extended Data Fig. 2g,h). Dual-NT, single-targeting and dual-targeting strains depleted on average in the expected order, from least to most (Fig. 2a). sgRNA position within the plasmid had a greater effect than it did in Msm (Fig. 2b), but the effect was modest and deemed acceptable, because our GI model accounts for sgRNA position. GIs were quantified, corrected for floor effects (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 2i,j) and aggregated at the gene-pair level to generate a GI score and confidence estimate, as in Msm.

a, Distribution of observed L2FC at generation 22 for dual-NT, single-targeting and dual-targeting constructs, as in Fig. 1b. b, Correlation of observed L2FC at generation 22 for single-targeting constructs differing only in sgRNA position. c, Expected versus observed L2FC at generation 25 for all dual-targeting constructs. Black line, x = y; red line, GAM fit. GI scores were computed as the median GAM residual per gene pair. d, Distribution of GI scores across all gene pairs. Shaded regions denote statistically significant (p > 0.5) interactions. e, Heat map of GI scores for all gene pairs, hierarchically clustered by Pearson correlation of GI profiles. Values beyond ±5 are clipped. f, Number of positive and negative GIs (p > 0.5) per gene. g, Distribution of pairwise GI profile correlations among all sgRNAs, and among sgRNAs targeting the same gene. h, GI scores for all genes paired with dnaJ1 (left) or with dnaJ2 (right). i, GI scores for all genes paired with murA (left) or with cwlM (right). j, GI scores for all genes paired with secA1 (left) or with secF (right). k, Left, dendrogram of all genes, clustered by GI profile correlation. Branches are coloured by nodes enriched (FDR < 0.005) for GO terms by Fisher’s exact test. Right, representative clusters (from top to bottom: fatty acid biosynthesis, arginine biosynthesis, nucleotide biosynthesis, folate metabolism, thiamine metabolism, menaquinone biosynthesis and protein degradation).

The Mtb GI map revealed nearly 6,500 interactions (p > 0.5), with negative GIs outnumbering positive ones (Fig. 2d–f and Supplementary Table 3). This 2.2% hit rate across all gene pairs parallels the Msm map. Most genes interacted with fewer than 12 partners, but a subset exhibited high connectivity (Fig. 2f), and 3.4% (26/762) of targeted genes showed no interactions under these conditions. As in Msm, sgRNAs targeting the same gene exhibited highly correlated interaction profiles (Fig. 2g), and GI strength did not correlate with gene vulnerability (Extended Data Fig. 2k). We observed strong negative GIs between dnaJ1 and dnaJ2 (ref. 21) and between cwlM and murA (ref. 22) (Fig. 2h,i). Further strong negative GIs recapitulated known or mechanistically plausible functional relationships, including (1) transcription factors and their targets (Extended Data Fig. 3a–c); (2) partially redundant enzymes (Extended Data Fig. 3d,e); and (3) functionally related genes within shared biological processes (Fig. 2j and Extended Data Fig. 3f). Reflecting the biological coherence of the data, clustering by GI profile similarity grouped genes with related functions (Fig. 2k).

To test platform reproducibility, we repeated the Mtb GI screen using a slightly higher concentration of anhydrotetracycline (ATc) to ensure saturating induction of dCas9 and sgRNA (Supplementary Table 3). We refer to the original and replicate screens as experiment 1 and experiment 2, respectively. The second screen showed slightly greater positional variability but also more pronounced depletion of single- and dual-targeting constructs (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b), resulting in a wider distribution of GI scores (Extended Data Fig. 4c–e) and a higher signal-to-noise ratio. Key benchmarks were again met, including concordance among replicates (Extended Data Fig. 2l–o), high GI profile similarity among sgRNAs targeting the same gene (Extended Data Fig. 4f) and a lack of correlation between GI score and gene vulnerability (Extended Data Fig. 2p). Most importantly, the replicate map recapitulated the functional information in the original. Summary metrics, including the overall hit rate (2.3%) and per-gene interaction number (Extended Data Fig. 4g), were comparable; specific GIs were reproduced across the two screens (Extended Data Figs. 3g–l and 4h,i); and functionally related genes clustered together (Extended Data Fig. 4j).

GI scores were strongly correlated between the Mtb experiments (R = 0.82; Extended Data Fig. 4k). However, concordance between interaction probabilities was lower (Supplementary Table 3), particularly near the boundary between the null and interaction distributions, where experiment-specific fits diverged. To reconcile these differences, we extended our statistical framework to jointly model GI scores from both experiments (Extended Data Fig. 4k). The model assigns each gene pair a joint probability and, when sufficiently confident, classifies the interaction as negative, positive or discordant. Joint modelling identified confident GIs for approximately 2.5% of Mtb gene pairs (p > 0.95) and likely GIs for 4.4% (p > 0.5).

Given the substantial but incomplete overlap between the two maps, we retained data from both screens. Unless otherwise specified, the individual Mtb GI scores and downstream analyses presented in the following sections are based on experiment 2, and the joint model provides an integrated assessment of interaction confidence across both experiments.

Having established platform robustness in both Mtb and Msm, we analysed GIs involving homologous genes targeted in both libraries. Consistent with comparative GI work in budding and fission yeast26, homologues showed a modestly higher GI profile correlation than did non-homologues (Fig. 3a,b), reflecting a mixture of conserved (for example, Figs. 1e,k and 2h,i) and non-conserved (for example, Extended Data Fig. 5a–c) interactions. A global comparison of GI scores for homologous gene pairs revealed limited correlation across species (R = 0.26; Extended Data Fig. 5d), which increased substantially when the analysis was restricted to gene pairs sharing the same biological process annotation (R = 0.57; Extended Data Fig. 5e and Supplementary Table 4). Likewise, within-process GIs were conserved at a higher rate than the overall set of interactions (Extended Data Fig. 5f). Together, these findings indicate that mycobacteria recapitulate the pattern of GI conservation observed in budding and fission yeast, in which interactions that link genes in the same biological process are preferentially conserved relative to interactions that link distinct processes26.

a,b, GI profile correlations between Msm and Mtb homologues in experiment 2 (a) and between identical genes across Mtb experiments (Mtb experiment 1 versus Mtb experiment 2; b). Each of the 100 black lines in each panel shows the density obtained using a random sample of non-homologous (a) or non-identical (b) gene pairs. c, Heat map of log2 odds ratio (OR), testing for enrichment or depletion of significant negative GIs (p > 0.5) within pathway pairs in Mtb. Gene pairs were categorized by GI presence or absence and pathway-pair membership, and association was assessed by Fisher’s exact test. Positive and negative log2(OR) values indicate more and fewer GIs than expected, respectively. Only results with |log2(OR)| > 2 and q < 0.0001 are shown. Hollow circles indicate pathway pairs that fail these thresholds after removing possible polar effects (gene pairs ≤ 5 genes apart). See Extended Data Fig. 5g for all significant (q < 0.05) pathway pairs. d,e, Distribution of s.c. ipTMs for co-folded Mtb protein pairs with mean s.c. ipTM ≥ 0.2 (d) and for all protein pairs (e). Black dots and grey lines represent the mean and s.d. of s.c. ipTMs across all pools. f, Distribution of PPI confidence across bins of GI score and GI profile correlation in Mtb. Gene pairs were binned by GI score (left) or by GI correlation (right), and the fraction of corresponding protein pairs falling into each mean s.c. ipTM category is shown. Per-bin gene-pair counts are indicated. PPI confidence: none (mean s.c. ipTM < 0.05), low (0.05 ≤ mean s.c. ipTM < 0.2), medium (0.2 ≤ mean s.c. ipTM < 0.4) and high (mean s.c. ipTM ≥ 0.4). g–n, AlphaFold-Multimer models and GI and PPI metrics for selected Mtb pairs: MurA and CwlM (g), DnaN and DnaE1 (h), DesA2 and DesA1 (i), EtfD and EtfB (j), Rv3212 and Rv1002c (k), AftD and TmaT (l), WecA and Rv3355c (m) and AftB and Rv3035 (n).

We next examined the functional organization of Mtb GIs by testing for enrichment of interactions within and between biological processes (Supplementary Table 4). We focused on negative GIs, because they are more abundant in our dataset and more likely to reflect functional relationships, following the precedent in yeast3. Gene pairs comprising genes in the same biological process were enriched for negative GIs (on-diagonal; Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 5g), consistent with limited tolerance for simultaneous knockdown within essential pathways. Negative GIs were also enriched among gene pairs spanning distinct biological processes—for example, genes involved in synthesizing different components of the cell envelope (such as arabinogalactan and lipoarabinomannan), and genes involved in DNA replication and DNA repair (off-diagonal; Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 5g). Beyond these process-level patterns, gene pairs with highly correlated GI profiles were themselves enriched for negative GIs (Extended Data Fig. 4l), consistent with the expectation that genes acting in the same pathway are more likely to share interaction partners and interact with each other3.

To investigate the molecular basis of GIs, we asked how frequently they reflect physical associations. Because no large-scale experimental protein–protein interaction (PPI) map exists for Mtb, we generated PPI predictions using pooled AlphaFold3 co-folding4,27 across the approximately 600,000 gene pairs screened in the Mtb and Msm GI libraries. We identified 15,240 candidate PPIs using a size-corrected interface predicted template modelling score (s.c. ipTM) cut-off ≥ 0.05 (Fig. 3d,e, Extended Data Fig. 6a–h and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3). Because size correction systematically reduces ipTM scores, this threshold is necessarily permissive, yet the overall hit rate (2.6%) remains low. Many of these candidates achieve higher ipTM scores when evaluated pairwise with AlphaFold-Multimer28. Consistent with observations in yeast3, gene pairs with negative GIs or highly correlated GI profiles were enriched for predicted physical interactions (Fig. 3f). Nevertheless, many lacked a predicted PPI, because GIs can arise from pathway-, process- or network-level relationships without direct binding. Overall, this resource identifies gene pairs that are both genetically and physically linked, providing a framework for predicting their molecular mechanisms. We present several representative examples spanning both known22,29,30,31 (Fig. 3g–j) and previously unrecognized (Fig. 3k–n) biological connections.

Previous studies have shown that GIs can predict drug–drug interactions5. To test whether this principle holds in our dataset, we analysed GIs among established drug targets.

One of the strongest negative GIs in both Mtb and Msm involved aspC (alanine aminotransferase16,32) and ddl (d-alanine-d-alanine ligase; Fig. 4a). Although previously unknown, this interaction is mechanistically plausible: AspC is crucial for biosynthesis of l-Ala, which is required by Alr (alanine racemase) to produce d-Ala, the substrate for Ddl (Fig. 4b). aspC also showed a negative GI with alr. Alr and Ddl are the targets of d-cycloserine33, a second-line agent for multidrug-resistant TB. Consistent with the GI data, CRISPRi-based chemical–genetic interaction (CGI) profiling of d-cycloserine identified aspC as one of the top sensitizing hits (Fig. 4c,d and Supplementary Table 5). Moreover, a paper published while we revised this one reported synergy between an AspC inhibitor and d-cycloserine34.

a, GI scores for all genes paired with aspC in Mtb. b, Pathway schematic illustrating the roles of AspC, Alr and Ddl in peptidoglycan biosynthesis. c,d, Volcano plots from Mtb CGI screens with d-cycloserine (an inhibitor of Ddl and Alr) at concentrations of 6.4 μM (c) and 19.1 μM (d). FDR was calculated using α-Robust Rank Aggregation (RRA) with one-sided tests for enrichment and depletion. e, GI scores for all genes paired with pptT in Mtb. f, Schematic highlighting PptT’s connection to the FAS-II mycolic acid biosynthesis cycle. PptT and the negative interactors discussed in the text are shown in bold. g,i,j,l, Checkerboard assay heat maps showing Bliss scores for the indicated drug pairs in Mtb. Dashed boxes outline the most synergistic area (MSA) and most antagonistic area (MAA).
